guidelineTitle: Computer aided detection and diagnosis of polyps in adult patients undergoing colonoscopy: a living clinical practice guideline
recommendationText: We suggest against the routine use of CADe colonoscopy

pico.population: Adults undergoing screening or surveillance colonoscopy
pico.outcomes: Colorectal cancer incidence, CRC mortality, post-colonoscopy CRC, adenoma detection rate, AMR, surveilance colonoscopy, perforation, bleeding, Advanced colorectal neoplasia detection rate, Serrated Sessile Polyp detection rate, Non-neoplastic polyps, Perforation or Bleeding, Adenomas per Colonoscopy, Advanced Adenomas per Colonoscopy, Serrated Polyps per Colonoscopy, Non-neoplastic polyps per Colonoscopy, Withdrawal Time

items.appraisal: The objective is clearly to determine the benefits and harms of CADe in adults undergoing colonoscopy and provide trustworthy guidance about its use. The document focuses explicitly on patient-important outcomes, including CRC incidence/mortality, burdens, and complications.

The clinical question is explicit and developed in PICO format. Population = adults undergoing colonoscopy; intervention = CADe; comparator = routine/non-CADe colonoscopy; numerous critical and important outcomes are prespecified; the principal efficacy evidence is RCT-based. The developers explicitly state that the panel formulated the question through discussion of population, intervention, outcomes and relevant subgroups.

Population and exclusions are unusually explicit: adults ≥18 undergoing colonoscopy for screening, surveillance, FIT/FOBT follow-up, or symptomatic evaluation. The recommendation specifically excludes colonoscopy for IBD history, abnormal imaging, and therapeutic interventions.

The international panel contained three patients, 11 healthcare professionals, and seven methodologists. It specifically included general practitioners, internists, gastroenterologists, patient partners, and health-research methodologists, with attention to geographic diversity, sex, and experience.

Exceptionally strong. Three patient partners participated throughout development, and a systematic review of patient values/preferences was also conducted. The patients helped identify priorities, participated in meetings, reviewed drafts, and validated the final recommendation. The limitations of the direct preference evidence are also explicitly acknowledged and influence the recommendation's weak strength.

The guideline is explicitly designed to provide clinicians and patients with decision guidance, including shared/individual decision-making. It also explains how the weak recommendation should be interpreted in settings where CADe is available.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: The guideline clearly reports systematic evidence acquisition: an updated systematic review/meta-analysis of all relevant RCTs, systematic patient-preference search, provider-trust review, and microsimulation. However, this nine-page guideline itself does not reproduce the full database-by-database search strategy, dates, and search strings for the main CADe review. Those methods reside primarily in linked companion evidence products/supplementary material. Under your strict Item 7 anchor, I therefore would not award 6–7 to this PDF alone.

The main evidence source is clearly restricted to RCTs evaluating CADe-assisted colonoscopy, with relevant indications and outcomes specified. The document also clearly states which clinical populations were outside its scope. However, the complete review-level inclusion/exclusion criteria—including all study-design, language, and setting criteria—are not reproduced here.

items.text: Strengths/limitations of body of evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: Outstanding. The guideline explicitly discusses absence of direct RCT evidence for CRC incidence/mortality, risk of bias from unblinded trials, uncertain generalisability across endoscopists, proprietary algorithms, model limitations, age indirectness, and weak evidence for patient preferences. It even explains why the 10-year modeling horizon was chosen.

items.text: Methods for formulating recommendations clearly described
items.appraisal: Five panel meetings are described, including scope definition, outcome prioritisation, evidence review, values/preferences, and provider-trust evidence. The panel then used a consensus-based GRADE approach and circulated the draft recommendation for approval. Most unusually, the paper reports the actual final vote: 13 members (60%) against versus nine (40%) for routine CADe.

items.text: Benefits, side effects, and risks considered
items.appraisal: Benefits, harms, and burdens form the core of the recommendation. The panel explicitly balances uncertain effects on CRC incidence/mortality against increased surveillance, overdiagnosis, anxiety, and procedural burden. The weak recommendation reflects placing greater value on avoiding burdens than on uncertain benefits.

The recommendation is directly accompanied by absolute effect estimates, certainty judgments, rationale, values/preferences, and an evidence profile. The linked MAGICapp also provides multilayered recommendations, evidence summaries, and decision aids.

items.text: External review by experts before publication
items.appraisal: External peer review is explicit and was managed by The BMJ; post-publication rapid-response review is also facilitated. However, individual external reviewer names, disciplines, and detailed review results are not provided in the guideline itself, preventing 6–7 under the supplied anchor.

This is genuinely a living guideline. Ongoing evidence surveillance is explicit, along with specific triggers: new CADe trials materially altering CRC incidence/mortality/burden estimates, technological changes affecting performance, or improved evidence about values/preferences. The microsimulation will be revised and the recommendation reassessed when appropriate.

Extremely clear: “For adults who have agreed to undergo colonoscopy, we suggest against the routine use of CADe (weak recommendation).” Population, intervention, direction, and recommendation strength are all explicit.

Routine colonoscopy and CADe-assisted colonoscopy are directly compared. The recommendation also explains when individual patients/clinicians may reasonably choose differently because it is weak/conditional.

The recommendation is prominent in the abstract and in the main text, and page 2 contains a full-page visual recommendation infographic contrasting routine colonoscopy with CADe, showing recommendation direction/strength, evidence profile, rationale, values/preferences, and practical issues.

The implementation section explicitly identifies endoscopist engagement, provider attitudes/trust, variable real-world use, device availability, technological performance, and clinical context as determinants of implementation. It even reports that endoscopists turned CADe on in only 52% of procedures when given a choice. The guideline acknowledges that fuller system-level feasibility, acceptability, equity, and resource assessment is planned for the next iteration.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: Strong. The guideline contains a visual recommendation infographic and points users to MAGICapp, which provides an expanded multilayered recommendation, evidence summaries, decision aids, and practical considerations for electronic use. This satisfies the supplied Item 19 anchor much more strongly than the AGA paper.

Resource burden is acknowledged—particularly additional surveillance colonoscopies and resulting costs/resources—but this first iteration deliberately adopts an individual-patient perspective. Formal cost-effectiveness, budget impact, resource use, equity, feasibility, and acceptability are explicitly deferred to a future system-level iteration. Therefore the current guideline should not receive 6–7 for this item.

There is strong evidence surveillance for updating the guideline, but that is not the same as clinical implementation auditing. The guideline does not establish formal audit indicators, target thresholds, audit frequency, or instructions for measuring adherence to its recommendation.

Funding is transparent: MAGIC provided methodological support and the project received EU Horizon Europe funding. However, the article does not explicitly state that the funder had no influence over the recommendation/content. Under the supplied strict Item 22 anchor, nonprofit/public funding without an explicit no-influence statement warrants 5–6 rather than 7.

Excellent. All authors completed BMJ Rapid Recommendations COI forms; MAGIC and BMJ judged that no panel member or co-chair had a financial COI; professional/academic interests were actively minimized; other coauthors' declared interests were assessed; and panel members were screened during selection. The paper additionally states that intellectual conflicts were minimized and managed.

items.text: The evidence supporting the recommendation is applicable to the clinical question at hand
items.rationaleA: The single recommendation is tightly and explicitly linked to a living systematic review of 44 RCTs (>30 000 participants) plus a linked microsimulation study, with GRADE certainty stated outcome by outcome ("very uncertain" for CRC incidence and post-colonoscopy cancer, "low certainty" for mortality), relative and absolute effects with confidence intervals (ADR RR 1.22, 1.16 to 1.29; 11 fewer CRC and 635 more surveillance colonoscopies per 10 000), and pre-specified MIDs (<10 CRC cases and <5 deaths per 10 000 deemed "trivial to no benefit"). Risk of bias (near-universal lack of blinding with endoscopist-judged outcomes), directness (no trial reported critical patient-important outcomes; model based on ages 60-69 and largely European inputs applied to all adults), and effect modification by indication, age, sex and FIT+ status are each addressed in the "Uncertainties" section. The weak strength and against-direction are congruent with the low/very low certainty and the panel's stated weighting. Publication bias and small-study effects are nowhere addressed in the guideline text, and consistency across the 40 pooled trials is asserted rather than characterised, which keeps this short of exemplary.
items.rationaleB: The single recommendation is tied to a living systematic review of 44 RCTs (30 674 participants) plus a linked microsimulation, with GRADE certainty stated outcome by outcome ("very uncertain" for CRC incidence and post-colonoscopy cancer, "low certainty" for mortality and surveillance burden) and effect sizes given with confidence intervals (ADR 37% v 45%, RR 1.22 (1.16 to 1.29)) and absolute terms (11 fewer CRC, 635 more surveillance colonoscopies per 10 000). Risk of bias, directness and consistency are addressed concretely in the "Uncertainties" section — unblinded trials with endoscopist-judged outcomes, population indirectness of a model built on ages 60-69 applied to adults ≥18, European versus North American inputs, and null subgroup analyses by indication, age and sex. The panel also set explicit MIDs (reduction below 10 CRC cases and 5 deaths per 10 000 = "trivial to no benefit"), and the weak recommendation is congruent with the low/very low certainty. Publication bias and any dose-response consideration are not discussed, and the critical outcomes rest entirely on modelling rather than direct trial data, which caps this below exemplary.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target users it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The problem is highly relevant to the target users (endoscopists, gastroenterologists, generalists) and the boundaries of the recommendation are stated precisely in the Remarks: it does not apply to colonoscopy for inflammatory bowel disease, abnormal imaging, or therapeutic interventions, and the rationale for grouping screening, surveillance, FIT+ and symptomatic indications is argued explicitly. The weak strength matches a close and uncertain benefit-harm balance, and the panel states that using CADe remains "an acceptable course of action" for a minority. However, the guideline itself undermines the actionability of the recommendation for its own target users by conceding that "it is unlikely that the gastroenterologist will consult the patient on whether the device should be turned on" and that use "may depend more on whether the device is available", then relocating the decision to the patient's choice of clinic; it gives the endoscopist no guidance on when to switch CADe off or how to handle a unit where it runs by default.
items.rationaleB: The question is squarely within endoscopists' scope of practice, and the recommendation is bounded explicitly by the "Remarks": it does not apply to colonoscopy for inflammatory bowel disease, abnormal imaging findings or therapeutic interventions, while the "Decision to group colonoscopy indications" box justifies applying it across screening, surveillance, FIT+ and symptomatic indications. The weak strength is correctly matched to the close benefit-burden balance and the low certainty, and the panel states that using CADe "would be an acceptable course of action" for a minority. The guideline is candid about a real misalignment for target users — "If available, it is unlikely that the gastroenterologist will consult the patient on whether the device should be turned on" — but having named that, it leaves the actionable decision (device acquisition, default on/off policy) to a future system-level iteration, so the recommended action sits slightly awkwardly against the actual point of decision.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target patients/populations it is intended for
items.rationaleA: Outcomes were generated by the panel and formally rated 1-9, with CRC-related mortality, CRC incidence and post-colonoscopy CRC designated critical and endoscopy surrogates (ADR, adenomas per colonoscopy, withdrawal time) explicitly demoted to "important but not critical" — and the microsimulation was commissioned precisely because no trial reported the critical outcomes. Burdens that patients care about (overdiagnosis, more frequent surveillance, health-related anxiety) are quantified or named and drive the recommendation. Tailoring is partly handled: pre-specified subgroups (FOBT/FIT+, older age, sex) showed no variability, and out-of-scope indications are excluded. Weaknesses are the acknowledged population indirectness (model ages 60-69 extrapolated to all adults ≥18 years) and the absence of any consideration of ethnicity, comorbidity, family history or hereditary risk.
items.rationaleB: Outcomes were formally prioritised by the panel (three patient partners included) on a 1-9 scale, with CRC-related mortality, CRC incidence and post-colonoscopy CRC incidence rated critical and endoscopic surrogates such as adenoma detection rate deliberately relegated to "important but not critical" — and the panel then weighed the critical outcomes most heavily, which is what drives the recommendation against a technology that only moves the surrogates. Burdens patients actually experience (overdiagnosis, more frequent surveillance, health-related anxiety) are explicitly modelled and quantified. Tailoring is addressed for indication, positive FOBT/FIT, older age and sex, all of which showed no effect modification, and the age-generalisability gap (model in 60-69 year olds, recommendation for adults ≥18) is acknowledged and reasoned through. No tailoring by ethnicity or comorbidity is offered, and importance-to-patients was established mainly by panel rating plus three patient partners rather than by direct patient elicitation.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target users
items.rationaleA: Clinician values were actively sought: the panel commissioned "a systematic review of studies evaluating healthcare providers trust in AI technology in gastroenterology care", and the text reports that "Gastroenterologists also have different perspectives, with varying attitudes and trust" and that endoscopists "turned on" CADe in only 52% of procedures when given the choice. Workflow effects are quantified (withdrawal time +0.57 minutes) and the guideline warns CADe "should not be a substitute for careful and thorough examination". Clinical flexibility is signalled through the weak recommendation and the concession that some clinicians will reasonably still use CADe. Still, provider attitudes are reported as evidence rather than integrated into any explicit judgement, the range of acceptable practice is never delimited, and nothing is said about new skills, training or how endoscopists should adapt routines around the tool.
items.rationaleB: The panel commissioned a dedicated systematic review of provider trust in AI in gastroenterology and reports that "Gastroenterologists also have different perspectives, with varying attitudes and trust," and the "Implementation and adaptation" section cites real-world uptake data (endoscopists "turned on" CADe in only 52% of procedures) and notes provider attitude and trust as a determinant of use. Eleven healthcare providers sat on the panel, and the weak recommendation explicitly licenses clinical flexibility, stating that some clinicians and patients may still reasonably choose CADe. Workflow acceptability is touched only lightly — increased withdrawal time (mean difference 0.57 minutes) and the risk of overreliance — with nothing on training, competency or the practicalities of adapting endoscopy routines, which are left to a later iteration.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target patients/populations
items.rationaleA: Three patient partners with lived experience of CRC screening participated "at every stage", helped set the MIDs ("based on both patient partner input and clinical experience"), and validated the final recommendation; in addition a dedicated systematic search of patient values and preferences was commissioned (supplemental material), identifying that patients value mortality reduction and quality of care but fear anxiety, overdiagnosis and more surveillance. The panel wrote an explicit values and preferences statement, judged that ">50% of well informed patients would not choose CADe assistance", flagged that with a weak recommendation "individual patients' values and preferences are likely to play a substantial role" through shared decision making, and points to multilayered decision aids in MAGICapp. The main limits are honestly stated: no CADe-specific preference studies exist, certainty about patient values is low, and the inference is the panel's own — and the guideline concedes patients may never actually be asked.
items.rationaleB: A systematic review of patient values and preferences was commissioned specifically for this guideline (supplemental material), its findings are reported concretely (patients value mortality reduction and quality of care, and worry about anxiety, overdiagnosis and more frequent surveillance), and its thinness is stated rather than glossed — only one study on AI in a GI setting, none on CADe. Three patient partners were engaged "at every stage," including validating the final recommendation, and the panel wrote an explicit values and preferences statement that is the stated pivot of the recommendation: "the majority (>50%) of well informed patients would not choose CADe assistance." The guideline differentiates where patient choice matters most ("individual patients' values and preferences are likely to play a substantial role... ideally through shared decision-making") and points to multilayered recommendations and decision aids on MAGICapp; the only real limitation is that panel inference substituted for direct evidence, which is itself transparently flagged as a driver of the weak strength and a target for updating.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of policy/decision makers
items.rationaleA: The system and payer perspective is deliberately out of scope: "this guideline focuses on the individual patient level" and "The next iteration of this guideline will consider evidence relating to healthcare systems and society ... resource use, acceptability, feasibility and equity." What remains is fragmentary — a note that in systems where patients pay out of pocket cost "could also be a consideration", an acknowledgement of increased population-level colonoscopy burden and unnecessary costs, and a genuinely policy-relevant critique of regulatory opacity (proprietary algorithms updated after FDA clearance "without formal regulatory reassessment"). There is no cost-effectiveness or budget-impact analysis, no equity analysis, no statement of what purchasers or health systems should do about CADe procurement, and no engagement with decision-makers as stakeholders.
items.rationaleB: This dimension is explicitly deferred: the guideline states it "focuses on the individual patient level" and that "future updates will take a societal and system level approach," with resource use, acceptability, feasibility, equity and formal cost-effectiveness all promised for the next iteration. What is present is fragmentary — an "Uncertainties" bullet on the lack of transparency in CADe regulatory approval (developers can modify algorithms after FDA clearance without reassessment), a passing note that out-of-pocket payment could matter to patients, and a health policy consultant on the panel — but none of it is converted into guidance for purchasers, payers or systems. Equity is named once, only as a future consideration, and no policy change is articulated despite the recommendation implying non-adoption of a technology systems are actively buying.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of the guideline developers
items.rationaleA: This is the guideline's strongest dimension. The panel states plainly that it "placed a higher value on avoiding burdens than on uncertain benefits", prints both candidate values-and-preferences statements ("Recommendation against" and "Recommendation for") that were put to a vote, and reports the vote itself (13 members, 60%, against; nine, 40%, for) and how the split was resolved into a weak recommendation. The method of integrating differing perspectives is described concretely (five web-conference meetings, outcome-importance survey, consensus with co-chair drafting and panel approval), and the divergence from the AGA and ESGE guidelines using the same evidence base is attributed explicitly to differing weighting of patient values. Competing interests were screened and intellectual conflicts "minimised and managed", so the declaration goes beyond bare COI disclosure to declared values that visibly shaped the recommendation.
items.rationaleB: The panel's own value judgment is stated as the explicit hinge of the recommendation: it "placed a higher value on avoiding burdens than on uncertain benefits," and the two competing rationale statements ("Recommendation against" versus "Recommendation for") are printed verbatim with the vote reported as 13 (60%) against and 9 (40%) for. The method for integrating differing perspectives is described — five facilitated meetings, consensus process, a formal vote, panel-agreed values and preferences statement — and the explicit MIDs are said to "reflect our consensus about what most well informed patients might consider meaningful, based on both patient partner input and clinical experience." Most tellingly, the guideline compares itself with the AGA and ESGE guidelines built on the same evidence base and attributes the divergent conclusion to differing value weighting, which makes the developers' values visible and falsifiable rather than implicit; competing-interest management is described as well but is not what carries this score.

items.text: The purpose of the recommendation is clear and actionable
items.rationaleA: The stated purpose — to provide "trustworthy guidance in response to potentially practice-changing evidence" at the level of the individual patient, as a living recommendation updated on MAGICapp — matches what is delivered: one actionable, clearly bounded recommendation with a defined trigger for updating (new trial data altering conclusions on incidence, mortality or burdens). Anticipated impacts on individuals are described in concrete numbers (635 more surveillance colonoscopies per 10 000, upward risk-category migration, health-related anxiety). What is missing is the organisational and system layer: the guideline explicitly defers cost-effectiveness, budget impact, feasibility and equity to "future updates", so the consequences of adopting a recommendation against a technology that units are already buying and installing are not spelled out.
items.rationaleB: The stated purpose — providing trustworthy, dynamically updatable guidance in response to potentially practice-changing evidence within the BMJ Rapid Recommendations series — is coherent with what the recommendation actually does: it prompts clinical discussion and shared decision-making about a technology in rapid uptake rather than mandating a practice change. Anticipated impacts on patients are described in quantified terms (635 more surveillance colonoscopies per 10 000, anxiety, overdiagnosis), and the panel is explicit that the guidance is intended to be actionable and transparent even under low certainty. Organisational and system-level impacts of adopting the recommendation, however, are named only as out of scope for this iteration, and the guideline does not say what a service that already owns CADe should do, so the implementation goal is only partly served.

items.text: The recommendation is feasible for local application and adoption
items.rationaleA: There is a section headed "Implementation and adaptation of the guideline", but it is largely a discussion of provider trust and living-update mechanics rather than implementation advice; the only concrete supports are the MAGICapp multilayered formats and decision aids and the note that shared evidence-to-decision tables allowed "adaptations for the North American and European context". The guideline never characterises the type or degree of change required, which matters because CADe "is being increasingly used in clinical practice" — de-implementation in units that already own the technology is the real task and is not addressed. Resource considerations, formal cost-effectiveness, personnel competencies and training, data or quality indicators for monitoring adoption, and strategies for overcoming acceptability barriers are all either absent or explicitly postponed to a future iteration.
items.rationaleB: There is a short "Implementation and adaptation of the guideline" section, but it is largely descriptive rather than enabling: it notes that utility depends on how endoscopists engage with the tool and cites the 52% turn-on figure, then defers cost effectiveness, budget impact and the upfront costs of buying or subscribing to CADe systems to future updates. The degree of change required from current practice is never characterised (CADe is described as "increasingly used," yet nothing addresses de-adoption or switching a purchased system off), and there are no monitoring criteria, quality indicators, training or competency requirements, or strategies for overcoming acceptability barriers. Support for local adaptation amounts to the MAGICapp multilayered format and decision aids plus the note that parallel AGA and ESGE versions provide "adaptations for the North American and European context."

guidelineTitle: GA Clinical Practice Guideline on Computer-Aided Detection–Assisted Colonoscopy
recommendationText: In adults undergoing colonoscopy, the AGA makes no recommendation on the use of CADe-assisted colonoscopy.

pico.population: Adults undergoing screening or surveillance colonoscopy
pico.outcomes: Colorectal cancer incidence, CRC mortality, post-colonoscopy CRC, adenoma detection rate, AMR, surveilance colonoscopy, perforation, bleeding, Advanced colorectal neoplasia detection rate, Serrated Sessile Polyp detection rate, Non-neoplastic polyps, Withdrawal Time

items.appraisal: The objective is explicit: determine the role of CADe-assisted colonoscopy and support endoscopists and patients in decisions about CADe for colorectal-polyp detection. The document also frames the expected patient benefit in terms of CRC incidence, CRC mortality, post-colonoscopy CRC, and colonoscopy quality.

An explicit foreground question is provided: in patients undergoing colonoscopy for screening, surveillance, or follow-up after positive FIT, should CADe-assisted colonoscopy versus standard colonoscopy be used? Population, intervention, comparator, and numerous critical/important outcomes are specified. Under your scoring anchor, this represents four PICOS components; study design is not part of the clinical question itself, so I score 6 rather than 7.

The population is clearly patients/adults undergoing colonoscopy for screening, surveillance, or follow-up after positive FIT. This is clinically specific, but comprehensive demographic characteristics, comorbidity/severity definitions, and guideline-level inclusion/exclusion criteria are not stated, preventing 7.

The multidisciplinary panel includes content experts, evidence-synthesis experts, and guideline methodologists, and author affiliations encompass gastroenterology, epidemiology, health economics/quality improvement, research, and methodology. Members' roles in question formulation, evidence review, EtD judgments, and recommendation development are explicitly described.

This is unusually strong. The developers conducted a protocol-based systematic review specifically to identify patient values and preferences, searched Embase and MEDLINE, summarized the findings, and incorporated uncertainty/variability in those preferences into the EtD deliberations. Although no patient appears to have sat on the panel, the supplied Item 5 anchor permits a high score where systematic collection, summary, and use of patient-preference evidence are demonstrated.

Both users and intended use are explicit. The target audience includes gastroenterologists, endoscopists, primary-care providers, people undergoing colonoscopy, administrators, and policy makers, and the document explains that it is intended to support rational informed decision-making rather than impose a standard of care.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: Multiple systematic reviews were used, including the principal CADe efficacy/safety review and separate reviews of patient preferences and provider trust. The patient-preference review gives databases and a search date—Embase/Medline on August 7, 2023—but the main guideline paper does not reproduce a complete, reproducible search strategy for the principal CADe review, including search terms. Under your strict Item 7 anchor, the guideline paper itself therefore does not warrant 6–7.

The principal evidence base is clearly identified as an SR/meta-analysis of RCTs, and the clinical PICO is explicit. The review included 44 RCTs involving >30,000 participants. However, the guideline itself does not comprehensively reproduce study-level inclusion and exclusion criteria, language criteria, or the screening procedure.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of the body of evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: Excellent. GRADE explicitly considers risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and publication bias. Table 2 then displays outcome-specific certainty judgments and reasons for downgrading; for example CRC incidence and PCCRC are rated very low certainty because of serious risk of bias/imprecision, while ADR evidence is downgraded for bias and publication bias.

items.text: Methods for formulating recommendations clearly described
items.appraisal: The GRADE EtD framework explicitly incorporated benefits/harms, certainty, resource use, equity, acceptability, feasibility, and values/preferences. Panel meetings and consensus procedures are described. Even more importantly, public-comment feedback changed the outcome: the initial conditional recommendation favoring CADe was reconsidered, a vote occurred because consensus was lacking, and the final result became “no recommendation.”

items.text: Benefits, side effects, and risks considered
items.appraisal: Central to the entire guideline. Potential reductions in CRC incidence/mortality and improved ADR are explicitly balanced against overdiagnosis, non-neoplastic polypectomy, increased surveillance colonoscopies, anxiety, procedural burden, costs, and resource use.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and supporting evidence
items.appraisal: Exceptionally strong. The recommendation is immediately accompanied by remarks, rationale, an evidence summary, and an outcome-specific GRADE table. The table reports absolute effects for CADe versus conventional colonoscopy and certainty for each relevant outcome.

The guideline explicitly states that it underwent public comment and external peer review before AGA Governing Board approval. However, reviewer identities, detailed review methods, and review findings are not reported. Under your Item 13 anchor, external review without those details falls around 2–3.

This is explicitly a living guideline. The paper states that it will be updated in approximately 1–2 years when new data become available. It also identifies the specific evidence gaps expected to trigger reconsideration, including critical long-term outcomes. Thus both an interval and evidence-based trigger are specified, although a fuller operational surveillance procedure is not described.

The central conclusion is explicit: “In adults undergoing colonoscopy, the AGA makes no recommendation on the use of CADe-assisted colonoscopy”, with “very low certainty of evidence.” The fact that it is a no recommendation does not make it ambiguous; it is a deliberate, clearly defined GRADE outcome.

The two relevant options—CADe-assisted versus standard colonoscopy—are explicitly compared for patient-important outcomes, surrogate outcomes, burdens, harms, and resource consequences. The lack of a preferred option is itself justified by the close balance and uncertain evidence.

On page 7, the central recommendation is displayed in a prominent boxed section with accompanying remarks. The rendered page also visually separates the recommendation from its rationale and evidence summary, making the key conclusion immediately identifiable.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: Excellent. A systematic review of provider attitudes identified concrete barriers including cost, accountability for incorrect diagnosis, medicolegal concerns, and distraction. The EtD discussion adds infrastructure, real-world effectiveness, acceptance, reimbursement, equity, racial/ethnic bias, and environmental concerns. These factors explicitly affected the recommendation.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: There is meaningful implementation discussion through the EtD framework and guidance for interpreting strong, conditional, and no recommendations. However, because the panel makes no recommendation, the document understandably supplies no ready-to-use implementation algorithm, checklist, decision aid, or CADe deployment protocol. Under your Item 19 anchor, substantial implementation discussion without an eligible implementation tool fits approximately 4.

Resource implications are detailed: increased follow-up colonoscopies, purchase/subscription costs, effects on population colonoscopy capacity, reimbursement, infrastructure, equity, and the need for cost-effectiveness studies are discussed. However, the development section explicitly states that the panel did not formally incorporate direct/indirect costs or cost-effectiveness into the recommendation itself. That prevents a 6–7.

The guideline suggests that endoscopy-unit leadership may need to promote uptake and monitor use, but it does not define guideline-specific implementation indicators, thresholds, audit frequency, or measurement procedures. ADR and PCCRC are outcome/quality metrics in the evidence base, not a formal audit framework for implementing this guideline.

Funding is exceptionally transparent: the guideline was fully funded by the AGA Institute with no outside agency or industry funding, and individual research grants are separately disclosed. However, there is no explicit statement that the AGA Institute itself had no influence on guideline content. Under your strict scoring anchor, professional-association funding without a formal no-influence statement is best scored 5–6 rather than 7.

COI management is strong. Members were selected after COI review; every panel member, chair, methodologist, and content expert completed disclosure forms before beginning work; disclosures had to be updated throughout development; and members were advised not to accept new paid speaking/consulting relationships during development and for 12 months after publication. Individual relevant conflicts are also disclosed—for example, consultancy/research relationships for some authors. I stop at 6 because the publication does not explicitly state recommendation-specific recusals or demonstrate how each existing COI did or did not affect voting.

items.rationaleA: The evidence base underpinning the single recommendation is exceptionally well characterised: Table 2 gives relative and absolute effects, NNTs and a GRADE certainty rating for every critical and important outcome, with footnotes that separately adjudicate risk of bias (lack of blinding of outcome assessors), inconsistency against a stated 1% MID, imprecision (CIs crossing harm) and publication bias ("Asymmetrical funnel plot with a signiﬁcant Egger's test"). Indirectness is handled explicitly by commissioning a microsimulation study because RCTs did not report CRC incidence/mortality, and residual confounding is probed by also reviewing an SR of 8 nonrandomized studies showing no ADR increase (RR 1.11; 95% CI 0.97-1.28). The 'No recommendation, very low certainty of evidence' output is transparently congruent with the certainty rating, and the Rationale section makes the evidence-to-recommendation link explicit, including why an 8% ADR gain (a surrogate) did not outweigh 635 more surveillance colonoscopies per 10,000. This is close to exemplary handling of evidence at the level of the recommendation.
items.rationaleB: The single recommendation rests on four explicitly described evidence bodies (an SR/meta-analysis of 44 RCTs, a commissioned microsimulation model, an SR of patient values, an SR of provider trust), and Table 2 grades every outcome with itemised footnotes for risk of bias ("inadequate/lack of blinding of outcome assessors"), inconsistency against a stated 1% MID, imprecision ("the 95% CI is wide and includes increased harms"), and publication bias ("asymmetrical funnel plot with a significant Egger's test"). Directness is handled candidly - ADR is labelled a surrogate and the long-term outcomes are model-derived, which is why they are rated down - and magnitudes are given as absolute effects with NNTs (11 fewer CRCs and 2 fewer CRC deaths per 10,000; 635 more surveillance colonoscopies per 10,000). The direction and definitiveness of the output are fully congruent with the certainty: "no recommendation ... very low certainty of evidence", with the Rationale section tracing exactly which uncertainties drove it. The nonlinear ADR-CRC relationship and its plateau above 45% is even considered as a dose-response issue.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target users it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The Target Audience section names gastroenterologists, endoscopists, primary care providers, people undergoing colonoscopy, administrators and policy makers, and the PICO (screening, surveillance, FIT-positive follow-up) matches the endoscopist's scope of practice precisely. The definitiveness of the statement is well aligned with the trade-off: the panel explicitly justifies non-directiveness by the "close tradeoff between desirable and undesirable effects" and by feedback in public comment that overturned a draft conditional recommendation. The limitation is that a 'no recommendation' gives target users no actionable direction - nothing is said about whether endoscopists with CADe already installed should keep using it, whether ADR-based credentialing should change, or how withdrawal-time effects should be handled - and the listed primary care and patient audiences have essentially no recommended action available to them, a mismatch the panel itself concedes when it says the decision "may not be conducive to a shared decision-making approach at the level of an individual person."
items.rationaleB: The target audience is named precisely (gastroenterologists, endoscopists, primary care providers, people undergoing colonoscopy, administrators, policy makers) and the problem - missed adenomas in >15 million annual US colonoscopies - is squarely within endoscopists' scope; the definitiveness of the statement is also well aligned with the closely balanced trade-off the panel describes. The critical weakness is that the output specifies no action: an endoscopist, unit director or payer deciding today whether to buy, enable or continue CADe gets no direction, not even interim advice, and the guideline gives no practical statement about what users should do while awaiting the planned 1-2 year update. It also fails to differentiate users despite having the material to do so - the microsimulation "incorporated different ADR ranges to simulate the performance of endoscopists with varying skill levels", yet no distinction is drawn between low-ADR and high-ADR endoscopists or between community and academic settings, which is instead relegated to an evidence gap.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target patients/populations it is intended for
items.rationaleA: Patient-important outcomes are prioritised properly: CRC-related mortality, CRC incidence and PCCRC were rated critical, and a microsimulation study was commissioned specifically because "existing randomized controlled trials" did not report them, with burden outcomes (surveillance colonoscopies per lifetime, perforation, bleeding, health-related anxiety, overdiagnosis) carried through to Table 2 and the Rationale. However, the importance of outcomes was set by the panel using "predeﬁned thresholds for the minimum clinically important difference... determined by clinical experts" rather than by patients, and no patient or public member is described on the panel. There is no tailoring of the position to any subgroup - nothing by age, sex, ethnicity, comorbidity, family-history risk, or by baseline endoscopist ADR, even though the model "incorporated different ADR ranges to simulate the performance of endoscopists with varying skill levels" and that stratification could plausibly have supported differentiated advice; the guideline instead lists diverse populations and settings only as an evidence gap.
items.rationaleB: Outcomes were explicitly ranked, with CRC-related mortality, CRC incidence and PCCRC rated critical and detection rates, colonoscopies per lifetime, perforation and bleeding rated important, and a microsimulation was commissioned precisely because RCTs did not report these patient-important endpoints - a substantive strength. Patient-relevant burdens are carried into the reasoning (635 more surveillance colonoscopies per 10,000, overdiagnosis, "increased health-related anxiety"), and prespecified MIDs were used. Weaker points: outcome importance was determined by panel judgement ("determined by clinical experts") rather than by any elicitation from patients, and there is essentially no tailoring by age, sex, ethnicity or comorbidity - the model simulates only individuals aged 60-69 with assumed 100% participation, and diversity of populations and settings appears only as a listed evidence gap.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target users
items.rationaleA: Clinician values were actively sought through a dedicated systematic review of provider trust in AI (2044 records, 13 studies included), and the findings are quantified and carried into the decision: 85% (95% CI 80%-90%) find AI in colonoscopy interesting, 74% expect better adenoma detection, but 43% are concerned about cost, 40% about accountability for incorrect diagnosis and 23% about medicolegal issues, with "some health care providers" finding CADe distracting. Acceptability and feasibility are formally judged in the Evidence to Decision framework, and workflow effects are quantified (withdrawal time +0.57 minutes) alongside the note that "endoscopy unit leadership may need to engage with endoscopists to promote uptake and monitor use." Most tellingly, target-user values demonstrably changed the output: "after signiﬁcant feedback during the public comment period, the panel reconvened and ultimately made a NO RECOMMENDATION statement." What is missing is any explicit statement of the range of practice that remains acceptable, or of new skills/training endoscopists would need, and the panel concedes "limited data on acceptability, especially by gastroenterologists."
items.rationaleB: The panel commissioned a dedicated SR of provider perspectives and trust (2044 records screened, 13 studies) and reports quantified acceptability data: 85% find AI in colonoscopy interesting, but 43% are concerned about increased costs, 40% about accountability for incorrect diagnosis, 23% about medicolegal issues, and some find CADe "too distracting in their daily practice". Workflow and adoption realities are addressed - trivial withdrawal-time prolongation, likely lower effectiveness in routine practice than in RCTs, and the need for "endoscopy unit leadership ... to engage with endoscopists to promote uptake and monitor use". Most tellingly, clinician values demonstrably changed the output: "after significant feedback during the public comment period, the panel reconvened and ultimately made a NO RECOMMENDATION statement." What is missing is any description of the range of CADe use acceptable to the clinical community or of where individual clinician discretion is more versus less appropriate.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target patients/populations
items.rationaleA: A protocol-driven systematic review of patient values was conducted (7101 records screened across Embase and Medline), and when only 2 directly relevant studies were found the search was broadened to an SR of 23 stated-preference studies on CRC screening; the specific findings are reported (>60% concerned about reduced personal contact with clinicians, >65% would choose an endoscopist using CADe, patient concerns about anxiety, overdiagnosis and more frequent surveillance). These findings visibly shape the decision - the panel concludes there "may be important uncertainty or variability in patient values and preferences", which is one of the stated grounds for withholding a recommendation - and the panel is candid that "no study... speciﬁcally evaluated patient values and preferences for AI-assisted colonoscopy." Weaknesses: the guideline states the decision "may not be conducive to a shared decision-making approach at the level of an individual person", which forecloses rather than differentiates the role of patient choice; family/caregiver perspectives are absent; and decision aids are mentioned only in the generic Table 1 legend, with no statement of whether one would be useful here.
items.rationaleB: Patient values were sought systematically rather than assumed - a protocol-driven search of Embase and Medline (7101 records) yielded only 2 directly relevant studies, so the panel broadened to an SR of 23 stated-preference studies on CRC screening, and reports both the favourable findings (>65% would choose an endoscopist using CADe) and the concerns (loss of personal contact, AI misuse, privacy, overdiagnosis, more frequent surveillance). This evidence visibly shaped the judgement that "there may be important uncertainty or variability in patient values and preferences". The guideline also explicitly locates where patient choice matters little: "as an intervention used primarily by endoscopists, the decision to use CADe may not be conducive to a shared decision-making approach at the level of an individual person." Against this, no patient, caregiver or public member sat on the panel, no statement is made about whether a patient decision aid would help (beyond the boilerplate Table 1 row), and the panel concedes "no study ... specifically evaluated patient values and preferences for AI-assisted colonoscopy."

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of policy/decision makers
items.rationaleA: System-level consequences are described concretely: 635 more surveillance colonoscopies per 10,000 over 10 years, "substantial increase in costs and a reduction of available resources for the coverage of the population", purchase models ("a ﬂat fee or subscription-based model") for a health system or a national screening programme, and the fact that "the costs of implementing a CADe system are not reimbursable through insurance." Health equity is treated seriously and in its own right - reduced equitable access, global inequity, racial and ethnic bias in training data sets creating mistrust, plus environmental impact. Two things hold the score down: the Methods state plainly that "the panel did not explicitly incorporate resource considerations (such as direct or indirect costs or cost-effectiveness)" into developing the recommendation, and no economic analysis was performed (cost-effectiveness is deferred to future research); and the guideline never says what policy or coverage decisions should follow - for example whether payers should reimburse, or whether CADe should be excluded from quality-measure sets pending better evidence.
items.rationaleB: Administrators and policy makers are named target users and the system-level consequences are described with unusual concreteness: a substantial increase in follow-up procedures, purchase "through a flat fee or subscription-based model" for a health system or national screening programme, and costs that "are not reimbursable through insurance". Health equity is genuinely engaged rather than box-ticked - reduced equitable access to clinicians who perform AI-assisted colonoscopy, global inequity, racial and ethnic bias in training data sets that "may introduce mistrust among patients of different backgrounds", plus environmental impact. Two things hold the score down: the Methods state plainly that "the panel did not explicitly incorporate resource considerations (such as direct or indirect costs or cost-effectiveness)" and no economic analysis was performed (it is listed as needed future work); and the guideline never says what policy or reimbursement changes should follow, leaving decision-makers with a described problem and no direction.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of the guideline developers
items.rationaleA: The panel's own value judgements are stated explicitly and are the visible hinge of the decision: "The panel placed a higher value on long-term outcomes of CRC incidence and mortality" than on the ADR surrogate, and it reasoned that the ADR gain "was primarily attributable to detection of diminutive to small polyps with low potential for progression" - a declared value that directly determined how benefits and harms were weighed. The integration method is described (GRADE Evidence to Decision framework, web-based meetings, consensus) and, unusually, the guideline discloses that consensus failed: "This was based on a vote, as there was a lack of consensus among the panel members." COI management is thorough (National Academy of Medicine standards, a bar on new speaking/consulting engagements until 12 months after publication, AGA-only funding, named disclosures for two panelists). It falls short of 7 because no vote tally or dissenting rationale is given, differing stakeholder perspectives are not reconciled in any described way, and the panel is composed of content experts and methodologists with no patient or payer representation reported.
items.rationaleB: The developers' own value judgement is stated openly and is the pivot of the recommendation: the panel "took a population perspective" and "placed a higher value on long-term outcomes of CRC incidence and mortality" than on the surrogate ADR gain, which is precisely why an 8% ADR increase did not translate into a favourable recommendation. The integration method is transparent - GRADE Evidence to Decision judgements on benefits/harms, values, equity, acceptability and feasibility, consensus where possible, and an explicit vote when it failed ("This was based on a vote, as there was a lack of consensus among the panel members"), with the EtD table supplied as supplementary material. COI handling is described in detail (National Academy of Medicine standards, disclosure updates, a moratorium on new industry engagements until 12 months post-publication, full AGA funding with no industry money). The gap is that although two panel members disclose relationships with CADe device manufacturers (consultancy for Fujifilm and Olympus; advisory roles), the guideline does not say how those interests were managed in the deliberation or the vote.

items.text: The purpose of the recommendation is clear and actionable
items.rationaleA: The stated objective was "to make a recommendation on the role of CADe-assisted colonoscopy", and on its own terms the document does not deliver one; what it does deliver is consistent with the broader stated aim of providing "guidance as the basis for rational informed decision making" rather than imposing a standard of care. Anticipated impacts of adoption are described well at each level - patients (overdiagnosis, health-related anxiety, more procedures), providers (distraction, accountability, medicolegal exposure), and systems (635 extra surveillance colonoscopies per 10,000, costs, resource diversion, equity, environmental impact) - and the living-guideline design, with a planned 1-2 year update and a structured Knowledge Gaps research agenda, gives the document a clear forward-looking purpose. The score is limited because a no-recommendation statement cannot prompt practice or policy change, and the guideline offers no interim guidance for the many units that have already deployed CADe or for payers currently deciding on coverage.
items.rationaleB: The stated objective is narrow and clear - "to make a recommendation on the role of CADe-assisted colonoscopy" - and the anticipated impacts of adoption on patients and systems are described well (surveillance burden, overdiagnosis, anxiety, cost, equity, environmental effect), which is the substance behind the panel's restraint. But the product does not deliver against its own implementation purpose: an explicit "no recommendation" cannot influence a health decision, prompt a practice change, or serve as a policy or performance measure, and Table 1's own footnote concedes the category means only that "further research is needed". Its real achievements are secondary purposes - naming the evidence gaps, warning future post-polypectomy surveillance guidelines to account for the changed detection landscape, and committing to a living update in 1-2 years - so the statement functions as a research agenda more than as guidance.

items.text: The recommendation is feasible for local application and adoption
items.rationaleA: This is the weakest domain. Implementation content amounts to a few scattered sentences: CADe "was judged to be feasible to implement", "endoscopy unit leadership may need to engage with endoscopists to promote uptake and monitor use", effectiveness "may be lower in clinical practice compared with its performance in RCTs", and a qualitative note on purchase models and non-reimbursement. There are no tools, no adaptation guidance, no personnel-competency or training requirements (indeed the effect of CADe on trainee polyp-recognition skills is flagged only as an unknown), no data or metrics for monitoring adoption, no strategies for overcoming provider or patient barriers, and no economic analysis - cost-effectiveness is explicitly excluded from the panel's deliberation and listed as a research need. The absence is partly explained by there being no recommendation to implement, but the guideline still does not tell users what degree of change from current practice is entailed or where local adaptation would be more or less appropriate.
items.rationaleB: This is the weakest domain. Beyond one sentence that "endoscopy unit leadership may need to engage with endoscopists to promote uptake and monitor use" and the caution that real-world effectiveness may be lower than in RCTs, there are no implementation tools, no algorithm or patient-facing material, no guidance on tailoring to community versus academic or resource-limited settings, and no criteria, indicators or data specifications for monitoring adoption or quality. Cost is discussed qualitatively (subscription/flat-fee purchase models, non-reimbursement) but no economic or cost-effectiveness analysis was undertaken - it is instead listed among knowledge gaps ("Cost-effectiveness studies are needed"). Nothing is said about the degree of change from current practice, training or competency requirements, or the acknowledged risk to trainee polyp-recognition skills beyond flagging it as unclear, and unresolved medicolegal and data-ownership barriers are named without any mitigation strategy.

guidelineTitle: Diagnosis and management of Barrett esophagus: European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ESGE) Guideline
recommendationText: more evidence is needed before AI can be generally accepted as an adjunct to – or a replacement of – the Seattle biopsy protocol during surveillance.

pico.intervention: AI-assisted endoscopic detection of dysplasia/early esophageal adenocarcinoma
pico.comparator: Standard high-quality endoscopy with Seattle biopsy protocol
pico.outcomes: Dysplasia detection rate, early cancer detection, diagnostic accuracy, missed lesion rate

items.appraisal: The guideline explicitly aims to optimize and harmonize diagnosis and care of patients with Barrett esophagus (BE), updating the 2017 statement in light of new evidence and adding recommendations on screening, surveillance, and management. It is intended as a practical guide even where evidence is weak.

Clinical questions were explicitly formulated and translated into research questions using the PICO format where appropriate. This directly satisfies the highest scoring anchor for foreground clinical questions.

The guideline clearly defines BE as ≥1 cm of columnar epithelium with intestinal metaplasia and then defines multiple clinically relevant subpopulations by BE length, dysplasia status, EAC stage, age, comorbidity, and treatment status. Screening recommendations further define high-risk populations by age, GERD, sex, obesity, smoking, ethnicity, and family history.

The 20-member group is international and includes extensive gastroenterology/endoscopy expertise plus histopathology expertise, with six taskforces covering chemoprevention, screening, surveillance, pathology/risk stratification, treatment, and post-treatment management. However, the core panel remains predominantly specialist gastroenterology/endoscopy rather than maximally multidisciplinary.

Patient preferences are explicitly incorporated into individual surveillance decisions—for example, comorbidity, life expectancy, and patient preferences should be considered. However, I found no evidence that patients or patient representatives were directly involved in the guideline-development group or that a guideline-specific patient consultation was performed. The mention of patient input through Heartburn Cancer UK concerns a separate research program, not clearly this guideline-development process.

The intended users are evident as clinicians managing BE—especially gastroenterologists/endoscopists, pathologists, and multidisciplinary expert centers—and the intended use is very clear. However, there is no single dedicated statement comprehensively enumerating all target professional users.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: Systematic searches were performed in MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library. However, the guideline does not provide search terms, search dates, or complete reproducible search strings. Under your strict Item 7 anchor, naming databases without specific search details supports approximately 3/7.

I did not identify explicit study inclusion/exclusion criteria, language restrictions, eligible study designs, or a systematic screening/selection process in the uploaded guideline and supplement. PICO formulation alone does not satisfy Item 8.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of the body of evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: Evidence certainty is formally assessed using GRADE, and the guideline repeatedly discusses study limitations, indirectness, lack of RCTs, retrospective designs, uncertainty, and areas requiring further research. Recommendations explicitly carry quality-of-evidence ratings ranging from high to very low.

items.text: Methods for formulating recommendations clearly described
items.appraisal: Excellent. Evidence and draft recommendations were discussed face-to-face, followed by online voting using a five-point Likert scale. Members could provide explanatory comments, recommendations were revised in response, and two voting iterations were required to finalize the document.

items.text: Benefits, side effects, and risks considered
items.appraisal: Benefits and harms are extensively balanced. Examples include benefits of cancer prevention and surveillance versus procedural burden, treatment complications, competing mortality, drug adverse effects, and overtreatment. The guideline explicitly individualizes surveillance according to likely benefit, comorbidity, life expectancy, and patient preferences.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and supporting evidence
items.appraisal: Very strong. Recommendations are embedded directly alongside the supporting studies and are individually assigned strength and quality-of-evidence ratings. For example, the chemoprevention and screening recommendations immediately follow the supporting evidence and specify strong/weak recommendation plus evidence quality.

The completed draft was reviewed by the ESGE Guideline Committee Chair, two external reviewers, ESGE national societies, and individual ESGE members before publication. The two external reviewers are named and explicitly thanked for their “critical review and appraisal.” The score stops short of 7 because the specific external-review findings and resulting changes are not comprehensively reported.

This document is itself an update triggered by new evidence, demonstrating that ESGE does revise its guidance. However, I found no prospective update interval, formal evidence-surveillance process, or explicit criteria for when this 2023 guideline will next be updated.

Recommendations are exceptionally specific, frequently giving exact populations, diagnostic/treatment actions, surveillance intervals, biopsy strategies, staging parameters, and thresholds. For example, surveillance differs by BE length at ≥1–<3 cm, ≥3–<10 cm, and ≥10 cm.

The guideline differentiates screening versus no screening, endoscopy versus nonendoscopic testing, various surveillance strategies, ablation versus surveillance, endoscopic resection versus multimodality therapy, and alternative ablation modalities. Options are linked to clinical circumstances and evidence certainty.

Excellent. Eleven Main Recommendations appear at the start of the guideline, while individual recommendations are boxed throughout. In addition, decision flowcharts visually summarize surveillance and post-treatment management. The surveillance flowchart on page 7 links BE length, visible lesions, pathology, biopsies, surveillance intervals, and referral to expert centers.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: Practical barriers and facilitators are extensively discussed: endoscopy availability, procedural time, expertise, training, cost, technological availability, patient fitness/preferences, quality of endoscopy, and need for expert centers. The guideline also explains barriers to implementation of newer AI and biomarker approaches because evidence remains immature.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: Strong implementation support. The guideline provides multiple flowcharts, explicit expert-center criteria, biopsy protocols, surveillance intervals, endoscopy-quality requirements, and procedural standards. The BE surveillance flowchart is directly actionable. Expert centers must also meet specified caseload, training, multidisciplinary, surgical-access, and database requirements.

Cost-effectiveness is considered repeatedly. The document discusses economic costs of population screening, cost-effectiveness of risk-targeted screening, nonsedated screening technologies, biomarkers, and surveillance strategies. It also considers practical procedural resources such as allocating ≥30 minutes for surveillance and 40 minutes for ultralong BE. A full guideline-wide economic evaluation is not performed, so I would stop at 6.

The guideline explicitly directs adherence to ESGE Performance Measures for upper-GI endoscopy and provides auditable quality standards such as inspection time, photodocumentation, classification systems, biopsy practice, and prospective registration of patients in expert centers. However, it does not provide a complete guideline-specific audit schedule or frequency for measuring these indicators. Under your anchor, explicit indicators/standards without monitoring frequency fits about 4.

I did not find a guideline-specific statement identifying who funded development and stating that the funding body had no influence, nor an explicit statement that no guideline-development funding was received. Under your strict Item 22 anchor, this warrants 1/7. Author research funding disclosures are not equivalent to a guideline-funding/no-influence declaration.

All participants declared potential conflicts, and detailed individual relationships with Medtronic, Fujifilm, Pentax, Olympus, Cyted, Lucid, and others are reported. However, the guideline does not clearly explain how these conflicts were managed during recommendation formulation, such as recusal from voting or exclusion from specific recommendations. Therefore, I would not award 7.
