items.text: The evidence supporting the recommendation is applicable to the clinical question at hand
items.rationaleA: Every one of the 22 recommendations carries an explicit GRADE strength and certainty label, the supporting narrative names study designs, effect sizes and confidence intervals (e.g. PPI meta-analysis OR 0.47, 95%CI 0.32-0.71; AspECT TR 1.27, 95%CI 1.01-1.58), and inconsistency and indirectness are handled openly (the French RFA trial's 13.5% progression is explained by a 35% CE IM rate; the AspECT composite endpoint and missing no-PPI arm are flagged as precluding conclusions). Harms are quantified alongside benefits (5% stricture with RFA, 12.2% AEs with cryoablation, LNM risks of ~2% vs ~20% for low- vs high-risk T1a). Against this, no risk-of-bias assessment, publication bias evaluation or Evidence-to-Decision table is presented in the document (data extraction is offloaded to an external evidence-table PDF), and strength is repeatedly incongruent with certainty: Recommendations 5, 20a, 20b, 20e, 21 and 22 are all 'strong' on 'weak', 'low' or 'very low' quality evidence, and the guideline justifies this only globally by its aim to 'deliver a practical guide, even when supporting evidence is weak'.
items.rationaleB: Every one of the 22 recommendations carries an explicit GRADE strength plus certainty label, the supporting narrative quantifies benefits and harms (e.g. RFA meta-analysis: 85% eradication of dysplasia, 0.4% annual progression, 5% strictures; cryoablation AEs 12.2%; LNM ~2% for low risk T1a vs ~20% for high risk T1a), confidence intervals are reported (PPI OR 0.47, 95%CI 0.32-0.71), and study-level limitations are named (AspECT "did not include a no-PPI group, and used a composite end point"; ablation-after-ER studies "mix patients with a visible lesion and patients with flat dysplasia"). Evidence tables are posted on the ESGE website rather than in the paper, and the article itself reports no risk-of-bias assessment, no consideration of publication bias, and no evidence-to-decision framework. Most damaging for this item is the repeated, unexplained discordance between strength and certainty: Recommendation 5 is "Strong recommendation, weak quality of evidence", Recommendations 20a, 20e and 21 are strong on "very low" evidence, and Recommendations 2a and 18 are strong on low evidence, with no stated justification for departing from the GRADE default.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target users it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The target users are endoscopists and GI pathologists, and essentially every recommendation is an act within their scope: minimum 1-minute inspection per cm of BE, photodocumentation, Prague/Paris classification, Seattle four-quadrant sampling every 2 cm, EMR for lesions of 20 mm or less versus ESD for suspected submucosal invasion (Rec 14), and p53 IHC to support dysplasia diagnosis (Rec 6a). Trade-offs are stated in terms clinicians act on: ablation after ER is weighed against 'the risks (especially strictures), costs, and the burden to the patient', and endoscopic resection is justified against esophagectomy mortality for low-risk T1b. Three flowcharts (Figs. 1-3) plus operational detail such as allocating 30 minutes (40 for ultralong segments) make the recommendations directly enactable; the main deduction is that several definitive 'strong' statements (e.g. Rec 20a requiring first post-EET follow-up in an expert center) rest on very low certainty without an explicit rationale for the definitiveness.
items.rationaleB: The recommended actions map directly onto what an endoscopist and GI pathologist actually do and are unusually operational: minimum 1-minute inspection per cm of BE, one photograph per cm, Prague and Paris classification, four-quadrant biopsies every 2 cm, EMR for lesions 20 mm or less with low probability of submucosal invasion versus ESD for Paris 0-Is/0-IIc and larger malignant lesions (Rec 14), and named surveillance intervals by segment length (Rec 9). Scope of practice is explicitly partitioned between community and expert centres: Rec 20a places the first post-EET endoscopy in an expert centre, and the text tells non-expert centres to take neo-squamocolumnar junction quadrant biopsies precisely because they lack EET expertise. The main gap is that the Scope and Purpose box never names the intended users or care settings, and some recommendations sit outside endoscopy practice (PPI chemoprevention in Rec 1a, primary-care Cytosponge case finding in Rec 3, chemo/radiotherapy decisions in Recs 17-18) without saying which professional is responsible.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target patients/populations it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The outcome set is patient-important and cancer-relevant - progression to HGD/EAC, cancer-specific and overall survival, recurrence, and procedural adverse events including strictures - and the recommended actions plausibly move these outcomes. Tailoring is genuine in places: surveillance intervals stratified by BE length, discontinuation at age 75 or life expectancy under 5 years (Rec 10) with the modelling study on sex and comorbidity giving stop-ages from 69 (women with comorbidity) to 81 (men without), and close surveillance rather than ablation in patients who are 'frail or have multiple co-morbidities'. However, the guideline never reports how the importance of outcomes to patients was determined, includes no quality-of-life, anxiety or patient-reported outcomes despite recommending decades of repeat endoscopy in a population with 0.3%-0.8% annual progression risk, and ethnicity appears only as a case-finding risk factor ('white ethnicity') with no discussion of applicability to non-white European populations.
items.rationaleB: The outcomes driving the recommendations are patient-important and plausibly modifiable by the recommended actions: progression to HGD/EAC, cancer-specific and overall survival, lymph node metastasis, stricture and other adverse events, and avoidance of unnecessary esophagectomy. Recommendations are meaningfully tailored to individual characteristics: segment length and dysplasia grade drive intervals, Rec 10 uses age 75 and life expectancy under 5 years, the discussion of Rec 10 cites modelling giving an optimal stop-age of 69 years in women with comorbidity versus 81 in men without, Rec 13's text carves out "patients who are frail or have multiple co-morbidities", and Rec 2b builds ethnicity, sex, obesity, smoking and family history into case finding. However, the guideline nowhere reports how the importance of any outcome to patients was determined, no patient or lay member sat on the 20-member panel, and outcomes patients typically care about most after a BE diagnosis - anxiety, quality of life, procedural discomfort, lifelong PPI burden - appear only as a single passing phrase about "the burden to the patient".

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target users
items.rationaleA: Clinician values were canvassed structurally: 20 panel members across six taskforces, two iterations of five-point Likert voting with free-text comments 'on the basis of which the recommendations were adjusted', plus circulation to two external reviewers, ESGE national societies and individual members. Workflow acceptability is explicitly considered - AAC is 'associated with very limited additional costs', virtual chromoendoscopy is already on all high-definition platforms, the extra pull-through 'translates to increased inspection time', and 30-40 minute procedure slots are demanded. Clinical flexibility is differentiated by setting: post-EET cardia biopsies 'have been abandoned in some expert centers' but are recommended 'in centers with no expertise in EET', and close surveillance is a 'valid alternative to ablation' in experienced centers. What is missing is any formal elicitation of user values or an analysis of acceptability barriers (the guideline itself cites repeated evidence of poor Seattle-protocol compliance without proposing how to shift that behaviour).
items.rationaleB: Clinician values were formally elicited within the panel through two iterations of anonymous five-point Likert voting with free-text comments "on the basis of which the recommendations were adjusted", and the draft went to ESGE national societies and individual members for comment; the acceptable range of practice in the clinical community is also described ("most experts adhere to a surveillance interval of 1-2 years" for ultralong BE; "random quadrant biopsies of the proximal cardia have been abandoned in some expert centers"). Workflow and skill acceptability are addressed concretely: at least 30 minutes per surveillance procedure rising to 40 for ultralong segments, virtual chromoendoscopy already present on all high-definition platforms with "very limited additional costs", and 30 supervised ER plus 30 ablation cases to acquire competence. Where clinical flexibility is appropriate is explicitly flagged - close surveillance "appears to be a valid alternative to ablation in individual cases" in expert centres. What is missing is any reported voting result or level of agreement per recommendation, and any elicitation of values from endoscopists outside the panel and expert-centre circle.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target patients/populations
items.rationaleA: Patient values are gestured at rather than incorporated: Section 6 says 'patient factors should explicitly be taken into consideration, such as co-morbidity, life expectancy, and patient preferences', Rec 17/18 defer to 'patient characteristics and patient preference' in the MDT, fundoplication 'may be discussed with patients as an alternative to a lifelong PPI', and post-EET stopping decisions should be individualised because 'patients and clinicians should discuss and individualize management decisions depending on the anticipated benefits and competing health concerns'. No patient, carer or lay representative sat on the guideline group, no patient values or acceptability evidence was sought (the burden and tolerability of Cytosponge versus sedated endoscopy, or of lifelong 3-5 yearly surveillance, is never examined), and no decision aid or tool is offered or even flagged as desirable. The mentions are real but generic, and none is operationalised into where patient choice should dominate versus be secondary.
items.rationaleB: Patient preference is invoked at exactly the decision nodes where it matters most and the guideline does distinguish these from the technical recommendations: Section 6 states that for the individual patient "co-morbidity, life expectancy, and patient preferences" must be taken into account and surveillance is only indicated if a finding would change management; Recs 16-18 make additional treatment versus strict endoscopic follow-up contingent on "patient characteristics and patient preference" in a multidisciplinary discussion; Rec 19's text says the risks and benefits of fundoplication "may be discussed with patients as an alternative to a lifelong PPI"; and the post-EET discussion says "patients and clinicians should discuss and individualize management decisions depending on the anticipated benefits and competing health concerns". Against this, no patient, carer or lay representative was on the panel, no patient values or acceptability evidence was sought or cited (the only acceptability data, on transnasal endoscopy and MACE comfort, sit unused in Appendix 2s), and no patient decision aid or communication tool is offered or even suggested despite Rec 21 stating that recurrence risks "can only be reliably communicated with patients" once defined.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of policy/decision makers
items.rationaleA: System-level considerations surface repeatedly but incidentally: population screening is recommended against partly because 'all-comer screening would lead to substantial economic costs' and case finding is confined to a high-prevalence group 'in order to be acceptable and cost-effective'; the cost-effectiveness of current surveillance intervals is acknowledged as 'in doubt' with citations to economic evaluations; routine post-EET four-quadrant biopsies 'add to the costs' and are discouraged; and the environmental/carbon footprint of redundant endoscopy is invoked twice. Section 9 on centralization is genuinely a service-configuration statement (case-volume thresholds, MDT access, prospective registry). But no decision-maker or payer was consulted, no resource-impact or budget analysis accompanies the recommendations, no health-equity considerations are raised at all - notably the ethnicity- and sex-based case-finding criteria and the mandatory referral to expert centers both have access implications that go unexamined - and the guideline never states what policy changes would be needed to deliver the recommended centralized model.
items.rationaleB: Several recommendations are frankly system-level and give decision-makers something to act on: the centralization section and Table 1 specify what a BE expert centre must be (at least 10 new HGD/early-cancer treatment cases per expert endoscopist per year, defined training volumes, multidisciplinary meetings, access to esophageal surgery, prospective registration of all BE patients), and cost arguments are used as an explicit reason for the direction of several recommendations - screening is confined to a select population "in order to be acceptable and cost-effective", all-comer screening "would lead to substantial economic costs", WATS3D is rejected partly on cost-effectiveness, and routine post-EET four-quadrant biopsies are rejected because they "add to the costs and have a negative impact on the environmental footprint". No economic or budget-impact analysis was conducted for this guideline, and nothing is said about reimbursement, Cytosponge or ESD availability, or the very uneven distribution of expert centres across European systems. Health equity is absent: the guideline does not discuss access disparities, nor the equity implications of building "white ethnicity" into case-finding criteria, nor of the acknowledged 50%-60% of BE cases without GERD symptoms who "will be missed".

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of the guideline developers
items.rationaleA: Developer values are visible in the text through explicit first-person judgements: 'the Working Group favors its use' for chromoendoscopy despite the evidence being 'weak', 'the Working Group feels that it is essential to allocate at least 30 minutes', the decision 'to keep the previous surveillance intervals unchanged' in the absence of new data, and the framing judgement that age alone 'is crude and insufficient' for post-EET decisions - all disclosing a pragmatic, interventionist stance also stated up front as the aim to give 'a practical guide, even when supporting evidence is weak'. Conflict-of-interest disclosure is unusually detailed and directly material (a co-founder/shareholder of Cyted and the institution that developed the Cytosponge sit on the panel that issues a strong recommendation for Cytosponge in Rec 3). Yet nowhere are the panel's values described as such, no method for weighing benefits against harms is set out beyond Likert voting, no COI management or recusal procedure is reported, and disagreements between members are not characterised.
items.rationaleB: Conflict-of-interest reporting is thorough and unusually candid - Fitzgerald's co-founder shareholding in Cyted Ltd, di Pietro's note that "the Cytosponge was developed by his institution", and industry ties for most authors are disclosed - but AGREE-REX asks about declared values, and the guideline describes no COI management or recusal procedure even though Rec 3 gives Cytosponge a strong recommendation. A few developer values do surface explicitly in the text: the stated aim "to deliver a practical guide, even when supporting evidence is weak", "the Working Group favors its use" for chromoendoscopy despite acknowledging the evidence is weak, and "the guideline working group feels that age alone should not drive post-EET surveillance decisions". These are isolated assertions; there is no account of what values the panel brought to weighing cancer prevention against procedural harm and burden, and the only integration method reported is Likert voting, with no mechanism described for reconciling differing stakeholder perspectives or for surfacing minority positions.

items.text: The purpose of the recommendation is clear and actionable
items.rationaleA: The purpose is stated plainly - to 'optimize patient management according to the best scientific evidence, and to harmonize the diagnosis and care for patients with BE' and to 'deliver a practical guide' - and the recommendations track it: harmonized definitions of 'recurrence of BE' versus 'recurrence of dysplasia' (Rec 21) are justified precisely because they let risks 'be reliably communicated with patients' and standardise the literature, and the quality standards of Rec 5 target the documented practice gap in Seattle-protocol adherence. Anticipated impacts are described in places (fewer redundant repeat endoscopies, reduced carbon footprint, avoidance of unnecessary esophagectomy in high-risk T1b via watchful waiting). What is absent is any structured account of the expected impact of adoption on patients, endoscopy units or health systems - for instance the capacity consequences of mandating 30-40 minute surveillance slots and expert-center referral for all BE 10 cm or longer, LGD, HGD and early cancer.
items.rationaleB: The stated purpose - to "optimize patient management according to the best scientific evidence, and to harmonize the diagnosis and care for patients with BE" and to be a practical guide - is well served by the recommendations, most obviously Rec 21's standardized definitions of "recurrence of BE", "recurrence of dysplasia" and "recurrence of cancer", the fixed interval schedules in Recs 9 and 22, and the three management flowcharts (Figs 1-3). Anticipated impacts are stated at several points: quality standards are "key to minimizing the risk of undetected lesions and avoiding redundant repeat endoscopies" and will "help to reduce the carbon footprint", automated TFF3 reading is noted as "significantly reducing pathologist workload", and watchful waiting after ER "might select patients in need of invasive (surgical) treatment, while preventing unnecessary surgery in the majority". There is, however, no dedicated statement of implementation goals or of the organizational and system-level consequences of adopting centralization, and no plan for monitoring whether the harmonization goal is achieved.

items.text: The recommendation is feasible for local application and adoption
items.rationaleA: The strongest implementability content is the expert-center specification carried over in Table 1 and Section 9: an annual case load of at least 10 new treated patients per expert endoscopist, a minimum of 30 supervised endoscopic resections and 30 ablations to acquire competence, mandatory MDT discussion, access to esophageal surgery, and prospective registration of all BE patients in a database - these cover personnel competencies, training and the data infrastructure needed to monitor adoption. Local adaptation is differentiated (expert versus non-expert center behaviour for post-EET biopsies and for surveillance instead of ablation), the flowcharts function as practical adoption tools, and cross-reference is made to the ESGE upper-GI performance measures. However, the guideline runs no economic analysis of its own recommendations, offers no audit criteria or implementation indicators tied to these 22 statements, gives no strategies for overcoming the poor protocol adherence it repeatedly documents, and provides no guidance on adapting the centralization model to European systems with very different endoscopy capacity and access.
items.rationaleB: The guideline supplies more implementation substance than most: it names the change required from current practice by citing evidence that endoscopists "systematically undersample" long-segment BE and that dysplasia detection falls when the Seattle protocol is not followed; it quantifies resource needs (30 minutes per surveillance procedure, 40 for ultralong segments); it specifies personnel competencies and training volumes for expert centres; it cross-refers to the ESGE Performance Measures for upper GI endoscopy as the quality-metric framework; and it requires prospective registration of all BE patients in a database, which is the data infrastructure for monitoring. It also differentiates where local adaptation applies, telling centres without EET expertise to take neo-squamocolumnar junction quadrant biopsies that expert centres may omit. Missing are any dissemination or implementation strategy, any barriers-and-facilitators analysis, any de novo economic or budget-impact analysis (cost-effectiveness is only cited from third-party literature and is repeatedly described as "in doubt"), any audit criteria derived from these specific recommendations, and any guidance for the many European settings without an expert centre, ESD capability or access to the Cytosponge.

guidelineTitle: S1 guideline for imaging diagnostics for skin diseases
source: Journal of the German Society of Dermatology (JDDG)
recommendationText: The data generated by all imaging methods is ideal for the application of AI‐based algorithms to increase diagnostic accuracy and support experienced users.

pico.population: Patients with suspected skin tumors or inflammatory/infectious skin diseases
pico.intervention: AI-assisted image analysis of dermatologic imaging
pico.comparator: Expert clinician interpretation without AI support

items.appraisal: The guideline's intent is clear: provide an overview of imaging devices/techniques, explain how they work, and summarize current evidence, indications and limitations for dermatologic diagnosis. The health intent and broad target population are identifiable, but expected patient-health benefits are not articulated as explicitly as in a high-scoring conventional CPG.

No formal PICO/PICOS questions are presented. However, the document systematically addresses clinically recognizable questions concerning the use of RCM, ex-vivo RCM, OCT, LC-OCT, MPT, optoacoustic techniques and other modalities for different skin diseases. Population and diagnostic intervention are generally clear, but comparator/outcomes/study design are not systematically specified.

The guideline broadly concerns people with skin tumors and inflammatory, infectious and parasitic dermatoses. Numerous disease-specific populations appear throughout, and children/pregnant women are mentioned for some modalities, but there is no comprehensive target-population definition with age, clinical status, severity, comorbidity and inclusion/exclusion criteria.

The guideline has a sizeable expert group from multiple dermatology departments, private dermatology practice and biological/medical imaging institutions. However, participation is predominantly dermatology/imaging based, with no clearly documented broader multidisciplinary representation such as primary care, pathology, nursing, health economics or patient representatives.
I found no evidence in the uploaded short version that patients/public representatives participated in development or that patient values, experiences or preferences were systematically collected.

The intended use—guidance regarding techniques, indications, evidence and limitations—is clear. The users are inferable as dermatologists and clinicians using dermatologic imaging, but they are not explicitly and comprehensively defined as a target-user group.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: The authors explicitly state that the guideline is based on a systematic literature search, which is stronger than no search statement. However, the uploaded short version provides no databases, search dates, search terms or reproducible strategy. Under the supplied AGREE II anchor, this supports only a low score.

No study-level inclusion/exclusion criteria, eligible designs, populations, language restrictions or screening/selection process are reported in the uploaded article. These may be in the full guideline report, but I cannot credit unseen material.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of the body of evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: A major strength. Each imaging modality has explicit limitations and the guideline repeatedly distinguishes established evidence from preliminary or experimental evidence. For example, OCT evidence for many inflammatory/infectious diseases is described as limited and the indications as experimental. LC-OCT evidence for inflammatory disorders is likewise explicitly characterized as preliminary.

items.text: Methods for formulating recommendations clearly described
items.appraisal: The guideline states that recommendations arose from the consensus of the expert group. However, the short version does not report voting, consensus thresholds, Delphi methods, meeting procedures, disagreement resolution or consensus results.

items.text: Benefits, side effects and risks considered
items.appraisal: Benefits and limitations are discussed extensively: diagnostic accuracy, avoidance of unnecessary excisions, safety, measurement limitations, artifacts, patient tolerability, costs and technical constraints. For example, RCM is associated with improved specificity, fewer unnecessary excisions and reduced healthcare costs, while its penetration depth and acquisition characteristics are explicitly discussed as limitations.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and supporting evidence
items.appraisal: The narrative consistently places references adjacent to clinical conclusions and recommendation-like statements. However, the uploaded short version does not contain the complete evidence-to-recommendation overview; it explicitly says that this table is in the long version. Consequently, I cannot verify a clear link for every formal recommendation.
I found no report in the uploaded short version of an external expert-review process, named external reviewers, review methodology or modifications following review.

A concrete validity endpoint is given: the guideline is valid until 30 September 2029. This provides an identifiable time point for reassessment, but no surveillance procedure, responsible updating group or explicit evidence-trigger criteria are described in the short version.

Many clinical conclusions are reasonably specific—for example which techniques are suited to particular tumors, when methods remain experimental, training requirements and important technical limitations. However, in this short version these statements are often embedded in narrative text rather than consistently presented as formally worded recommendations.

Excellent. The guideline systematically distinguishes RCM, ex-vivo RCM, OCT, LC-OCT, MPT, optoacoustic imaging, multispectral analysis, Raman spectroscopy, MIS and LIPS according to resolution, penetration, measurement time, interpretation requirements, cost and indications. Table 1 provides a particularly useful side-by-side comparison.

Modality headings, indication sections, limitation sections and the comparison table make the clinical content navigable, but the short version lacks a prominent consolidated set of formal key recommendations. The authors state that the complete recommendations/statements overview is in the long version.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: Strong. Practical barriers are considered for individual technologies: required dermatopathology expertise and training, penetration depth, measurement duration, patient movement, lesion morphology, device accessibility, artifacts and equipment requirements. For RCM, for example, training, shallow penetration, small measurement field and the need for patients to remain still are explicitly discussed.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: Table 1 is a useful practical comparison tool, allowing clinicians to compare modalities by resolution, depth, acquisition time, interpretation requirements, cost and primary indication. The guideline also advises training for several modalities. However, there is no structured implementation algorithm, checklist, pathway or ready-to-use decision-support tool in the uploaded short version.

Resource implications are unusually visible. Table 1 gives approximate equipment costs—for example RCM €70,000–185,000, LC-OCT about €150,000, MPT €290,000–325,000, and MSOT €350,000–500,000—and identifies training requirements. MPT also explicitly carries high purchase and maintenance costs and requires a specialized room. However, there is no formal economic evaluation or explanation of how costs systematically altered recommendations.

I found no guideline-implementation quality indicators, adherence targets, audit frequency or defined monitoring framework. References to imaging used for disease/treatment monitoring concern patient assessment rather than auditing guideline implementation.

The short version states only that open-access funding was enabled and organized by Projekt DEAL. That concerns publication access, not necessarily guideline-development funding, and there is no explicit declaration that a guideline funder did not influence content. Under the strict supplied Item 22 anchor, this scores 1.

The article acknowledges that conflicts of interest exist as a reporting element and directs readers to the long version for them. However, the uploaded version neither reports the individual declarations nor describes how they were collected or managed. This meets only the lower “COI mentioned incompletely” anchor.

guidelineTitle: CAR/CSTR Practice Guideline on CT Screening for Lung Cancer
organization: Canadian Association of Radiologists (CAR) + Canadian Society of Thoracic Radiologists (CSTR)
recommendationText: Any use of Health Canada approved AI/CAD software for facilitation of workflow should be performed with radiologist oversight.

pico.population: High-risk individuals undergoing LDCT lung cancer screening
pico.intervention: AI-based pulmonary nodule detection and risk stratification systems
pico.outcomes: Diagnostic accuracy, number of interval follow-up LDCT exams, costs associated with follow-up of screen-detected lung nodules

items.appraisal: The objective, intended users and anticipated benefit are explicit. The update aims to support diagnostic-imaging departments in implementing organized lung-cancer screening using LDCT in appropriately selected high-risk individuals, with reduction of lung-cancer mortality as the principal health benefit.

The guideline clearly addresses the major foreground issues—who should be screened, screening interval/duration, LDCT technique, reporting, quality assurance, AI, personnel requirements and program organization—but these are not formulated as explicit PICO/PICOS questions. Population, intervention and outcomes are generally identifiable, but not systematically specified as formal health questions.

The target screening population is described in substantial detail. Eligibility generally includes age approximately 50–55 to 74–80 years, ≥20 years of daily smoking, current/former smoking status and a PLCOm2012 6-year risk threshold of 1.5–2%. Explicit exclusions include suspicious symptoms/nodules, major comorbidity limiting survival and inability to undergo CT.

Six authors from diagnostic/medical imaging departments across several Canadian institutions are identified. External review involved the Canadian Association of Medical Radiation Technologists, Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care and Canadian Partnership Against Cancer. However, the actual guideline-development group appears heavily radiology-focused rather than broadly multidisciplinary.

The guideline strongly endorses shared decision-making with potential screening participants, but I found no evidence that patients or members of the public participated in guideline development or that patient preferences were systematically elicited during development. Clinical shared decision-making is not equivalent to AGREE II stakeholder participation.

Exceptionally clear. The guideline explicitly identifies radiologists, medical radiation technologists and administrators working in diagnostic-imaging departments in Canada and explains that its purpose is to assist departments/clinics with organized screening implementation and individual screening requests.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: The authors state that they reviewed relevant literature and based recommendations on current literature and evidence-informed expert opinion, but no databases, search dates, search terms or reproducible search strategy are reported.

No formal study inclusion/exclusion criteria, eligible study designs, language restrictions or screening/selection process for the supporting literature are reported. The screening-program eligibility criteria described later concern patients, not evidence selection.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of the body of evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: The guideline is very transparent about uncertainty. It distinguishes robust RCT evidence from questions unlikely to receive adequately powered trials, discusses limitations of annual vs biennial evidence, uncertainty regarding AI, harms of screening and limitations of risk models. The lack of a formal certainty-of-evidence framework prevents 7.

items.text: Methods for formulating recommendations clearly described
items.appraisal: The document states that recommendations were based on the current literature and evidence-informed expert opinion. However, it does not report voting, Delphi methods, consensus thresholds, disagreement resolution or how the working group converted evidence into the final ten recommendations.

items.text: Benefits, side effects and risks considered
items.appraisal: Excellent. Benefits are weighed explicitly against radiation exposure, anxiety, false positives, invasive procedures, overdiagnosis, mortality related to work-up, competing mortality and resource burdens. The guideline emphasizes that the benefit–harm balance is narrow and optimized by limiting screening to high-risk individuals.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and supporting evidence
items.appraisal: Supporting trials, modeling studies and program data are discussed immediately before the corresponding recommendations. For example, screening frequency, eligibility thresholds, resource impacts and AI recommendations are accompanied by specific cited evidence. The link is strong, but there is no formal evidence-to-recommendation table or graded certainty/strength system.

CAR members reviewed earlier drafts, and three external organizations—CAMRT, CTFPHC and CPAC—are explicitly acknowledged for review and feedback. This is meaningful external review, but the review method, specific comments and resulting modifications are not described sufficiently for 6–7.

The authors explicitly state that lung-cancer screening is rapidly evolving and that the guide “will be revised as needed.” This establishes an intention to update but provides no interval, formal surveillance strategy or explicit general trigger criteria.
The ten summary recommendations are highly specific: they give risk thresholds, screening intervals, training requirements, reporting requirements, quality monitoring and AI oversight requirements.

The guideline compares organized vs opportunistic screening, annual vs biennial screening, different eligibility approaches, Lung-RADS vs PanCan protocols, CT technical options and AI-supported workflows. It also explains when screening should stop.

All ten recommendations are consolidated in Table 2, “Summary of CAR/CSTR Recommendations.” Appendix A separately provides the technical CT protocol and Appendix B the quality indicators, making essential guidance easy to identify.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: This is a major strength. The guideline discusses geographic, cultural, psychosocial, systemic and socioeconomic barriers; provincial CT capacity; workforce training; software requirements; equity; wait times; resource availability and health-system collaboration. It explicitly warns that failure to address barriers could worsen disparities.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: Excellent. It supplies a detailed CT screening protocol in Appendix A, standardized reporting advice, training requirements, accreditation/QA recommendations, Lung-RADS guidance and external implementation resources. It also points to an available structured screening-report example and an accredited CAR training program.

Costs and system capacity are considered directly. Ontario modeling across 576 scenarios found LDCT screening cost-effective and annual screening more cost-effective than biennial screening; real-world program data are used to examine effects on CT wait times. Eligibility thresholds are also explicitly linked to affordability and provincial CT capacity.

Outstanding. Recommendation 9 requires regular quality monitoring, indicator tracking and peer learning. Appendix B then provides explicit measurable indicators, including screening appropriateness, smoking-cessation documentation, adherence to annual follow-up, 6-month and 3-month surveillance compliance, diagnostic delay, invasive-procedure rates, PPV, mortality, cancer-detection rates, resection rate and stage distribution. Several indicators include explicit timing windows and measurement definitions.
The authors explicitly state that they received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication. Under the supplied AGREE II anchor, an explicit no-funding statement warrants 7.

The publication explicitly states that the authors declared no potential conflicts of interest concerning the research, authorship or publication. However, it does not describe how declarations were collected or how conflicts would have been managed. Under your strict anchor, reporting presence/absence alone does not warrant 5–7.

items.text: The evidence supporting the recommendation is applicable to the clinical question at hand
items.rationaleA: The 'Summary of Current Evidence', 'Harms and Limitations' and 'Overdiagnosis' sections give a substantive narrative account of magnitude of benefit and harm (NLST 20% and NELSON 24% lung cancer mortality reduction, NNS 320, 16 procedure-related deaths in the CT arm so that 'for every 4 lung cancer deaths prevented, one person died'), and some risk-of-bias/precision commentary (MILD 'likely underpowered', NELSON 'limited by a relatively low number of women enrolled'). However, no formal certainty-of-evidence system (GRADE or otherwise) is applied, no confidence intervals or publication-bias assessment appear, and none of the 10 recommendations in Table 2 carries a strength or certainty label. Evidence-to-recommendation links must be inferred from the preceding prose; the developers openly substitute 'evidence-informed expert opinion' where RCT data are lacking without saying which recommendations rest on it. Recommendation 1 ('All provinces and territories should implement an organized lung cancer screening program') is stated as definitively as Recommendation 7, despite resting on very different evidence.
items.rationaleB: The narrative 'Summary of Current Evidence', 'Harms and Limitations' and 'Overdiagnosis' sections give a genuinely substantive account of magnitude of benefit and harm (20% and 24% mortality reduction in NLST/NELSON, NNS 320, 16 deaths within 60 days of an invasive procedure, one radiation-induced cancer per 108 screen-detected cancers), and directness/precision limits are occasionally flagged ('MILD ... was likely underpowered', NELSON 'limited by a relatively low number of women'). However there is no systematic appraisal of risk of bias, no publication-bias or consistency assessment, and the developers openly rely on 'evidence-informed expert opinion' where RCT data are absent. Critically, the 10 statements in Table 2 carry no certainty-of-evidence rating, no strength label and no citations, so congruence between recommendation strength and evidence certainty cannot be judged and the evidence-to-recommendation link is only implicit (e.g. Recommendation 4 on annual versus biennial screening rests on acknowledged underpowered and 'forthcoming' data yet is stated with the same 'should' as Recommendation 1).

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target users it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The target users are named precisely in the Introduction ('radiologists, medical radiation technologists, and administrators working in diagnostic imaging departments in Canada'), and most recommendations sit squarely inside that scope of practice: accredited training and minimum reading volumes (Rec 6), standardized reporting and nodule classification (Rec 7), quality monitoring and peer learning (Rec 9), radiologist oversight of AI/CAD (Rec 10), plus the Appendix A acquisition protocol. The narrow benefit-harm trade-off is stated explicitly ('the harm benefit ratio of lung cancer screening is narrow and is optimized when screening is limited to those with a high risk'), and this aligns with the directive Rec 3 against enrolling ineligible people. Alignment is weaker for Rec 1 (a provincial policy action) and Rec 5 (shared decision-making by 'a health care professional with expertise in lung cancer screening'), which fall outside radiology practice and sit awkwardly against the guideline's own statement that it is 'not intended to... influence referring providers'.
items.rationaleB: Target users are named precisely in the Introduction ('radiologists, medical radiation technologists, and administrators working in diagnostic imaging departments in Canada'), and the recommendations sit squarely inside that scope: accredited training and minimum reading volumes (Rec 6), standardized reporting and nodule classification (Rec 7), quality monitoring and peer learning (Rec 9), radiologist oversight of AI/CAD (Rec 10), plus a fully specified CT protocol in Appendix A. The document explicitly disclaims any intent to 'replace evidence-based recommendations or influence referring providers', which keeps the actions aligned to radiology practice, and the narrow harm-benefit ratio is used directly to justify Recommendation 3 (not enrolling ineligible people) and the critique of opportunistic screening. Marks are lost because Recommendation 1 (provinces and territories should implement organized programs) lies outside the target users' scope of practice, and because every recommendation is worded with an undifferentiated 'should', giving no gradation of definitiveness even where the evidence is weak.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target patients/populations it is intended for
items.rationaleA: Patient-important outcomes drive the document: lung cancer and all-cause mortality, stage distribution and 5-year survival, anxiety and HRQoL (Pan-Canadian Early Detection study data showing no clinically significant HRQoL change but a minority with increased anxiety), procedural complications and 30-day mortality, and overdiagnosis. Tailoring is addressed for age and sex (higher radiation-induced damage in younger and female patients; greater NELSON benefit in women), comorbidity and life expectancy (stopping rules for 'metastatic cancer', 'advanced dementia'), risk level via PLCOm2012, and for First Nations and low-socioeconomic-status Canadians in the Equity section. What is missing is any account of how the importance of these outcomes to patients was determined — no patient survey, panel member or preference study is cited, so outcome selection is entirely developer-determined.
items.rationaleB: Outcomes addressed are patient-important and go well beyond test performance: lung-cancer and all-cause mortality, stage at diagnosis and 5-year survival, procedure-related death and complications, overdiagnosis, radiation-induced cancer, and explicitly anxiety and health-related quality of life (the Pan-Canadian HRQoL/anxiety analysis, reference 34). Tailoring is handled in several places: sex differences in NELSON benefit and in radiation susceptibility, age limits of 50-55 to 74-80, comorbidity-based stopping rules ('metastatic cancer', 'advanced dementia'), education and race within PLCOm2012, and the Equity section on First Nations and low-socioeconomic-status Canadians. What is missing is any statement of how the importance of these outcomes to patients was determined - no patient survey, rating exercise or patient representative is reported anywhere, so outcome selection rests on developer judgement.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target users
items.rationaleA: Target-user acceptability is addressed concretely: workflow and workload effects (Tammemägi data showing 'no impact on CT wait times at sites where lung cancer screening was implemented'), new competencies required (QUEST accredited training, double reading of the first 15 positive screens, minimum volumes with the note that 'test banks or CME courses can be used to augment volumes'), and infrastructure burden ('Lung-RADS requires only a standard PACS system' whereas PanCan 'requires either specialized software'). Clinical flexibility is deliberately signalled — a choice among Lung-RADS, LU-RADS and PanCan, and the acknowledgement that 'the number and minimum size of nodules to be reported may vary between institutions'. However, radiologists' values were not formally elicited; the only evidence of consultation is the Acknowledgments' thanks to 'CAR members who took the time to review and provide their feedback on earlier drafts' and to CAMRT, with no description of what that feedback changed.
items.rationaleB: Acceptability and workflow issues for radiologists and technologists are handled concretely: new skills and training burden (accredited QUEST training, minimum 300 chest CTs including 100 lung screens annually, double reading of the first 15 positive screens), reporting workflow (structured templates, the Ontario Health sample report), technology prerequisites ('Lung-RADS requires only a standard PACS system' whereas PanCan 'requires either specialized software'), and the system-level worry about CT wait times, which is answered with Tammemagi's finding of 'no impact on CT wait times'. The acceptable range of practice is described rather than dictated - Lung-RADS, LU-RADS and PanCan are all presented as legitimate options, and reporting thresholds 'may vary between institutions'. The Acknowledgments record review by CAR members and by CAMRT, but no systematic elicitation of target-user values (survey, Delphi, vote) is reported, and the guideline does not say which recommendations permit clinical flexibility and which do not.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target patients/populations
items.rationaleA: Recommendation 5 makes patient values central — screening 'should be a shared decision-making process between potential participants and a health care professional' including smoking cessation counselling — and the Harms section requires that anxiety, overdiagnosis, false positives and radiation 'should be communicated to patients', noting that 'Patients and providers may overestimate the benefits... and underestimate the harms'. Continuation of screening is explicitly left to 'the patient, their health care provider, and in some cases, the screening program', and cultural and psychosocial barriers to uptake are named. Against this, no patient, survivor, family or caregiver representative is identified anywhere in the working group or review list, no patient values or preference literature is cited, and — despite mandating shared decision-making — the guideline never mentions patient decision aids or any supporting tool, which is a clear omission at the recommendation level.
items.rationaleB: Recommendation 5 places patient values at the centre of the eligibility decision - screening 'should be a shared decision-making process between potential participants and a health care professional with expertise in lung cancer screening' with smoking-cessation counselling - and the harms section states that harms 'should be communicated to patients' and warns that 'patients and providers may overestimate the benefits ... and underestimate the harms'. Continuation of screening to the upper age limit is likewise left to 'the patient, their health care provider, and in some cases, the screening program'. Against this, no patient, family or caregiver input was sought at any point in the document, no patient decision aid is recommended or referenced despite shared decision-making being a formal recommendation, and burden and motivation factors for participants (travel, repeat annual scans, follow-up procedures) are only alluded to through the low real-world uptake figure rather than considered as preferences.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of policy/decision makers
items.rationaleA: The document is written with system decision-makers in view: Recommendation 1 is addressed to provinces and territories, Figure 1 maps current program status, and the 'Impact of Lung Cancer Screening on Health Systems' section confronts anticipated cost and wait-time concerns with Ontario modelling of 576 scenarios and real-world pilot metrics. Resource-constrained policy choices are explicitly linked to the recommendation itself — the 1.5%-2% PLCOm2012 threshold in Rec 2 is justified because a 2% risk 'has a cost effectiveness ratio of just under $50 000, which has been a threshold selected by several Canadian provinces as a balance of efficient detection of cancer and affordability', and thresholds 'may in part be dependent on the CT scanning capacity of the province'. A full Equity section covers socioeconomic, First Nations and race-based disparities and the contested race variable in PLCOm2012, warning that failure to act 'may result in lung screening programs that exacerbate disparities'. What is absent is any budget-impact or staffing analysis and any concrete statement of which policy or funding changes provinces should make; the rich equity analysis shrinks to the single phrase 'in a timely and equitable manner' in Rec 1.
items.rationaleB: This is the guideline's strongest values dimension. Recommendation 1 is an explicit policy statement to provinces and territories, and the 'Impact of Lung Cancer Screening on Health Systems' section engages directly with decision-maker concerns about cost and wait times, citing the Ontario microsimulation of 576 scenarios and the roughly $50,000 cost-effectiveness ratio at a 2% PLCOm2012 threshold 'selected by several Canadian provinces as a balance of efficient detection of cancer and affordability to the health care system'. Equity is treated at length and with candour - socioeconomic gradients, First Nations survival disparities, the contested use of race in PLCOm2012 (some provinces 'use the PLCOm2012 risk model without race'), and the warning that failure to address barriers 'may result in lung screening programs that exacerbate disparities'. Policy-relevant infrastructure is named (CAR accreditation, provincial quality programs, the CPAC quality indicators in Appendix B), and CPAC and the CTFPHC reviewed the draft; the gap is that decision-makers' needs were not formally elicited and no costing is offered at the level of an individual imaging department.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of the guideline developers
items.rationaleA: Beyond the bare 'The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest' and the funding statement, the guideline says almost nothing about the values the six-author working group brought to the recommendations. There is one implicit value declaration in the Introduction — 'Rather than avoid assessing practices for which there is no or limited RCT evidence, we have reviewed the relevant literature to provide rationale for decisions' and reliance on 'evidence-informed expert opinion' — but it is never developed into an account of how the group weighed mortality benefit against radiation, overdiagnosis and procedural death. No consensus method, voting rule, or mechanism for reconciling the differing perspectives of CAR members, CAMRT, CTFPHC and CPAC reviewers is described, so the reader cannot tell whose judgement produced statements such as 'the harm benefit ratio... is narrow'.
items.rationaleB: The developers do declare one methodological value openly - 'Rather than avoid assessing practices for which there is no or limited RCT evidence, we have reviewed the relevant literature to provide rationale for decisions' - and a professional one, that 'radiologists take responsibility for appropriate use of health care resources', which visibly drives Recommendation 3 and the anti-opportunistic-screening stance. Beyond that the item is essentially unaddressed: the Working Group's composition, disciplines and the method for reaching agreement (consensus, voting, handling of dissent) are never described, and there is no account of how developer values shaped the interpretation of the benefit-harm trade-off, for instance in choosing a 1.5%-2% risk threshold or endorsing screening past three rounds against the CTFPHC position. The 'declared no potential conflicts of interest' and no-funding statements are relevant but, on their own, do not meet this item.

items.text: The purpose of the recommendation is clear and actionable
items.rationaleA: The implementation goal is stated plainly — the guide 'aims to assist diagnostic imaging departments and clinics in implementing organized lung cancer screening programs and addressing individual requests for screening' — and Recommendations 6-10 plus Appendices A and B map directly onto that operational purpose. Anticipated impacts on individuals (mortality reduction, earlier-stage diagnosis, anxiety, procedural harm) and on systems (cost-effectiveness, negligible wait-time effect, low real-world uptake) are described with data. The weakness is an internal inconsistency of purpose: the guideline disclaims any intent to 'replace evidence-based recommendations or influence referring providers', yet Rec 1 is an advocacy statement aimed at provinces and Rec 5 assigns work to referring clinicians, and no anticipated organizational impact (staffing, navigator roles, capacity) of adopting Rec 1 is quantified.
items.rationaleB: The implementation goal is stated plainly in the Introduction - to 'assist diagnostic imaging departments and clinics in implementing organized lung cancer screening programs and addressing individual requests for screening' - with explicit scope limits (post-diagnosis management excluded, referring providers not targeted), and the ten recommendations map cleanly onto that goal, mixing advocacy (Rec 1), practice standardization (Rec 6, 7, 10) and quality/system change (Rec 8, 9). Anticipated impacts are described at all three levels: for individuals (mortality reduction, stage shift, anxiety and procedural harm), for organizations (training volumes, accreditation, multidisciplinary team access, AI oversight) and for systems (cost-effectiveness, wait times, equity of access). It falls short of the top of the scale only in that no anticipated magnitude of change is attached to adopting the specific recommendations, and the Conclusion frames several key issues (biennial screening, equitable access) as unresolved 'areas of investigation' without a research agenda or update timetable beyond 'this guide will be revised as needed'.

items.text: The recommendation is feasible for local application and adoption
items.rationaleA: This is the guideline's strongest dimension. Appendix A gives an operational CT protocol with both minimum and preferred parameters (>=16 vs >=64 detector rows, CTDIvol <=3.0 mGy minimum and <=1.5 mGy recommended, slice reconstruction <=1.25 mm), Appendix B supplies two complete sets of implementation and quality-monitoring metrics (6 National Lung Cancer Roundtable and 10 Canadian Working Group indicators covering early reassessment rate, PPV, 30-day mortality, non-malignant resection rate and stage distribution), and personnel competencies are specified with named accredited training (CAR LSAP, QUEST) and reading volumes. Local adaptation is explicitly anticipated — 'provinces and regions may have varying resources for lung cancer screening and may need to adjust their practices accordingly' — with alternative reporting systems whose differing software and cost implications are laid out, cost-effectiveness thresholds, and a pointer to a sample structured report from Ontario Health. Gaps remain: no dissemination plan, no costing of program start-up or non-radiologist staffing, and no explicit strategies for overcoming provider or patient acceptability barriers despite naming 'geographic, cultural, psychosocial, and systemic barriers to screening'.
items.rationaleB: The guideline is unusually well equipped for local adoption: Appendix A gives a parameter-by-parameter CT protocol with minimum and preferred values (>=16 versus >=64 detector rows, slice reconstruction <=1.25 mm, CTDIvol <=3.0 mGy minimum and <=1.5 mGy preferred), Appendix B lists 16 quality indicators from the National Lung Cancer Roundtable and the CPAC working group for monitoring adoption, and named training and accreditation routes (QUEST, CAR LSAP), a sample structured report from Cancer Care Ontario, and a defined minimum report content set are all provided. Local adaptation is explicitly flagged - 'provinces and regions may have varying resources ... and may need to adjust their practices accordingly', risk thresholds 'may in part be dependent on the CT scanning capacity of the province', and Lung-RADS training is recommended specifically 'in regions where there is no established provincial program'. Cost and cost-effectiveness are cited at the program level. What is absent is any explicit characterization of the size of the gap between current and recommended practice, a dissemination strategy, and concrete tactics for overcoming the acceptability and access barriers the Equity section itself identifies as decisive.

guidelineTitle: JCS/JHRS 2022 Guideline on Diagnosis and Risk Assessment of Arrhythmia
organization: Japanese Circulation Society (JCS) & Japanese Heart Rhythm Society (JHRS)
recommendationText: Auxiliary use of an AF diagnosis function using an AI algorithm may be considered

pico.population: Patients with suspected or confirmed arrhythmias

items.appraisal: The objectives are very clear: proper diagnosis and risk assessment of arrhythmia, improvement of symptoms/QOL/prognosis, and prevention of sudden cardiac death. The guideline explicitly states that it focuses on the diagnosis component of arrhythmia care and aims to provide a comprehensive diagnostic/risk-assessment guide.

The guideline is organized around clinically specific diagnostic problems—e.g., which diagnostic tests should be used for particular arrhythmias, syncope, genetic disorders and risk assessment—but it does not formulate a formal set of PICO/PICOS questions. Population, diagnostic intervention and outcome are often inferable, but not systematically specified for each foreground question.

The guideline covers patients undergoing diagnosis/risk assessment for suspected or established arrhythmias and related disorders, with many sections defining disease-specific subgroups. However, there is no overarching population section with comprehensive age, disease-severity, comorbidity and inclusion/exclusion criteria.

The development group is extensively identified by name, institution and role. It includes cardiologists/arrhythmia experts, clinical laboratory/genetics expertise, intensive-care expertise and pediatric cardiology in the Independent Assessment Committee. However, the core working group remains predominantly cardiovascular/arrhythmia specialists rather than a broadly multidisciplinary panel including primary care, nursing, patient representatives or allied health.

I found no evidence that patients, caregivers or the public participated in guideline development or that their views were systematically collected. Patient consent/preferences are discussed in specific areas such as genetic testing, but that is clinical care rather than stakeholder involvement in guideline development.

The intended users and intended use are explicit. The guideline is designed not only for arrhythmia specialists but also for general clinicians and physicians involved in medical checkups, and it explains how the guideline should support diagnostic testing and risk assessment in routine practice.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: The guideline states that evidence-based materials from Europe/USA, Japanese research and previous related guidelines were examined, but it does not report databases, search dates, search terms or a reproducible systematic-search strategy. The very large bibliography demonstrates extensive evidence use but does not itself satisfy AGREE II systematic-search reporting.
I found no explicit study inclusion/exclusion criteria, screening process, eligible study designs, language criteria or PICO-based evidence-selection rules.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of the body of evidence clearly stated

items.text: Methods for formulating recommendations clearly described

This describes the broad method but not a fully transparent consensus/voting process, disagreement resolution method or recommendation-by-recommendation voting results.

items.text: Benefits, side effects and risks considered

Excellent. Numerous dedicated recommendation tables show COR/LOE, and the guideline contains many diagnostic algorithms and flowcharts. The syncope pathway, for example, visually moves from initial assessment to risk stratification, targeted testing and treatment.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice

guidelineTitle: Singapore tuberculosis (TB) clinical management guidelines 2024: A modified Delphi adaptation of international guidelines for drug-susceptible TB infection and pulmonary disease
source: Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore
recommendationText:
The panel recognises that a number of automated CAD-AI products have been certified by the Health Sciences Authority, Singapore and more are expected in the future. Some products have been deployed in other countries for chest X-ray screening for TB disease in various settings. While multiple studies have demonstrated comparable diagnostic performance (relative to a human radiologist) for the detection of chest X-ray changes associated with pulmonary TB, such findings will have to be validated within the local practice setting in Singapore. At present, deployment of CAD-AI products will require a human-in-the-loop, where a certified radiologist is still needed to provide a final read. In addition, due consideration must be given to the fact that current products have narrow capabilities, with potential to miss other non-specified abnormalities on a chest X-ray. (De novo)
The panel also recommended vigilance in this rapidly evolving field and timely updates of major developments. (De novo)

items.appraisal: The objective is explicit: provide healthcare professionals in Singapore with evidence-based, locally contextualised best practices for screening, diagnosis and treatment of adults and children with drug-susceptible TB infection and pulmonary disease. The intended benefit is standardisation/improvement of TB management and contribution to TB elimination.

Excellent. The guideline addresses 25 explicit clinical questions, covering screening, diagnosis, treatment selection, monitoring and follow-up. Questions are directly stated throughout—for example, indications for screening, diagnostic tests, regimens and monitoring.

The target population is clearly delineated as adults and children with drug-susceptible TB infection or pulmonary TB disease in Singapore. Extrapulmonary TB and drug-resistant TB are explicitly excluded, and numerous recommendations identify specific populations such as PLHIV, children, pregnant women and immunocompromised patients.

Strongly multidisciplinary. The panel includes infectious-disease specialists, pediatricians, respiratory physicians, diagnostic radiologists, laboratory medicine/microbiology specialists, primary-care physicians and public-health professionals, supported by a Public Health Translational Team. Affiliations and roles are extensively reported.

Patient preferences and values are explicitly incorporated into clinical recommendations—for example, TB preventive treatment is to be decided jointly with patients/legal guardians considering benefits, risks, preferences and values. However, I found no evidence that people with TB or patient representatives participated directly in guideline development or that patient views were systematically collected for this guideline.

The target users are explicitly healthcare professionals in Singapore, and the intended use—screening, diagnosis and treatment of drug-susceptible TB—is clearly stated. The guideline additionally identifies the National TB Programme as the principal implementation body.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: The developers systematically reviewed major English-language national and international TB guidelines published between 1 January 2016 and 5 March 2023, then performed additional targeted primary-literature searches for newer areas such as CAD-AI, NGS and VOT. This is clearly systematic at the guideline-selection level, but the uploaded article does not provide a fully reproducible database-by-database primary search string, preventing 6–7 under the supplied scoring anchor.

Eligibility for source guidelines is reasonably clear: major national/international TB management guidelines, English language, 2016–March 2023. The source guidelines are listed individually. However, detailed study-level inclusion/exclusion criteria for the supplementary targeted primary-literature reviews are not comprehensively reported in the uploaded article.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of the evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: Evidence limitations and inconsistencies are repeatedly made explicit. Examples include weak evidence regarding sequential IGRA/TST testing, insufficient data on rifapentine in pregnancy, uncertainty around treatment extension and the need for local validation of CAD-AI. The source guidelines were also formally appraised with a modified AGREE II instrument.

items.text: Methods for formulating recommendations clearly described
items.appraisal: Excellent. A 2-round modified Delphi was used, with consensus defined as agreement or no objections from any panel member. Recommendations are explicitly labelled Adopted, Adapted or De novo.

items.text: Benefits, side effects and risks considered
items.appraisal: Benefits and harms are explicitly balanced throughout. Treatment decisions consider hepatotoxicity, adherence, drug interactions, adverse events, patient burden and clinical benefit. Patient preferences are also incorporated. The guideline specifically states that decisions should consider benefits, risks, preferences and values.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and supporting evidence
items.appraisal: Strong linkage. Recommendations are followed by detailed “Remarks” sections explaining the supporting guidelines, studies and rationale. Recommendations are also identified as adopted, adapted or de novo, making their evidentiary origin transparent.

Drafts were circulated to several external Singapore stakeholder bodies, including the Academy of Medicine chapters for family medicine, pediatrics, infectious diseases and respiratory medicine. The Ministry of Health's Agency for Care Effectiveness provided a separate methodology review, and relevant changes were incorporated.

A concrete update is scheduled: the National TB Programme will convene a multidisciplinary team in 2026 to conduct a new systematic review of available guidelines and evidence. The guideline additionally calls for timely updates in rapidly changing fields such as CAD-AI. A more comprehensive general trigger/criteria framework would be needed for 7.

Excellent specificity. Recommendations clearly identify populations, interventions, doses, durations, thresholds and clinical circumstances. For example, adult TB-infection regimens distinguish 4R, 6H/9H, 3HR, 3HP and 1HP and specify which are preferred or alternatives.

Preferred and alternative diagnostic/treatment approaches are systematically compared, with explicit criteria for different age groups, risk groups and clinical circumstances. The guideline also clearly indicates situations in which an option is not recommended.

Each clinical question has a prominently labelled Recommendation(s) section followed by explanatory remarks. Tables summarize screening indications and treatment regimens, making core recommendations straightforward to locate.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: Implementation factors are considered extensively and locally. Examples include drug availability, cost, adherence barriers, resource constraints, acceptability of DOT/VOT, patient autonomy, laboratory availability, CAD-AI validation and system infrastructure. Table 4 explicitly identifies education, financial/transport support, healthcare-worker training, integration with other care and observed treatment as implementation enablers.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: The guideline provides numerous practical tools: regimen tables, screening tables, management of treatment interruptions, detailed appendices, recommendations for PLHIV, CAD-AI information and a dedicated appendix on enablers for treatment adherence. These are highly implementation-oriented, though not packaged as a single formal implementation toolkit.

Resource and cost implications are repeatedly integrated into recommendations. For example, a shorter rifapentine regimen has higher drug cost but this is expected to be offset by reduced treatment duration for patients and the National TB Programme. Screening cost-effectiveness, test costs, drug availability and resource constraints are also considered.

The guideline contains detailed clinical monitoring instructions for TB therapy, but AGREE II Item 21 concerns monitoring/auditing of guideline implementation. I found no comprehensive implementation-performance indicators, target adherence thresholds or specified audit frequency. Therefore clinical follow-up recommendations should not be mistaken for formal guideline audit criteria.

The guideline explicitly states that the work was funded by the Ministry of Health Singapore. However, there is no explicit statement that the Ministry had no influence on the guideline content or recommendations. Under your strict Item 22 anchor, government/nonprofit funding without a no-influence statement supports approximately 5–6, so I assign 5.

COIs are explicitly reported: one panel member received speaking fees from Qiagen, conference sponsorship from MSD and a grant from Institut Mérieux; the other panel members report no potential conflicts. However, the publication does not comprehensively explain how declared conflicts were collected and managed during recommendation development, preventing 7.
