items.text: The evidence supporting the recommendation is applicable to the clinical question at hand
items.rationaleA: The Remarks under most of the 25 questions do engage with the evidence in a substantive way: directness and precision are named (T-SPOT.TB may be more sensitive "albeit with wide confidence intervals in meta-analyses"; 1HP rests on "a single randomised clinical trial in PLHIV living in a high TB prevalence region"), magnitude is quantified (third sputum sample yields "2-3% on average"; nasopharyngeal aspirate NAAT sensitivity "approximately 46% versus 73% in gastric aspirate"; pyrazinamide >15% of interruption-causing adverse events in the elderly), and consistency across the 15 source guidelines in Table 1 is tabulated. What is missing is any formal certainty-of-evidence rating or strength-of-recommendation label: the (Adopted)/(Adapted)/(De novo) tags describe provenance, not confidence, no GRADE or equivalent is applied, risk of bias and publication bias are never addressed, and no evidence profile is attached to any individual recommendation. Congruence also fails in at least one place - Question 20 says the Panel "strongly recommended" extending treatment to 9 months while the same Remarks concede "current evidence does not suggest this results in lower relapse rates" and that WHO recommends against it. Coverage of primary literature was also only a "targeted search approach" limited to CAD-AI, NGS and VOT.
items.rationaleB: The Remarks under many questions do engage with substance of evidence - nasopharyngeal aspirate NAAT sensitivity of "approximately 46% versus 73% in gastric aspirate" (Q13), the "marginal additional diagnostic yield for a third sample (2-3% on average)" used to set the 2-sample minimum (Q14), pyrazinamide accounting for ">15%" of treatment-limiting adverse events in the elderly (Q18), and non-inferiority results from TBTC Study 31 and SHINE - and the panel occasionally names imprecision explicitly ("albeit with wide confidence intervals in meta-analyses" for T-SPOT.TB, Q3). But no recommendation carries a certainty-of-evidence rating or a strength grade; the (Adopted)/(Adapted)/(De novo) labels describe provenance from source guidelines, not evidential support. Risk of bias of primary studies, consistency, publication bias and confounding are never addressed, and the only source-quality appraisal is a "modified AGREE II" assessment of the parent guidelines relegated to Appendix S1. Congruence between certainty and definitiveness is therefore untestable at recommendation level: Q20 uses "strongly recommended" for treatment extension while the same Remarks concede "current evidence does not suggest this results in lower relapse rates" and that WHO advises against it.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target users it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The target users ("healthcare professionals in Singapore") and the boundary of their remit are clearly set: extrapulmonary and drug-resistant TB are excluded, with an explicit referral rule that "All persons with rifampicin- or multidrug-resistant TB should be referred to the TB Control Unit (TBCU) at Tan Tock Seng Hospital", and special populations are to be managed "by or in close consultation with the relevant clinical specialists". Recommended actions sit squarely within the users' scope of practice and are operationally specific - which test at which age (Q3, Q4), sample types and minimum sample number (Q13, Q14), weight-based dosing in Tables 3 and 5, follow-up intervals (Q10, Q23), and an interruption algorithm in Table 6. The main weakness is definitiveness: with no strength grading, many statements are permissively hedged ("Re-treatment of individuals re-exposed to infectious TB can be considered", Q11; "CT thorax may be considered", Q15) so users cannot tell where the harm-benefit trade-off is close versus clear-cut, and three regimen recommendations (3HP, 1HP, 2HPMZ/2HPM) are contingent on rifapentine that is "not available in Singapore at the time of writing".
items.rationaleB: Scope is explicit about users and boundaries - "providing healthcare professionals in Singapore with evidence-based and contextualised best practices", with extrapulmonary and drug-resistant TB excluded and an unambiguous referral pathway ("All persons with rifampicin- or multidrug-resistant TB should be referred to the TB Control Unit (TBCU) at Tan Tock Seng Hospital"). Recommendations are operationally specific and matched to Singapore's practice reality: mg/kg dosing in Tables 3 and 5, sample numbers and timing, follow-up intervals of 2-4 and 4-6 weeks, and explicit local contextualisation (NAAT widely available so AFB smear was debated; WGS "primarily used for public health surveillance"; tNGS assays "none are available in Singapore"). Weaknesses: the guideline never differentiates what a polyclinic family physician, a radiologist and a TBCU specialist should each do, several recommendations are conditional on a drug that does not exist locally ("should rifapentine become available in Singapore", Q6, Q7, Q18, Q19), and the absence of any strength grading leaves definitiveness signalled only by verb choice ("can be", "may be considered", "should").

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target patients/populations it is intended for
items.rationaleA: Patient-important outcomes are visible throughout and are quantified locally - "treatment completion, relapse and case fatality rates are 65%, 6.1% and 0.4%, respectively, in 2020" - alongside harms that patients feel (hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, ethambutol ocular toxicity, "lengthy duration, pill burden and side effects") and post-TB lung disease as a late outcome (Q25). Tailoring is a genuine strength: recommendations are stratified by paediatric age band (infants <6 months, 6 months to <2 years, 2-5 years with/without BCG, >=5 years), PLHIV and CD4 count, pregnancy and breastfeeding, age >70 years for pyrazinamide, and immunocompromising conditions in Table 2. The gap is provenance of outcome importance: nowhere does the guideline report how outcomes were prioritised from the patient's standpoint, and no patients, families or caregivers took part in the panel or the 2-round Delphi - the weighting of, for example, shorter duration against a single-trial evidence base was made by clinicians alone.
items.rationaleB: Outcomes that matter to patients recur throughout - treatment completion, relapse, hepatotoxicity, isoniazid peripheral neuropathy (driving universal pyridoxine), ethambutol ocular toxicity, and a whole question (Q25) devoted to post-TB lung disease as "under-recognised but contribute[ing] significantly to excess morbidity and mortality". Tailoring is a genuine strength: age-banded paediatric testing (IGRA at >=5 years, TST at 6 months to <2 years, Q4), regimen tables split by adults/PLHIV/children, pyrazinamide avoidance above 70 years, exclusions for pregnant and breastfeeding women, and non-severe childhood disease qualifying for 2HRZ(E)/2HR. What is missing is any account of how the importance of these outcomes to patients was established - no patient or caregiver representative appears among the Panel or the stakeholder bodies consulted (all professional colleges), and patient-relevant groups named in the text such as "the homeless, prisoners" and migrants from high-burden countries are explicitly pushed out of scope.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target users
items.rationaleA: Clinician values were structurally sought - a 21-member multidisciplinary panel spanning infectious diseases, respiratory, paediatrics, radiology, microbiology and polyclinic family medicine reached consensus defined as "agreement or no objections from any Panel member", and drafts went to the Academy of Medicine chapters and colleges with "relevant changes incorporated". Acceptability and workflow reasoning is explicit and repeatedly decisive: IGRA is preferred "despite higher test costs" because of "their ease of testing and convenience"; stool NAAT is rejected because of "familiarity of obtaining induced sputum or gastric fluid samples at present coupled with additional laboratory processing steps for stool"; pyridoxine is given to all adults "to simplify implementation"; AFB smear is retained "since these results still guide contact tracing operations"; CAD-AI is bounded by a "human-in-the-loop" requirement. Flexibility is differentiated in places (paediatric specialist consultation for the shortened 2HRZ(E)/2HR regimen; visual assessments "at the discretion of the treating specialist"), but no formal survey of users was undertaken, dissent within "majority opinion" positions is unquantified, and the acceptable range of alternative actions is not described.
items.rationaleB: Clinician acceptability visibly shapes recommendations: IGRAs are preferred "despite higher test costs... in view of their ease of testing and convenience" (Q3); TST is retained in young children because "phlebotomy is challenging" (Q4); stool NAAT is rejected "in view of the familiarity of obtaining induced sputum or gastric fluid samples at present coupled with additional laboratory processing steps" (Q13); AFB smear is kept because "these results still guide contact tracing operations" (Q12); and pyridoxine is given to all adults "to simplify implementation" (Q6). The 21-member Panel spans family medicine, polyclinics, paediatrics, radiology, microbiology, ID and respiratory medicine, and a draft went to Academy of Medicine chapters for review, so a range of practitioner views was structurally represented. Flexibility is signalled but only loosely - "These guidelines are not intended to replace the clinical judgment of the healthcare practitioner" and visual assessments left "at the discretion of the treating specialist" - and no systematic elicitation of target users' values (survey, focus group, formal acceptability assessment) is reported.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target patients/populations
items.rationaleA: Patient values are named as a decision input - "The decision to start TB infection treatment should be made jointly between the individual or his/her legal guardian, and the physician, taking into consideration the benefits and risks of treatment as well as the individual's preferences and values" - and burden/acceptability drive several recommendations: self-administered TB infection treatment is the default because "Enforcing observed treatment for TB infection can pose a significant barrier for treatment"; VOT is endorsed as "patient autonomy-enabling"; Q21 states "the least restrictive and effective interventions should be applied, with patients meaningfully involved in treatment-related decisions". Table 4 operationalises this with treatment literacy, counselling, and "food, financial and transport subsidies", and the text calls for support to be "developed in collaboration with persons with TB disease", while acknowledging the tension of "Balancing patient rights/choices with public health and safety". However, no patient, family or community representative sat on the panel or the stakeholder review list, patient preferences were never empirically elicited, and the guideline nowhere states that decision aids or patient tools would be beneficial or where choice should weigh most heavily.
items.rationaleB: There are real, load-bearing statements: TB infection treatment "should be made jointly between the individual or his/her legal guardian, and the physician, taking into consideration the benefits and risks of treatment as well as the individual's preferences and values"; "Enforcing observed treatment for TB infection can pose a significant barrier for treatment" (Q8); VOT is framed as "cost-effective and patient autonomy-enabling"; and Q21 concludes that "the least restrictive and effective interventions should be applied, with patients meaningfully involved in treatment-related decisions". Table 4 operationalises burden and motivation through enablers - treatment literacy, counselling, "food, financial and transport subsidies" - and the text calls for adherence interventions "developed in collaboration with persons with TB disease". However no patients, former patients, families or advocacy groups were on the Panel or in the stakeholder consultation, nothing describes how patient values were actually sought, no decision aid or patient-facing tool is offered or even recommended, and the balance between individual rights and compulsory public-health measures is asserted rather than resolved.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of policy/decision makers
items.rationaleA: Decision-maker needs are structurally embedded: the update was "commissioned" by the National TB Programme, funded by the Ministry of Health, and reviewed for methodology by the Agency for Care Effectiveness, and the Implementation Considerations section assigns delivery to the National TB Programme and TBCU including "sourcing for rifapentine through the Global Drug Facility" - a concrete procurement action. Resource and system reasoning appears in the recommendations themselves: systematic screening of people with diabetes, substance use and elderly in long-term care was rejected because it "might not be cost-effective in Singapore"; the higher cost of rifapentine "will likely be offset by the shorter duration of treatment for both the individual and the national programme"; WGS is endorsed partly because "the output can also be used for national TB surveillance" and could "eliminate the requirement for phenotypic testing". Against this, no formal economic evaluation or budget impact analysis is presented, health equity is never treated as an explicit consideration, and the populations where equity most bites - "migrants from high TB burden countries, prisoners and healthcare workers" - are deliberately placed out of scope.
items.rationaleB: This is written from within the health system: the update was "commissioned" by the National TB Programme, funded by MOH, methodologically reviewed by the Agency for Care Effectiveness, and "will largely be implemented by the National TB Programme team". Resource and system-level reasoning is explicit in several recommendations - systematic screening of people with diabetes, substance use and elderly in long-term care was rejected because it "might not be cost-effective in Singapore"; rifapentine's "higher cost of the drug regimen will likely be offset by the shorter duration of treatment for both the individual and the national programme"; routine WGS "could eliminate the requirement for phenotypic testing" and its output "can also be used for national TB surveillance"; CAD-AI is tied to Health Sciences Authority certification. Local programme performance data (treatment completion 65%, relapse 6.1%, case fatality 0.4% in 2020) grounds the policy case. Health equity is the clear gap: migrants from high-burden countries, prisoners and healthcare workers are named only to be declared out of scope ("will not be further discussed here"), and no formal economic analysis or costed policy change is presented.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of the guideline developers
items.rationaleA: The Panel's value positions are frequently made visible at the point of decision - precaution ("As a precautionary measure, the Panel elected to adopt WHO's recommendation" on re-exposure), deference to existing local practice (pyrazinamide avoided from age >70 "based on existing practice in Singapore" among proposed thresholds of >65 to >80), simplicity of implementation (universal pyridoxine), and conservatism in the face of weak data ("In view of the weak evidence, the Panel chose not to recommend sequential or parallel IGRA/TST testing... despite such recommendations in several guidelines"). Conflicts of interest are disclosed for one author and denied for the rest. But the item asks for more than this: nowhere does the guideline state up front what values the developers brought, how benefits were weighed against harms as a matter of declared principle, or by what method divergent views were integrated - "majority opinion" and "majority consensus" are invoked (e.g. on screening in diabetes and the >=15 mg prednisolone/>8 week steroid threshold) without reporting the split, the voting rule, or how minority positions were resolved beyond "no objections".
items.rationaleB: The panel's own reasoning is unusually visible at the level of individual decisions - "the majority opinion of the Panel was that systematic TB screening... might not be cost-effective", "the Panel's majority consensus in the absence of clear evidence was a corticosteroid dose of >=15 mg prednisolone equivalent", "As a precautionary measure, the Panel elected to adopt WHO's recommendation" (Q11), and the >70-year pyrazinamide threshold set "based on existing practice in Singapore" - which makes the underlying values (precaution, alignment with international norms, implementation simplicity, deference to established local practice) inferable. But those values are never declared up front, and the integration method is thin: consensus is defined only as "agreement or no objections from any Panel member", with no voting thresholds, no record of dissent, and no procedure for reconciling differing stakeholder perspectives beyond circulating a draft. Conflict-of-interest reporting is minimal and one disclosure is directly germane - a Panel author "received speaking fees from Qiagen", manufacturer of the QuantiFERON assay discussed in Q3 - with no management or recusal described.

items.text: The purpose of the recommendation is clear and actionable
items.rationaleA: The implementation goal is stated plainly - to provide "evidence-based and contextualised best practices" and, in the Clinical Impact box, "to standardise and improve the clinical management of TB infection and disease in Singapore, contributing to the global goal of TB elimination" - and the 25 recommendations map cleanly onto that scope of screening, diagnosis, regimen selection, monitoring and follow-up, with nothing recommended that falls outside it. Anticipated impacts are described for several specific recommendations: shorter regimens "aiming to increase adherence and expedite completion", VOT as "a cost-effective and patient autonomy-enabling alternative to DOT", routine WGS potentially eliminating phenotypic drug susceptibility testing, and CAD-AI needing local validation before deployment. What is not described is the aggregate anticipated impact on organisations and systems - no expected change in the 65% completion rate or the 6.1% relapse rate is projected, and no estimate is given of the laboratory, radiology or clinic workload consequences of moving to IGRA-first testing, two-sample collection or expanded follow-up.
items.rationaleB: The implementation goal is stated plainly in the Clinical Impact box - "to standardise and improve the clinical management of TB infection and disease in Singapore, contributing to the global goal of TB elimination" - and the 25 recommendations map onto it coherently, covering the full pathway from screening through diagnosis, regimen selection, monitoring and post-treatment evaluation. Anticipated impacts are described for several specific recommendations: shorter and less frequent regimens "aiming to increase adherence and expedite completion", VOT as an equivalent but less restrictive alternative to DOT, and WGS potentially removing phenotypic DST for pan-sensitive isolates. What is absent is any quantified expectation of what adoption should achieve - given that the guideline itself reports a 65% treatment completion rate, no target, indicator or anticipated organisational burden is attached to the recommendations.

items.text: The recommendation is feasible for local application and adoption
items.rationaleA: This is the weakest dimension. The entire "IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS" section is a single paragraph that names the implementing bodies (National TB Programme, TBCU at Tan Tock Seng Hospital), mentions "their dissemination and education of TB care providers" without saying how, and flags rifapentine sourcing; the only other implementation content is a two-line scheduled review in 2026. The type and degree of change from current practice must be inferred from the "What is New" box rather than being set out recommendation by recommendation, and several recommendations are unimplementable as written until a drug arrives. There are no audit criteria or quality indicators, no monitoring data requirements, no cost or budget figures, no economic analysis, no statement of personnel competencies or training needed for IGRA, WGS or CAD-AI deployment, no strategies for overcoming provider or patient acceptability barriers, and no differentiation of which recommendations need local adaptation - which is a notable omission for a guideline whose own method was guideline adaptation. Table 4 (enablers, incentives and adherence interventions) and the supplementary appendices on adherence and interruptions supply partial substitutes, which is why this is not scored lower.
items.rationaleB: The IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS section is a single paragraph: it names the responsible bodies (National TB Programme at NCID; TB Control Unit at Tan Tock Seng Hospital), states the recommendations "will largely be implemented by the National TB Programme team, including their dissemination and education of TB care providers", and identifies one concrete supply action, "sourcing for rifapentine through the Global Drug Facility"; a review is scheduled for 2026. Change from current practice is discernible in places (2 samples rather than the 3 most guidelines recommend, IGRA over TST despite cost, VOT alongside DOT), and Table 4 lists adherence enablers including subsidies and "Healthcare worker education and training". But there are no implementation tools, no audit or quality-improvement criteria, no monitoring data requirements, no costing, no training competencies, and no differentiation of where local adaptation applies across polyclinic, general hospital and TBCU settings; the requirement that CAD-AI "findings will have to be validated within the local practice setting in Singapore" is stated without any pathway, threshold or responsible party.

guidelineTitle: The 2019 Genitourinary Pathology Society (GUPS) White Paper on Contemporary Grading of Prostate Cancer
recommendationText:
While there is active research and promise in this area, the findings are premature for recommendations of digital pathology/
artificial intelligence in routine clinical application.

items.appraisal: The objective is explicitly stated as “to update grading recommendations” in the setting of persistent controversies and uncertainty in prostate cancer grading. The health/clinical intent is clear, and the topic and target clinical condition are explicit. A fully articulated expected patient-health benefit is less explicit than in a conventional CPG, preventing 7.

The paper addresses a series of clearly defined grading controversies—percent Gleason pattern 4, tertiary patterns, global vs highest score, Grade Groups, cribriform carcinoma, intraductal carcinoma, molecular testing, and AI/novel grading. However, these are expert-derived topics rather than formal PICO questions with all PICOS elements.

The guideline applies to patients with prostate cancer being evaluated on biopsy, TURP, or radical prostatectomy specimens, with many recommendations further restricted by Grade Group or specimen type. These populations are clinically specific throughout the paper, but there is no single formal population section with comprehensive inclusion/exclusion criteria.

Exceptionally broad expert participation for this topic. The paper includes a large international group of genitourinary pathologists, and clinician surveys included urologists, medical oncologists and radiation oncologists. The society itself was designed to include these groups.

No patient or public representatives are reported, and I found no method for eliciting patient experiences, preferences or values during development. Clinician surveys are valuable stakeholder input but do not satisfy the AGREE II requirement for the target population/patient perspective.

Pathologists are the primary intended users, with strong attention to how pathology reporting affects urologists, oncologists and radiation oncologists. The intended use—standardizing grading/reporting to support prognosis and management—is clear. However, the target users are not summarized in a dedicated explicit statement.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: The stated data source is a critical review of the literature combined with surveys. No databases, search dates, full search strings or reproducible systematic-search strategy are reported. This therefore falls well below a formal systematic evidence search.
I found no formal inclusion/exclusion criteria, study-design eligibility rules, language criteria or systematic study-selection process.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of the evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: The paper repeatedly discusses limitations, conflicting evidence, reproducibility issues, lack of studies and areas where evidence is insufficient for recommendations. For example, it explicitly states where no study exists and where more data are required. It also distinguishes mature evidence from preliminary evidence in areas such as AI. The assessment is strong, although not a formal certainty-of-evidence framework.

items.text: Methods for formulating recommendations clearly described
items.appraisal: The paper explains that recommendations were generated by integrating critical literature review, expert deliberation/consensus and pathology/clinician surveys. However, it does not report a standardized voting threshold, Delphi method, formal consensus rules or systematic process for resolving disagreement across all recommendations.

items.text: Benefits, side effects and risks considered
items.appraisal: For a diagnostic/pathology guideline, benefits and harms are considered mainly through consequences of grading/reporting decisions—risk stratification, eligibility for active surveillance, potential overtreatment, prognostic precision and effects on therapeutic decisions. For example, percent pattern 4 is explicitly connected to active-surveillance eligibility and treatment decisions. This is meaningful but less formal than an explicit benefit–harm framework.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and supporting evidence
items.appraisal: A major strength. Individual sections review the evidence, survey data and clinical rationale immediately before explicit recommendation tables. Table 3, for example, clearly distinguishes recommendations from questions where more data are required. This structure is repeated for other working groups.

I found no description of an independent external expert-review process before publication, reviewer identities, review methodology or how external comments modified the recommendations. Journal peer review cannot be assumed to fulfill the AGREE II external-review criterion unless explicitly described as part of guideline development.

The paper frequently identifies areas where future research may alter recommendations, but no formal updating interval, evidence-surveillance process, trigger criteria or responsible update group is provided.

Recommendations are highly specific. For example, the paper states when percent Gleason pattern 4 should be reported and gives precise reporting increments; other sections provide equally specific instructions for tertiary pattern 5, IDC-P and MRI-targeted biopsies.

Alternative grading/reporting approaches are explicitly compared, with recommendations made where evidence/practice patterns support one approach and “require more data” statements where no position is justified. Table 5 is a good example.
Each working group has a dedicated summary table of recommendations, with newly introduced GUPS recommendations emphasized in bold. This makes key recommendations extremely easy to identify.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: Practical barriers are discussed within individual topics, including interobserver variability, sampling error, uncertainty in small-volume disease, geographic practice variation and clinical interpretability. For example, the paper discusses how limited cancer volume can make percent pattern 4 unreliable and recommends communication with clinicians. However, there is no systematic implementation-barrier assessment.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: The recommendation tables are useful practical aids, and the paper gives detailed reporting instructions that could directly guide pathology practice. However, there is no dedicated implementation toolkit, checklist, reporting template, algorithm or structured implementation program.

Resource issues are only occasionally touched upon—for example, molecular assays are described as expensive and AI may affect workflow or efficiency. There is no systematic resource-use or economic analysis informing the recommendations.
I found no formal monitoring indicators, audit standards, adherence measures, target thresholds or recommended audit frequency for implementation of the grading recommendations.

I found no guideline-specific funding statement describing who funded development or explicitly stating that funding bodies did not influence the recommendations. Under the strict scoring anchor in your supplied AGREE II prompt, this warrants a score of 1.

Financial interests are disclosed: one author reports advisory/consulting relationships and the paper states that the other authors have no relevant financial interests. However, the document does not describe the process used to collect/manage COIs or explain how conflicts did or did not influence recommendation formulation.

guidelineTitle: Use of Computer-Assisted Detection (CADe) Colonoscopy in Colorectal Cancer Screening and Surveillance: Use of Computer-Assisted Detection (CADe) Colonoscopy in Colorectal Cancer Screening and Surveillance
recommendationText:
The panel believes that most well-informed patients who have already decided to undergo colonoscopy for screening or surveillance would favor CADe assistance during colonoscopy. This is due to the potential benefits, although limited, of reduction in colorectal cancer incidence and mortality.
This recommendation is weak, because the evidence is limited with considerable uncertainty of the evidence estimates, the absolute benefits for colorectal cancer incidence and mortality are small, and there is patient burden associated with CADe (more polyp overdiagnosis and more colonoscopy surveillance).

pico.population: Adults undergoing colonoscopy for CRC screening, surveillance
pico.outcomes: Primary outcomes were: CRC-related mortality, CRC incidence, and post-colonoscopy CRC incidence. Secondary outcomes were: adenoma detection rate, advanced adenomas per colonoscopy, serrated polyps per colonoscopy, adenomas per colonoscopy, adenoma miss rate, polypectomies of nonadenomatous polyps per colonoscopy, colonoscope withdrawal time (inspection time), number of colonoscopies per lifetime, perforations, and bleeding events.

items.appraisal: The objective, health intent, expected outcomes, and target population are explicit. ESGE aims to provide clinical guidance on the benefits and harms of AI CADe during colonoscopy, specifically for CRC screening and surveillance. The anticipated benefit is reduction of CRC incidence/mortality, balanced against burdens such as overdiagnosis and additional surveillance.
An explicit clinical question and complete PICO are provided: adults undergoing colonoscopy; CADe-assisted colonoscopy; colonoscopy without CADe; and clearly specified primary and secondary outcomes.

Adults ≥18 years are specified, together with indications. The final recommendation is restricted to screening and polyp surveillance, and inflammatory-bowel-disease surveillance is explicitly excluded from the evidence question. The panel further explains why symptomatic indications were excluded from the ESGE recommendation.

ESGE recruited experts with colonoscopy/CADe expertise; 23 members from 15 countries, including 8 women and 15 men, were selected. Authors and institutional/geographical affiliations are comprehensively reported. However, the ESGE voting panel itself is primarily a gastroenterology/endoscopy expert panel rather than a fully multidisciplinary stakeholder panel.

Patient values/preferences were explicitly incorporated into the evidence framework, and an evaluation of values/preferences was commissioned. However, the panel found no directly relevant studies of patient preferences for CADe colonoscopy, so the BMJ panel made its “best inferences” and ESGE adopted that approach. Thus patient preferences influenced the recommendation, but direct target-population evidence/participation was limited.
The guidance is intended to inform clinical use of CADe during screening/surveillance colonoscopy and explicitly discusses implications for clinicians and patients, including shared decision-making.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: The guidance explicitly relies on BMJ/MAGIC PICO searches, evidence synthesis, and a systematic review of RCTs. The commissioned systematic review included 44 RCTs (>30,000 patients). However, this ESGE document does not reproduce database names, search dates, complete search strings, or a reproducible search strategy. Under the supplied AGREE II anchor, that prevents a 6–7.

PICO eligibility is clearly defined, including population, intervention, comparator and outcomes, with IBD surveillance explicitly excluded. It also identifies the systematic review as one of RCTs. Nevertheless, complete systematic-review inclusion/exclusion criteria are not reproduced in this document.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: Evidence certainty is explicitly evaluated. The panel identifies low/very-low certainty for critical CRC outcomes, lack of RCT evidence for CRC incidence/mortality, modeling limitations, risk of bias and publication bias. The evidence tables on pages 4–5 make these judgments particularly transparent, displaying absolute effects and certainty ratings for each outcome.

Exceptionally transparent. All members reviewed the evidence and discussed it; two mutually exclusive recommendations were formulated; the panel agreed that either recommendation would be weak; anonymous voting was conducted; and results are reported numerically: 13/19 (68.4%) for CADe versus 6/19 (31.6%) against.

items.text: Benefits, side effects and risks considered
items.appraisal: Benefits and harms are central to the recommendation. Potential reductions in CRC incidence/mortality are balanced against overdiagnosis, additional polypectomy, increased surveillance, anxiety and procedure-related harms. The modeling tables quantify both benefits and burdens.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and supporting evidence
items.appraisal: There is a direct and unusually transparent evidence-to-recommendation link. Absolute estimates, certainty ratings, benefit/harm trade-offs and patient preferences lead directly into the recommendation. The final statement explicitly explains that it is weak because evidence is uncertain, absolute benefits are small and patient burden increases.

items.text: External review by experts before publication
items.appraisal: I found no description of external review by independent experts before publication, including reviewer identities, review methodology or resulting modifications. Collaboration with BMJ/MAGIC and use of externally generated evidence are not equivalent to external review of the ESGE statement itself.

ESGE explicitly states that it currently makes no recommendation for clinical indications other than screening/surveillance and will provide recommendations when more evidence becomes available. This provides an evidence-based update trigger, but no update interval or formal surveillance/updating procedure is specified.

The recommendation specifies the target population, intervention, clinical setting, direction and strength. Most informed patients already choosing screening/surveillance colonoscopy are expected to favor CADe, but the recommendation is explicitly weak.

The two alternatives—colonoscopy with CADe versus without CADe—are directly compared. The document even presents the panel with mutually exclusive “for” and “against” recommendation formulations and explains the different weighting of benefits and burdens behind each.
The recommendation is visually prominent in the Summary and again in a dedicated RECOMMENDATION box on page 6. Evidence tables on pages 4–5 also clearly display effects and certainty.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: Major determinants of adoption are discussed: uncertainty of benefit, differences in endoscopist ADR, overdiagnosis, additional surveillance, patient anxiety, harms/burdens and variability in patient values/preferences. These factors clearly influence the recommendation, but there is no systematic implementation-barrier assessment.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: The paper explains that a weak GRADE recommendation implies shared decision-making and that patients may reasonably choose CADe or no CADe. However, it does not supply an eligible implementation tool such as a patient decision aid, algorithm, checklist, implementation protocol or audit instrument.

Increased lifetime surveillance colonoscopies and procedure burden are quantified: modeling estimates 635 additional patients per 10,000 requiring surveillance over 10 years with CADe. This is important resource-use information, but no formal economic/cost analysis or budget-impact evaluation is reported in this document.

Relevant measurable outcomes—ADR, CRC incidence, mortality, additional surveillance, bleeding and perforation—are defined, but these are primarily evidence outcomes rather than a specified clinical audit/monitoring framework. No monitoring frequency or explicit audit standards are provided.

I found no explicit guideline-specific statement identifying funding for development and declaring that the funder had no influence, nor an explicit statement that no funding was received. Under the strict Item 22 anchor supplied in your appraisal prompt, this scores 1.

This is a major strength. All applicants completed COI forms; only members without financial interests in entities associated with CADe products could vote, while members with relevant associations could participate but had no recommendation voting rights. The final publication additionally reports individual author conflicts.

items.text: The evidence supporting the recommendation is applicable to the clinical question at hand
items.rationaleA: The single recommendation rests on a named systematic review of 44 RCTs (>30 000 patients) plus a commissioned microsimulation model, and Tables 1-3 give absolute effects with 95%CIs and GRADE certainty ratings per outcome, explicitly attributing downgrades to "serious risk of bias" and "serious publication bias" (e.g. ADR, adenomas per colonoscopy). Directness is handled unusually well for this topic: the guideline states the RCTs "found none that have investigated the primary outcomes of CRC incidence and mortality" and uses modelling to bridge the surrogate ADR to patient-important endpoints, then downgrades that modelling to low/very low certainty. Strength is explicitly congruent with certainty - "This recommendation is weak, because the evidence is limited with considerable uncertainty" - and both the benefit magnitude (11 fewer CRCs, 2 fewer deaths per 10 000) and the harm magnitude (635 more needing surveillance per 10 000) are quantified. Falls short of 7 because confounding in the ADR-CRC observational link underpinning the model is not appraised, and the model's assumptions (100% participation, ages 60-69) are described but their effect on the recommendation is never discussed.
items.rationaleB: The single recommendation rests on an explicitly reported evidence base: a systematic review of 44 RCTs (>30 000 patients), a microsimulation model, and GRADE certainty ratings given outcome-by-outcome in Tables 1-3, with absolute effects and 95%CIs (e.g. CRC incidence 'Difference: 11 fewer per 10 000 (95%CI 35 fewer-17 more)') and named reasons for downgrading ('Due to serious risk of bias', 'Due to serious publication bias'). Directness is handled openly, the review 'found none that have investigated the primary outcomes of CRC incidence and mortality', so modelled surrogate-to-outcome inference is flagged as low/very low certainty, and the weak strength of the recommendation is explicitly justified by that uncertainty and by the small absolute benefit. Weaknesses: heterogeneity/consistency across the 44 trials is never discussed, no dose-response or confounding treatment is offered despite the model relying on an observational ADR-CRC association [3], and the reader must go to the BMJ/MAGIC source documents for any evidence profile detail beyond the three summary tables.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target users it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The problem is squarely within European endoscopists' practice, and the recommendation's scope is drawn tightly and explicitly: it applies only to "primary screening or colonoscopy after positive FIT testing" or polyp surveillance, with symptomatic patients and IBD surveillance deliberately excluded and ESGE stating it "does not provide any recommendation" for other indications. The weak, non-directive strength is well matched to the close benefit-harm balance the panel describes, and the stated implication - "shared decision-making between patients and their health care providers" - is an action endoscopists can take. Weaker on the practice-context detail that would let a user act: the model deliberately stratified by ADR thresholds "to simulate the performance of endoscopists with varying skill levels," yet the recommendation never differentiates low-ADR from high-ADR endoscopists, and no guidance is given on which CADe devices, settings or units the statement applies to.
items.rationaleB: The clinical problem (variable ADR, CADe devices 'have entered the market in many countries') is squarely within European endoscopists' scope, and the panel deliberately narrowed the recommendation to the population its evidence covers, applying it 'only to patients who undergo colonoscopy for screening ... or polyp surveillance' and stating that 'ESGE does not provide any recommendation regarding CADe for patients who undergo colonoscopy for indications other than screening or polyp surveillance'. The weak strength is well matched to the close benefit-harm balance and is explained in GRADE terms, with the stated implication of shared decision-making. However, the recommended action itself is left abstract: nothing is said about which CADe systems, how they should be used alongside adequate withdrawal technique, or whether the advice differs for high- versus low-ADR endoscopists, even though the model itself simulated 'endoscopists with varying skill levels'.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target patients/populations it is intended for
items.rationaleA: Outcomes are genuinely patient-important and were prespecified as primary: CRC-related mortality, CRC incidence and post-colonoscopy CRC incidence, with burdens (non-neoplastic polypectomy, extra surveillance, "increased health-related anxiety and overdiagnosis," perforation, bleeding) carried through to Table 3 and into the recommendation text. The recommended action plausibly moves these outcomes, and the guideline is candid that the effect on mortality is "trivial or no benefit." How the importance of these outcomes to patients was established is thin - the panel concedes it "did not find relevant studies on values and preferences for CADe" and "made the best inferences about what most patients would want." There is no tailoring by age, sex, comorbidity or family history, and the modelled population is only ages 60-69 while the recommendation is issued for all adults undergoing screening or surveillance, an extrapolation gap the statement never flags.
items.rationaleB: Patient-important outcomes drove the evidence base by design: primary outcomes were CRC-related mortality, CRC incidence and post-colonoscopy CRC, and burdens were quantified (635 more individuals per 10 000 needing follow-up over 10 years; no excess perforation or bleeding), with overdiagnosis and 'increased health-related anxiety' named explicitly. The recommendation plausibly connects the action to these outcomes via ADR. Tailoring is thin, however: the model is restricted to ages 60-69 with assumed 100% participation, and there is no differentiation of the advice by age, sex, family history, comorbidity or life expectancy, despite the Discussion acknowledging overdiagnosis depends on 'the patient's remaining lifetime'.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target users
items.rationaleA: Clinician values were captured procedurally rather than substantively: 19 eligible endoscopist votes split 13 for / 6 against, reported transparently with the minority rationale ("absolute net benefits ... were too small to justify the harms"), and the Discussion states clinicians "may choose CADe or not ... depending on their values and preferences," which does signal where clinical flexibility is appropriate. But the panel is 23 self-selected ESGE members, not a sampled clinical community, and no wider survey or consultation of endoscopists is reported. Acceptability and workflow factors that determine whether endoscopists adopt CADe - the 0.53-minute longer withdrawal time is measured but never discussed as a workload issue, and training, alert fatigue, deskilling and unit-level integration go unmentioned - are entirely absent.
items.rationaleB: Clinician values were captured, but only through the panel itself: 23 members from 15 countries, an anonymous vote of 13 for versus 6 against, and an explicit statement that this 'shows that there is considerable uncertainty of the evidence and its interpretation, and variation of values and preferences amongst the ESGE panel members'. The weak recommendation expressly leaves room for clinical flexibility ('clinicians and patients may choose CADe or not ... depending on their values and preferences'). What is missing is any consideration of acceptability and feasibility for endoscopists in practice, no discussion of new skills or training, workflow disruption, added withdrawal time as a unit-level cost (the 0.53-minute difference is reported as data but never as an acceptability issue), de-skilling, or over-reliance/alert fatigue, and no wider survey of the endoscopy community beyond the 19 voters.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target patients/populations
items.rationaleA: The recommendation is written as a values statement about patients - "most well-informed patients who have already decided to undergo colonoscopy ... would favor CADe assistance" - and each of the two ballot options makes the underlying value trade-off explicit (avoiding cancer versus avoiding overdiagnosis, anxiety and extra surveillance). The statement is clear that patient choice carries large weight here, noting "values and preferences vary across different settings and contexts, and for different patients" and that the weak recommendation implies shared decision-making. However, no actual patient input was obtained: the Methods promise "an evaluation of values and preferences of patients undergoing colonoscopy [10]" but the same section then says no relevant studies were found and preferences were inferred, and no patient or lay member sat on the panel. No decision aid or patient-facing tool is offered or even recommended, despite a weak recommendation whose whole implication is a shared conversation.
items.rationaleB: Patient values are the explicit hinge of the recommendation, which is framed as a judgement about what 'most well-informed patients who have already decided to undergo colonoscopy ... would favor', and both candidate statements spell out the competing value placed on avoiding cancer versus avoiding surveillance, anxiety and overdiagnosis. The guideline is honest about the evidentiary gap: 'The BMJ panel did not find relevant studies on values and preferences for CADe in colonoscopy. Thus, the BMJ panel made the best inferences about what most patients would want, and the ESGE panel followed the same approach', with only an indirect patient/physician perspectives study [10] cited. Against this, no patients or lay members sat on or voted in the panel, no patient decision aid or communication tool is offered or even recommended despite the panel invoking shared decision-making, and burden factors such as bowel preparation for extra surveillance procedures go unexamined.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of policy/decision makers
items.rationaleA: The document is written for clinicians and does essentially nothing for the people who buy CADe or run screening programmes. Its own model predicts 635 more individuals per 10 000 needing follow-up colonoscopy over 10 years - a substantial capacity and cost consequence for national screening services - yet this is reported only as a harm to patients and never translated into system, workforce or budget implications. There is no cost or cost-effectiveness consideration anywhere, no comment on device procurement, reimbursement or regulation, and no consideration of health equity or of differences between well-resourced and less-resourced European settings beyond the passing remark that values vary "across different settings and contexts."
items.rationaleB: This dimension is essentially untouched. CADe is a purchased commercial technology and the recommendation would generate 635 additional follow-up colonoscopies per 10 000 patients over 10 years, yet there is no cost, cost-effectiveness, budget-impact, procurement, regulatory or endoscopy-capacity analysis anywhere, and that surveillance excess is framed only as patient burden. Health equity is never mentioned, despite screening programme structures differing markedly across the European countries the statement addresses, and no guidance is given to payers or national screening programmes on whether to fund or mandate CADe. The only near-policy remark is the generic line that 'Values and preferences vary across different settings and contexts'.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of the guideline developers
items.rationaleA: This is the statement's strongest dimension: the two candidate recommendations name the developers' value positions outright - the against option "placed higher value on avoiding the burdens than on the uncertain benefits," the for option "places greater value on the potential of avoiding colorectal cancer and death" - so the reader can see exactly which value judgment produced the published text. The method for integrating differing perspectives is described and executed: an anonymous online ballot between two mutually exclusive prespecified options, with the 68.4%/31.6% split, the one abstention and the dissenting reasoning all reported, and the Discussion concedes "variation of values and preferences amongst the ESGE panel members." Independence is protected by excluding members with financial interests in CADe products from voting, with individual disclosures listed. Short of 7 because the integration method is a bare majority vote with no attempt at consensus or weighting, and no non-endoscopist perspectives (patients, payers, methodologists external to BMJ/MAGIC) were brought into that vote.
items.rationaleB: The developers' value judgements are made unusually visible: the two pre-specified voting options each state the value trade-off in words ('the panel placed higher value on avoiding the burdens than on the uncertain benefits' versus 'places greater value on the potential of avoiding colorectal cancer and death'), the anonymous vote count is published, and the dissenting minority's reasoning is reported (that '9 fewer cancers and 2 fewer cancer deaths per 10 000 patients were too small to justify the harms'). Conflicts of interest were used substantively rather than merely disclosed, since 'Only members without financial interests in entities associated with CADe products were eligible as voting members'. It falls short of the top of the scale because a simple majority vote is the only mechanism for integrating divergent perspectives, no attempt is made to reconcile or weight the minority position, and no prior values or predispositions of individual panellists are characterised beyond financial interests.

items.text: The purpose of the recommendation is clear and actionable
items.rationaleA: The Scope and Purpose box states the aim plainly and the recommendation matches it, including the explicit statement that it "replaces previous ESGE recommendations for CADe in colonoscopy [7]" - so the intended decision-influencing role is clear. The Discussion articulates a further implementation goal, that transparent voting "encourages endoscopists and the public to make their own, informed choices," and the weak-recommendation implication of shared decision-making is spelled out. What is missing is any description of anticipated impact from adoption: beyond the per-10 000 event counts in the tables, the statement never says what would change for patients, endoscopy units, or screening systems if the recommendation were taken up, and it sets no advocacy or policy objective.
items.rationaleB: The SCOPE AND PURPOSE box states the aim plainly and the statement positions itself in the practice landscape, noting it 'replaces previous ESGE recommendations for CADe in colonoscopy [7]', which is an important signal for users given the earlier, more favourable 2022 ESGE position. The stated implementation intent is deliberately modest and consistent with the weak recommendation: to provide 'a transparent decision-making process at ESGE' that 'encourages endoscopists and the public to make their own, informed choices'. But anticipated impacts of adoption are described only for patients (more surveillance, overdiagnosis) and not at all for endoscopy units, screening programmes or health systems, and no reversal is offered for the practical question the change of position creates for centres that already bought CADe on the strength of the 2022 statement.

items.text: The recommendation is feasible for local application and adoption
items.rationaleA: There is no implementation content at all. The statement never characterises the change required from current practice (it does not say how widely CADe is already deployed, nor whether units without it should acquire it or units with it should keep using it), gives no resource, cost or cost-effectiveness guidance, no training or competency requirements, and no advice on tailoring to local screening programmes despite the recommendation spanning primary-colonoscopy and FIT-based systems that it elsewhere distinguishes. Most conspicuously for ESGE, which cites its own work on "barriers to dissemination and implementation of quality measures" [4], no monitoring criteria, audit data or quality indicators are proposed for tracking CADe use or its downstream surveillance burden. The only gesture toward local context is the remark that values "vary across different settings and contexts," which carries no actionable advice.
items.rationaleB: Implementability is the weakest domain. The statement offers no description of the type or degree of practice change required, no implementation tools, no resource or cost considerations, no training or competency requirements for CADe use, no audit or quality indicators for monitoring adoption, and no strategies for addressing acceptability barriers, this despite ESGE's own cited work on 'Overcoming the barriers to dissemination and implementation of quality measures' [4]. The only gesture toward local context is the observation that 'Values and preferences vary across different settings and contexts', plus the deferral that 'ESGE will provide recommendations for clinical indications when more evidence becomes available'. Nothing tells a European endoscopy unit what to actually do on Monday morning.

guidelineTitle: ESR Essentials: arti cial intelligence in breast imaging—practice recommendations by the European Society of Breast Imaging
organization: European Society of Breast Imaging (EUSOBI) / European Society of Radiology (ESR)
recommendationText:
While some AI algorithms may have clinical potential,
their use should be regarded as optional. Unless AI is
used as a standalone tool for imaging evaluation, the
final image interpretation responsibility lies with the
radiologist, and available AI tools can only be regarded
as a tool to assist the radiologist in this task.

pico.population: Women undergoing breast cancer screening or diagnostic breast imaging

items.appraisal: The health intent is clear: to guide clinical use of AI in breast imaging, particularly regarding diagnostic accuracy, workflow efficiency and safe implementation. Expected benefits such as workload reduction and improved diagnostic performance are explicit. However, the overarching target patient population is not defined as comprehensively as required for the highest AGREE II scores.

The review addresses clinically relevant questions concerning AI in mammography, DBT, ultrasound, MRI, contrast-enhanced mammography and LLMs, but these are not formulated as structured clinical/PICO questions. Interventions are identifiable, but population, comparator and outcome elements are not systematically specified for each question.

Different clinical groups are discussed—screening populations, symptomatic women, high-risk women and patients with established breast cancer—but there is no formal guideline-level definition of the target population with eligibility characteristics or inclusion/exclusion criteria. The patient summary distinguishes some of these groups.

Authors, affiliations and geographical locations are extensively reported, with expertise strongly concentrated in radiology/breast imaging. Relevant specialist expertise is therefore strong, but the group is not broadly multidisciplinary—for example, there is no documented patient representative, oncologist, surgeon, health economist, implementation scientist or technologist/AI governance specialist in the recommendation group.

A useful patient summary is provided, but I found no evidence that patient/public views, experiences or preferences were systematically sought during development. A patient-facing summary is not equivalent to stakeholder participation under AGREE II.

The intended users are predominantly radiologists/breast-imaging professionals, and the intended use is clear: AI should currently function as an assistive tool, with final image interpretation remaining the responsibility of the radiologist. The document could score 7 if the intended user groups were explicitly enumerated in a dedicated section.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: No reproducible systematic literature-search methodology is reported: no databases, search dates, complete search terms or formal search strategy are given. The paper cites systematic reviews and many primary studies, but using systematic reviews as evidence is not the same as performing/reporting a systematic search for guideline development.
No explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria, study-design eligibility rules, screening procedure or article-selection methodology are reported.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of the body of evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: This is one of the paper's methodological strengths. It repeatedly distinguishes robust from preliminary evidence and clearly identifies limitations such as lack of long-term outcomes, limited DBT evidence, absent post-implementation evaluation, poor real-world MRI validation and very early CEM/LLM evidence. The score does not reach 6–7 because there is no formal systematic certainty assessment of the complete body of evidence.

I found no reported consensus method, Delphi process, voting procedure, threshold for agreement or method for resolving disagreement. Society endorsement is reported, but endorsement is not a description of recommendation formulation.

items.text: Benefits, side effects and risks considered
items.appraisal: Benefits and disadvantages are explicitly balanced. The paper discusses diagnostic accuracy and workload reduction alongside uncertainty about long-term outcomes, cost-effectiveness, governance, safety, inappropriate extrapolation across platforms, regulatory issues and the need for post-market monitoring.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and supporting evidence
items.appraisal: The three key recommendations provide a stated Level of evidence: Moderate, and the subsequent modality-specific sections summarize supporting studies and their limitations. Evidence and recommendations are therefore closely connected, although not through a fully systematic recommendation-to-evidence framework.

items.text: External review by experts before publication
items.appraisal: The document states that it was endorsed by the ESR Executive Council and EUSOBI Executive Committee in August 2025. However, it does not describe an independent external expert-review methodology, identify external reviewers or report how review comments affected the final recommendations.

No formal updating interval, surveillance process, trigger criteria or responsible updating group is reported. The recommendation for continued post-market surveillance of AI products concerns the technologies themselves, not a procedure for updating this guidance.

The recommendations are generally clear—for example, AI in mammographic screening may be implemented but requires rigorous post-market surveillance, and AI should currently be considered an aid rather than an autonomous substitute for the radiologist. Some wording remains intentionally cautious (“seems,” “can be used,” “optional”), appropriate to the evidence but slightly reducing specificity.

The document clearly distinguishes AI applications according to mammography, DBT, ultrasound, MRI, CEM and LLMs, and indicates where clinical use is reasonable, optional, unsupported or confined to research. For example, MRI AI beyond conventional CAD is explicitly not yet recommended.
The three principal recommendations appear in a dedicated “Key recommendations” section and include explicit evidence levels. They are also reinforced by Key Points and the concluding summary.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: Several major implementation barriers are identified: need for governance, absent long-term outcomes, insufficient post-implementation evidence, regulatory concerns, lack of large-scale validation, limited cost-effectiveness evidence and technological/model-specific limitations. However, these factors were not collected using a formal implementation assessment process.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: The paper provides meaningful implementation advice, particularly the WHO four-phase evidence framework in Figure 1 and recommendations for post-market surveillance. The figure helps users judge the maturity of AI applications across imaging modalities. However, it does not provide a ready-to-use implementation checklist, decision aid, governance template, procurement tool or clinical implementation protocol.

Workload, reading time, resource-limited environments and cost-effectiveness are discussed. Indeed, the authors explicitly note that cost-effectiveness and large-scale validation studies remain lacking. These considerations are meaningful but fall short of a systematic economic/resource assessment.

The paper explicitly states that implementation should include rigorous post-market surveillance and identifies concrete outcomes to monitor: recall rates, biopsy rates and cancer-detection rates. This satisfies the presence of indicators, but no monitoring frequency, thresholds or measurement protocol is provided.

The paper reports only that open-access funding was provided by Università della Svizzera italiana. There is no explicit statement about funding of the recommendation-development work itself or that funding sources had no influence over recommendations. Under the strict scoring anchor in your AGREE II prompt, absence of a guideline-specific funding/no-influence statement warrants a low score.

Individual author relationships are disclosed in substantial detail, including consulting fees, grants, honoraria, advisory-board roles and relationships with AI/imaging companies. However, the document does not explain how conflicts were collected, evaluated or managed during recommendation formulation, or whether conflicted individuals were restricted from particular decisions.

guidelineTitle: AGA Clinical Practice Update on Screening and Surveillance in Individuals at Increased Risk for Gastric Cancer in the United States
recommendationText: Artificial intelligence tools appear promising for the detection of early gastric neoplasia in the adequately visualized stomach, but data are too preliminary to recommend routine use.

pico.population: Individuals undergoing upper endoscopy for gastric cancer screening/surveillance

items.appraisal: The objective, population and intended health benefit are explicit: provide best-practice advice for primary and secondary prevention of gastric cancer in the US, particularly through H. pylori eradication and endoscopic screening/surveillance of high-risk populations.

The CPU does not formulate formal PICO questions, but its clinical issues are very clearly operationalized through 15 Best Practice Advice statements addressing whom to screen, modality, biopsy, surveillance, treatment and discontinuation. This is strong but short of a fully specified PICO-question framework.

Excellent definition of the target population and important subgroups. It specifies increased-risk US populations and risk determinants including immigrant status, family history, hereditary syndromes, H. pylori, smoking and socioeconomic factors. It also explicitly excludes cardia GC and identifies other topics outside scope.

Four named authors and their institutions are clearly reported, all with relevant gastroenterology/endoscopy expertise. However, this is a relatively small expert-author group rather than a broadly multidisciplinary guideline panel incorporating multiple relevant professional disciplines.

Patient preferences are considered in individual clinical decisions—for example whether surveillance should continue—but I found no reported method for systematically obtaining patient/public views during development. Thus, preferences are considered, but there is no documented patient-engagement methodology.

The document was commissioned to provide timely guidance on a clinically important topic for AGA membership, and the recommendations clearly target gastroenterologists/endoscopists and other clinicians managing high-risk patients. The intended users are therefore apparent, although not comprehensively defined in a dedicated target-user statement.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search evidence
items.appraisal: This is a major limitation. The authors state that the advice was drawn from a review of published literature and expert opinion and explicitly state that systematic reviews were not performed. No reproducible database/search-date/search-string strategy is reported.
No explicit systematic inclusion/exclusion criteria, study-design criteria, PICO eligibility criteria, language restrictions or screening process are reported.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of the body of evidence described
items.appraisal: The CPU is unusually transparent about evidence limitations. It acknowledges limited US evidence and reliance on indirect evidence and expert opinion and repeatedly identifies uncertainties and evidence gaps. However, there is no formal systematic assessment of certainty/quality across the body of evidence.

All authors contributed to drafting/revising the Best Practice Advice statements and approved the manuscript. However, no formal consensus method, voting threshold, Delphi process, disagreement-resolution procedure or results of recommendation deliberation are reported.

items.text: Benefits, side effects and risks considered
items.appraisal: Benefits and harms are meaningfully balanced. For endoscopic screening, the CPU discusses mortality benefit, procedure harms, costs, resource utilization and environmental implications. It also considers life expectancy, treatment fitness, complications and patient preferences when deciding when surveillance should stop.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and supporting evidence
items.appraisal: Each Best Practice Advice statement is followed by explanatory evidence with citations, making the evidence-to-advice connection readily identifiable. For example, the H. pylori recommendation is supported by RCT/meta-analysis and observational evidence. The score is not 7 because the evidence was not systematically graded and the authors explicitly state that formal evidence-quality/strength ratings were not performed.

The CPU underwent internal review by the AGA CPU Committee and external peer review through the standard procedures of Gastroenterology. The external review is clear, but reviewer identities, methodology and resulting modifications are not comprehensively reported.

I found no explicit updating procedure specifying a review interval, criteria/triggers for updating, or a defined updating process. Discussion of future evidence gaps and iterative modification of practice does not constitute an AGREE II updating procedure.

Excellent. Recommendations clearly specify populations, actions and often technical details. For example, biopsy advice specifies a minimum of five biopsies, anatomical sites and separate specimen jars.

Different options are clearly differentiated according to risk and findings: no further screening versus continued screening, surveillance intervals, repeat endoscopy, H. pylori treatment, ESD and surgical referral.

The 15 recommendations are prominently labeled BEST PRACTICE ADVICE and presented separately from supporting discussion. Additionally, the clinical pathway on page 8 visually integrates screening findings with surveillance/treatment decisions.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: Strong implementation discussion. The CPU explicitly identifies system- and patient-level barriers including access, insurance coverage, language, education, economics, transportation and cultural barriers, and discusses the need for stakeholder engagement and equitable access.

The guideline provides substantial practical guidance and an actionable clinical pathway (Figure 1, page 8) linking findings to surveillance and treatment. It also describes preprocedural, intraprocedural and postprocedural implementation pillars in Figure 2. This is considerably stronger than implementation discussion alone.

Cost-effectiveness, limited endoscopic resources, resource utilization, insurance coverage and environmental sustainability are explicitly discussed. The document cites cost-effectiveness analyses of adding EGD to CRC screening in selected high-risk populations.

The CPU calls for quality metrics/detection metrics and adherence to high-quality endoscopy standards, but it does not provide a comprehensive audit framework with clearly defined indicators, measurement methods and monitoring frequency.

Funding is disclosed: Shah receives a Veterans Affairs Career Development Award. However, there is no explicit statement that the funder had no influence on development or content. Under the supplied scoring anchors, this prevents a 7.

Detailed individual COIs are disclosed for all four authors, including consultancy relationships, stock ownership and research support. However, the document does not clearly explain how these conflicts were managed or prevented from influencing the recommendations, preventing a 7.
