items.text: The evidence supporting the recommendation is applicable to the clinical question at hand
items.rationaleA: The narrative supporting several statements reports effect magnitude and precision well (endoscopic screening RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.48-0.70; H pylori eradication RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.40-0.72, NNT 72), explicitly weighs directness ('data supporting GC screening in high-risk populations in the United States are limited and clinical guidance is based more so on indirect evidence and expert opinion'), and argues against lead-time bias/overdiagnosis as an explanation for the stage shift. However, the Methods state plainly that 'systematic reviews were not performed' and the statements 'do not carry formal ratings regarding the quality of evidence or strength', so risk of bias, publication bias and certainty are never assessed and strength-certainty congruence cannot be verified. Several operationally important statements rest on unreferenced expert opinion - the minimum of 5 biopsies in BPA 5, the 3-year interval in BPA 9, the 1 cm/2 cm carcinoid thresholds in BPA 13 - and no evidence-to-decision link is made at the level of an individual BPA. The consistently hedged wording ('intervals are not well defined', 'should be considered') at least keeps the definitiveness of most statements roughly proportionate to the thin evidence base.
items.rationaleB: The narrative supporting the 15 Best Practice Advice statements cites quantitative effect estimates with precision (endoscopic screening RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.48-0.70; H pylori eradication RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.40-0.72, NNT 72) and is candid about directness, stating that US guidance rests "more so on indirect evidence and expert opinion, rather than rigorous direct evidence" and that the supporting meta-analysis is "all from East Asia"; it also addresses lead-time bias, endoscopic miss rates (~10%), interobserver variability in dysplasia, and limitations of the Markov cost-effectiveness model that "did not consider other individual-level risk factors." However, the METHODS explicitly concede that "systematic reviews were not performed" and the statements "do not carry formal ratings regarding the quality of evidence or strength," so there is no risk-of-bias, consistency, or publication-bias appraisal and no certainty rating anywhere. Harms are dismissed in a single line ("Serious harms of nontherapeutic upper endoscopy are very low") with no quantification of overdiagnosis or cumulative procedural burden, and evidence-to-recommendation links are never made explicit at the level of an individual BPA. The definitiveness of statements such as BPA 2 ("Endoscopy is the best test") and BPA 4 ("H pylori eradication is essential") outruns the self-declared indirect evidence base.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target users it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The target users are unmistakably US gastroenterologists and endoscopists, and every action named sits squarely within their scope: performing high-definition white-light endoscopy with image enhancement and adequate inspection time (BPA 3), taking Sydney-protocol biopsies into two labelled jars (BPA 5), negotiating pathology reporting standards locally (BPA 7), and referring dysplasia to expert centres for ESD (BPA 10-11). Benefit-harm trade-offs are stated in terms clinicians act on - 'serious harms of nontherapeutic upper endoscopy are very low' with 'the main considerations are cost, resource utilization, and environmental considerations' - and the direction and strength of each statement track that trade-off, e.g. the deliberate refusal to endorse AI ('data are too preliminary to recommend routine use'). Scope boundaries are explicit (cardia GC, hereditary diffuse GC and detailed GIM surveillance are excluded and cross-referenced to other documents), so users know where the advice stops. It falls short of 7 only because some statements (screening initiation age of 45, BPA 9 intervals) leave the user without an actionable default when risk factors conflict.
items.rationaleB: The problem and the recommended actions sit squarely within US gastroenterologists' and endoscopists' scope: BPA 3 specifies high-definition white-light endoscopy with image enhancement, mucosal cleansing, inspection time and photodocumentation; BPA 5 gives an operational biopsy protocol (updated Sydney System, minimum 5 biopsies, antrum/incisura and corpus in separately labelled jars); BPA 7 directs endoscopists to negotiate reporting standards with local pathologists; and Figure 1 supplies a complete clinical pathway from index EGD to management. Where the action exceeds the general endoscopist's competence the guideline routes the user onward rather than overreaching (BPA 10 refer to an experienced GI pathologist and a center with expertise; BPA 11 ESD "at a center with endoscopic and pathologic expertise"). Two things hold this short of the top: some statements are aspirational or system-directed rather than actionable at the bedside (BPA 6 on the "unmet need for improved training"; BPA 15 on health equity), and because no formal benefit-harm trade-off was weighed, the strength of the wording is not calibrated to that trade-off.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target patients/populations it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The outcomes driving the advice are ones patients care about - GC mortality, stage at diagnosis, 5-year survival (32% in the US vs >70% in Korea/Japan) - and the recommended actions plausibly move them, since the whole rationale is the shift toward curable early-stage disease. Tailoring is genuinely detailed: Table 1 individualises eligibility by age 45+, country of origin, immigrant generation, first-degree family history (start 10 years earlier), acculturation/ethnic enclave, persistent poverty, tobacco and diet, and BPA 14 tailors de-escalation to fitness for treatment and life expectancy rather than an age cut-off. What is missing is any account of how the importance of these outcomes to patients was determined - no patient or community input is reported anywhere - and patient-side harms (procedural risk, sedation burden, false reassurance, anxiety from indefinite surveillance) are dismissed in a single clause rather than weighed.
items.rationaleB: The outcomes driving the advice are unambiguously patient-important - GC mortality, stage at diagnosis, curative endoscopic or surgical resection, and 5-year survival ("a dismal 32%") - and the recommended actions plausibly move them, as argued from the South Korea and Japan stage-shift data. Tailoring is the document's strongest feature: Table 1 stratifies by immigrant generation and region of origin, first-degree family history (screen 10 years earlier than the youngest affected relative), non-White race/ethnicity with disaggregation by country of origin, hereditary syndromes, smoking >20 pack-years, diet, and persistent-poverty residence, with an age-45 start justified against colonoscopy timing, and BPA 14 de-escalates by fitness and life expectancy. What is missing is any account of how the importance of these outcomes to patients was determined - no patient-reported outcomes, no patient representation, and no attention to downsides patients would weigh (procedural anxiety, repeat endoscopy burden, out-of-pocket cost, overdiagnosis of indolent lesions).

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target users
items.rationaleA: Acceptability and workflow are considered concretely: adding screening EGD at the time of screening colonoscopy to fit existing practice, the 'unmet need for improved training, especially in the United States' in recognising GIM and dysplasia, the call for image libraries, CME and detection metrics, and BPA 7's instruction to 'work with their local pathologists to achieve consensus' on reporting - all of these speak to new skills and adapted routines. The document also differentiates where clinical flexibility applies, repeatedly conceding that 'the optimal screening intervals in such scenarios are not well defined' while being firm on ESD referral to expert centres. But no clinician values or preferences were actually sought - the panel is four subspecialist authors and the only external input reported is journal and committee peer review - and there is no discussion of what range of practice the wider US gastroenterology community would find acceptable, e.g. whether general endoscopists will accept the added biopsy and inspection-time burden.
items.rationaleB: Clinician acceptability is touched on in several concrete ways: the workflow-friendly strategy of adding EGD at the time of screening colonoscopy, the acknowledged skills gap ("these findings often go undiagnosed when endoscopists are unfamiliar with the characteristic visual features"), the call for "training, continuing medical education, image libraries" and detection metrics, and explicit resource and "green endoscopy" considerations. Clinical flexibility is deliberately signposted - BPA 13 distinguishes "may consider resecting gastric carcinoids <1 cm" from "should endoscopically resect lesions measuring 1-2 cm," and repeated admissions that "intervals are not well defined" leave room for judgement. But no clinician values were actually sought: the panel is four authors, review was limited to the CPU Committee and journal peer review, and there is no survey, Delphi, voting record, or description of what range of practice the wider US gastroenterology community would find acceptable - notable given the update asks users to adopt screening where "there are no established screening guidelines for GC."

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target patients/populations
items.rationaleA: Patient preference is written into the recommendations themselves rather than merely mentioned: BPA 8 makes continuation of screening after a normal index EGD contingent on 'that individual's risk factors and preferences', BPA 14 balances 'patient life expectancy, perceived benefit... risk of complications, and personal preferences', post-resection surveillance continues 'unless the patient's health status or preference indicates otherwise', and pre-resection counselling about possible surgery is required. Burden and access barriers are named for the specific populations targeted - 'language, education, economic, transportation, and cultural barriers are overrepresented' - with culturally and linguistically aligned patient navigators proposed. Against this, no patients, families or community representatives were consulted, no evidence on patient values or willingness to undergo repeated endoscopy is cited, and no decision aid or patient-facing tool is offered or even recommended despite the advice hinging on preference-sensitive choices.
items.rationaleB: Patient preference is written into the recommendations themselves rather than merely gestured at: BPA 8 makes continued screening after a normal index EGD contingent on "that individual's risk factors and preferences"; BPA 14 balances "patient life expectancy, perceived benefit... risk of complications, and personal preferences"; surveillance after resection continues "unless the patient's health status or preference indicates otherwise"; and pre-resection counselling that surgery may follow is explicitly required. Population-level acceptability barriers are named with unusual specificity - "language, education, economic, transportation, and cultural barriers" - together with "culturally and linguistically aligned patient navigators" as an uptake intervention. Nevertheless the guideline nowhere reports that patient, family or community values were sought or how they were elicited, includes no patient or community representative among the four authors, and never states whether patient decision aids would help despite building several statements on shared decision making.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of policy/decision makers
items.rationaleA: Health equity is not an afterthought here but the organising argument - BPA 15 is itself an equity statement, and the text quantifies disparity (2- to 14.5-fold higher noncardia GC incidence in non-White groups; 43% higher GC mortality in persistent-poverty counties) while flagging the goal of 'moving away from race and ethnicity-based clinical decision making'. System-level levers are named explicitly: insurance coverage of screening procedures 'through stakeholder engagement', the NCI funding-to-lethality ranking of 19th and the need to amplify research funding, endoscopic capacity and resource utilisation, green endoscopy, and the three-pillar pre-/intra-/post-procedural framework in Figure 2. Cost-effectiveness evidence is invoked on both sides (EGD at colonoscopy is cost-effective; universal H pylori screening and biennial stand-alone EGD are not). It stops short of higher scores because no policy or payer decision-makers were engaged, and no budget-impact or capacity modelling is offered for what US-wide risk-based screening would actually cost or require.
items.rationaleB: A dedicated "Implementation and Sustainability" section and Figure 2 (pre-, intra- and postprocedural pillars) frame the advice explicitly for system-level actors, and specific policy levers are named: insurance coverage - "ensuring that GC screening procedures are covered by insurance through stakeholder engagement" - equitable access to endoscopy and to oncologic services, and correction of the finding that GC "ranked lowest (19th) in terms of National Cancer Institute funding-to-lethality ratio." Health equity is not an afterthought but the organising value of BPA 15 and of the disparity analysis (43% higher GC mortality in persistent-poverty counties; up to 14.5-fold risk in Korean Americans), with the footnote to Table 1 committing to "moving away from race and ethnicity-based clinical decision making." Cost-effectiveness evidence is cited on both sides (EGD-at-colonoscopy cost-effective; universal H pylori screening and biennial stand-alone EGD not). It falls short of the top marks because no payer, health-system or public-health decision-maker input was sought, no budget-impact or resource-requirement estimate is offered for a US screening program, and the policy asks remain advocacy statements rather than costed, addressed recommendations.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of the guideline developers
items.rationaleA: A clear value position is visible - the authors argue that weak direct evidence should not delay action ('the lack of strong scientific evidence has not delayed other countries... regardless, this should not delay current GC prevention and early detection efforts') and that equity is a legitimate ground for recommending screening - but this stance is asserted in the discussion rather than declared as a value the panel brought, and its effect on how benefits and harms were weighed is never made explicit. No method for eliciting, integrating or reconciling differing views among the four authors is described; the Author Contributions note says only that 'all authors contributed to drafting and revising the Best Practice Advice statements'. Conflicts of interest are disclosed in detail (consultancies with Olympus, Fujifilm, Boston Scientific, Medtronic, research support from AI Medical, stock holdings), which is relevant given statements about endoscopic technology and AI, but disclosure alone does not satisfy this item and no management of those conflicts is described.
items.rationaleB: The document discloses authorship contributions, funding (a VA Career Development Award) and detailed conflicts of interest, several of which bear directly on the advice - consultancies with Olympus, Medtronic, Boston Scientific, Fujifilm and research support from AI Medical alongside BPA 3 and BPA 6 on endoscopic platforms, image enhancement and artificial intelligence - but discloses no management of those conflicts. A value position is clearly operating and is even visible in the text ("the lack of strong scientific evidence has not delayed other countries... from advocating for and implementing risk-based GC screening" and the framing that equity considerations justify acting on indirect evidence), yet it is never declared as the panel's own value judgement or examined for how it tilted the benefit-harm interpretation toward action. There is no described method for integrating values, no consensus, voting or disagreement-resolution procedure among the four authors, and no mechanism for incorporating differing stakeholder perspectives.

items.text: The purpose of the recommendation is clear and actionable
items.rationaleA: The stated objective - 'to provide best practice advice for primary and secondary prevention of GC in the context of current clinical practice and evidence in the United States' - is matched item-for-item by the 15 statements, which cover who to screen, how to perform and document the examination, what to do with each finding, and when to stop. The document is openly and coherently an advocacy instrument as well as a practice one, calling for research funding, insurance coverage, training infrastructure and equity action, and it describes anticipated impacts at each level: for patients, a stage shift toward curable disease modelled on Korea and Japan; for endoscopy units, higher detection standards and ESD capacity; for the system, programmatic screening sustained by the three foundational pillars of Figure 2. The main gap is that no US-specific projection of benefit, harm or volume is offered, so the anticipated impact remains argued by analogy rather than estimated.
items.rationaleB: The stated objective - "to provide best practice advice for primary and secondary prevention of GC in the context of current clinical practice and evidence in the United States" - is matched by the statements themselves, which span primary prevention (BPA 4, H pylori test-and-treat including familial-based testing), secondary prevention (BPA 1-3, 8-9), management (BPA 10-13), de-escalation (BPA 14) and equity/policy (BPA 15). Anticipated impacts are described at every level with reference cases rather than assertion: population impact via the Korean and Japanese stage shift (60%-70% of GCs now diagnosed at a curable stage; survival >70%), organisational impact via pathology reporting consistency, training and ESD capacity, and system impact via insurance coverage and research funding. The document also explicitly frames itself as filling a guidance gap ("There are no established screening guidelines for GC"), so the advocacy purpose and the recommendation set are congruent. It stops short of exemplary because the anticipated magnitude of impact in the US - how many cancers or deaths averted, at what endoscopic volume - is never estimated.

items.text: The recommendation is feasible for local application and adoption
items.rationaleA: The change required from current US practice is stated frankly - endoscopists are 'unfamiliar with the characteristic visual features' of GIM and dysplasia, risk-stratification parameters 'are inconsistently reported on US pathology reports', and ESD proficiency is still concentrated in high-volume centres - and Figure 1 gives a usable clinical pathway from index EGD through each finding. Resource and cost considerations are handled seriously (cost-effectiveness of EGD at the time of colonoscopy, the non-cost-effectiveness of universal H pylori screening and biennial stand-alone EGD, endoscopic capacity, environmental sustainability), and dissemination factors, training needs, pathologist-endoscopist coordination and patient navigation are all named. What is missing is anything the reader can pick up and use: no quality indicators with thresholds (detection metrics 'should be established' but none are specified), no audit or monitoring dataset, no local adaptation guidance for differing practice settings, and no patient-facing or implementation tools accompany the advice.
items.rationaleB: The degree of change from current US practice is stated plainly and is large - from no organised screening to risk-based opportunistic screening, standardised Sydney-System biopsy sets, standardised pathology reporting, and referral pathways to ESD centres - and Figure 1 plus Figure 2 give usable adoption scaffolding. Resource and cost considerations are handled seriously for a practice update: existing cost-effectiveness analyses are cited for and against specific strategies, the "main considerations are cost, resource utilization, and environmental considerations," and personnel competency needs (endoscopist detection skills, gastric ESD proficiency, experienced GI pathologist review) are repeatedly specified. Dissemination barriers are enumerated concretely (language, education, transportation, insurance, access). The gap is measurement and adaptation: the guideline says "detection metrics established and adhered to" but defines no target thresholds, specifies no audit or monitoring data, offers no quality indicators analogous to adenoma detection rate despite invoking that analogy, and provides no guidance on which statements need local adaptation versus uniform application.

guidelineTitle: The Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian Sleep Society Guideline on the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea in children
source:
Canadian Journal of Respiratory, Critical Care, and Sleep
Medicine
organization: The Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian Sleep Society
recommendationText: We suggest that the following tests should not be used to diagnose osa in children: Physiological measures of airway function analyzed with machine learning algorithms

pico.intervention: Physiological measures of airway function analyzed with machine learning algorithms
pico.comparator: Physiological measures of airway function analyzed without machine learning algorithms

items.appraisal: The objective is explicit: help clinicians choose appropriate testing to identify OSA in children, through evidence-based recommendations, with the intended benefit of improving care and clinical outcomes. The guideline also explicitly excludes treatment. This provides the health intent, target population, and expected benefit required for the top anchor.

The foreground question is explicit: whether alternative measures should be used to diagnose OSA in children. Population = children with suspected OSA; intervention = alternative diagnostic tests; comparator = PSG; outcome = diagnosis/diagnostic accuracy. Thus, four PICOS components are identifiable, but a study-design component is not part of the stated clinical question. The supplied rubric awards 6 for four PICOS elements and 7 for all five.

The guideline states that it applies to all children <18 years with suspected OSA. Age and clinical status are clear, but detailed guideline-population characteristics such as severity/staging, sex, and explicit population-level inclusion/exclusion criteria are not comprehensively specified.

There were 14 voting members spanning pediatric respiratory/sleep medicine, neurology/sleep medicine, otolaryngology, general pediatrics, family medicine and fellows, supported by a methodologist, knowledge-mobilization specialist and project manager. Participating professional organizations are identified, and author affiliations provide institutions/geography.

No child or parent with OSA lived experience sat on the panel, but KidsCan YPRAG youth underwent a structured 60-minute consultation involving review of materials and open-ended questions. A summary was supplied to the chair and explicitly presented to the panel during recommendation formulation. This is substantially more than merely stating that preferences were considered.

Target users are explicitly identified and their intended use is clear: practitioners making diagnostic decisions, including GPs, pediatricians, subspecialists, ENT specialists, psychologists/psychiatrists and NPs, plus policy makers, patients/families, researchers and knowledge-translation specialists.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search for evidence
items.appraisal: Databases are identified—MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library and PubMed—as are the general MeSH/free-text concepts, date range and exact initial/update dates. The article states that the detailed reproducible strategy is in OLS eTable 1/eAppendix 1. Under your scoring prompt, database + search terms + search time supports about 5, while 6–7 requires a complete strategy. Because that OLS was not part of the uploaded file, I score this conservatively.

Eligibility is detailed: children 0–17, laboratory PSG as reference standard, alternative diagnostic test as index test, no study-design restriction, language restrictions specified, dual independent screening and consensus resolution. Quantitative-synthesis eligibility is also explicitly defined.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of evidence clearly stated
items.appraisal: QUADAS-2 was used for risk of bias/applicability and GRADE assessed risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias and effect magnitude. The guideline then discusses heterogeneity, inconsistent OSA definitions, lack of replication, limited data in younger children and exclusion of children with comorbidities, and uses these limitations to constrain recommendations.

The process is unusually explicit: four virtual sessions, presentation of GRADE summaries, draft → discussion → revision → voting; a five-option vote; predefined 80% acceptance threshold; repeat discussion/revision when threshold not met; and final online confirmation.

items.text: Benefits, side effects and risks considered
items.appraisal: The recommendation process explicitly considered the balance of desirable/undesirable effects, preferences, resource use, equity, acceptability and feasibility. The recommendation text also discusses concrete benefits and harms—for example improved access versus safety risks of unmonitored testing, including accidental strangulation/entanglement.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and evidence
items.appraisal: Table 1 directly pairs recommendations with certainty of evidence, strength of recommendation and corresponding evidence tables/figures. The surrounding recommendation sections then explain the underlying studies and quantitative results.

The CTS independently invited four external and two internal content experts; one internal reviewer conducted an AGREE appraisal. The lead author responded to comments, the manuscript was revised, reviews and the AGREE II scoresheet went to the CRGC, and final organizational approval followed. The named expert reviewers and affiliations are also reported.

There is an explicit three-year review interval or earlier update if needed, a standing CTS Sleep Assembly committee, continuous McMaster Plus alerts starting from the final search date, and new evidence is specified as a trigger for considering a timely update.

Recommendation 1 specifies the test, position in pathway (“alternative/2nd line”), population (>5 years, otherwise healthy), precise clinical circumstance (PSG effectively absent), evidence quality and recommendation strength. Recommendations 2–3 similarly use explicit directive language.

PSG remains the diagnostic standard; L3/HSAT is identified as a conditional second-line alternative; PSQ/oximetry are adjuncts but not stand-alone diagnostic tests; numerous other approaches are explicitly advised against. Selection criteria and relative positioning are therefore clear.
Recommendations are numbered and prominently formatted, and Table 1 summarizes them together with evidence certainty, recommendation strength, clinical remarks and evidence sources.

items.text: Facilitators and barriers to application described
items.appraisal: Important barriers/facilitators are discussed in meaningful detail: limited PSG access, wait/travel burden, regulatory and funding differences, provider training, home-testing preferences, safety, and equity. These considerations explicitly affected the recommendations—the “effectively absent” PSG condition is an example. The guideline also states that implementation will require pediatric L3/HSAT standards, regulatory/funding changes, education and training.

items.text: Advice/tools for putting recommendations into practice
items.appraisal: There is useful clinical guidance and “clinical remarks,” but the uploaded guideline does not provide a dedicated implementation tool such as an algorithm, checklist, pathway, audit instrument, decision aid or ready-to-use protocol. Indeed, it says standards for L3/HSAT testing/reporting and provider education still need to be developed. Under your Item 19 rubric, implementation discussion without a qualifying practical tool falls in the lower-middle range.

Resource use was expressly considered during recommendation formulation. The text addresses family travel/time costs, possible health-system savings, PSG expense and provincial/territorial funding coverage. However, there is no formal economic evaluation or sufficiently detailed cost-effectiveness analysis to justify 6–7 under the supplied rubric.

I found no implementation audit criteria, measurable quality indicators, target standards, measurement frequency or instructions for assessing adherence to the recommendations. References to physiological “monitoring” concern diagnostic technology, not auditing guideline implementation.

items.text: Funding body did not influence guideline content
items.appraisal: The guideline explicitly states functional/editorial independence, no direct external funding, and that no funder participated in collection, review, analysis or interpretation of evidence or decisions concerning key messages. It separately states no funding associated with the work. This directly meets the highest scoring anchor.

Members declared potential conflicts on establishment of the panel and annually thereafter; declarations are available through CTS, and members were selected according to the CTS Conflict of Interest Policy. This demonstrates systematic collection and a management framework, but the article itself does not describe individual conflicts or explicitly explain how each conflict did/did not influence recommendation deliberations, so I would stop short of 7.

items.text: The evidence supporting the recommendation is applicable to the clinical question at hand
items.rationaleA: Each of the three recommendations carries an explicit certainty rating in Table 1 tied to named evidence tables, underpinned by a registered systematic review (CRD42020157842) with QUADAS-2 risk-of-bias assessment, GRADE certainty grading, and sROC meta-analysis reporting sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios and I-squared inconsistency (Table 2), with directness limitations quantified (67% of L3/HSAT studies excluded comorbidities; only one study included children under 2). Precision is transparently reported, including absurdly wide intervals such as LR+ 10.78 (0.007-15562.6), and the text warns that 'inconsistency was high for sensitivity or specificity for all comparison so results must be interpreted with caution'; harms (accidental strangulation with unmonitored testing) are weighed explicitly. The main defect is congruence: Recommendation 1 is graded 'Strong' on 'Low to Moderate' certainty with acknowledged non-generalizability, and no GRADE justification is offered for this discordance. Minor internal inconsistencies also appear between the abstract (62%/26% comorbidity exclusion, 13% under 2 years) and the body (58%/17%, 12%), and between the stated median sample sizes (38 vs 96).
items.rationaleB: Each of the three recommendations carries an explicit GRADE certainty rating linked to named evidence tables (Table 1), and the underlying systematic review used QUADAS-2 for risk of bias, reported sensitivity/specificity with 95% confidence intervals and I2 statistics (Table 2), and flagged that "Inconsistency was high for sensitivity or specificity for all comparison so results must be interpreted with caution." Directness is handled unusually well: the panel repeatedly quantifies indirectness (67% of L3/HSAT studies excluded comorbidities, only one study included children <2 years, median age 10.7 years) and uses it to narrow Recommendation 1 to "otherwise healthy children over 5-years of age." Weaknesses are that publication bias is listed as a GRADE component considered but never reported as a finding in the main text, QUADAS-2 summaries sit only in the online supplement, and Recommendation 1 is graded Strong on Low-to-Moderate evidence — a discordant pairing justified narratively by access and equity but not framed as an explicit GRADE discordant-recommendation rationale.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target users it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The 'Target population and users' section names the intended users concretely (general practitioners, general pediatricians, pediatric subspecialists, otolaryngologists, child psychiatrists and psychologists, nurse practitioners) and qualifies them as those who 'have the appropriate training to make diagnostic decisions about OSA', and all three recommendations are ordering/interpretation decisions squarely within that scope. Conditions of use are operationally specified (L3/HSAT only for otherwise healthy children over 5 years where PSG access is 'effectively absent'), and Recommendation 2 usefully preserves the adjunct roles clinicians already use PSQ and oximetry for (screening, triage, post-operative risk). Weaknesses: the 'Strong' grade on Recommendation 1 sits uneasily with the acknowledged evidence limitations and the strangulation risk, and 'effectively absent' is deliberately left for users to operationalise, with the panel conceding it 'may vary across jurisdictions'. Including child psychiatrists and psychologists among target users also stretches the alignment between scope of practice and the recommended actions.
items.rationaleB: Target users are named specifically ("general practitioners, general pediatricians, pediatric subspecialists, otolaryngologists, child psychiatrists, child psychologists and nurse practitioners") and the clinical problem — PSG being inaccessible in most jurisdictions — is precisely the one these clinicians face, with the panel itself including family medicine, otolaryngology and pediatrics. The recommended actions are concrete and within scope, and the "clinical remarks" rows in Table 1 usefully bound them (age, comorbidity, strangulation risk). However, the fit is uneven across the user list: several named users (child psychiatrists, psychologists, many GPs) cannot order or interpret L3/HSAT, and the guideline concedes that uptake "will require the development of standards for L3/HSAT testing and reporting in children ... and education and training for providers" without saying what those are. No diagnostic algorithm or pathway is provided, and Recommendations 2 and 3 tell users what not to use without offering a fallback for the large groups Recommendation 1 excludes (children under 5, children with comorbidities) where PSG is effectively absent.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target patients/populations it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The Introduction grounds the problem in patient-important outcomes (learning and memory, behaviour, mood, metabolic and cardiovascular sequelae, healthcare utilisation), and the guideline is candid that the reviewed evidence measures diagnostic accuracy rather than these outcomes, even noting that 'the AHI does not accurately predict OSA-related morbidity or outcomes in adults or children'. Tailoring is a genuine strength: recommendations are bounded by age (over 5 years; data gap under 2), by medical complexity, and the Discussion documents differential PSQ performance in craniofacial disorders, sickle cell anemia, Marfan syndrome and asthma (sensitivity 0.37-0.84 across comorbidity groups). The limiting factor is that the recommended alternative pathway excludes children under 5 and children with comorbidities, who are precisely the groups facing the greatest access barriers, leaving them without an actionable option; and how the importance of outcomes to patients was determined rests on a single youth consultation.
items.rationaleB: Tailoring is a genuine strength: the recommendations are explicitly conditioned on age (<2, <5, >5 years) and medical complexity, and the Discussion documents differential test performance in craniofacial disorders, sickle cell anemia, Marfan syndrome, asthma and Down syndrome, with an explicit equity observation that lack of alternatives "may perpetuate limitations in access to diagnostic testing and health disparities in children at risk for OSA." The Introduction connects OSA to outcomes children and families care about (neurocognition, behavior, mood, metabolic and cardiovascular consequences) and the Discussion cites the three adenotonsillectomy RCTs showing gains in behavior and quality of life. The limitation is that the review's own outcomes are purely diagnostic-accuracy metrics (sensitivity, specificity, AUC); no downstream patient-important outcome was measured, no outcome-prioritisation exercise with patients is reported, and the consequences of false positives and false negatives for a child are only asserted in passing rather than modelled.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target users
items.rationaleA: Target-user values were captured structurally: the 14-member voting panel was constituted from nominations by the CSS, Canadian Paediatric Society, College of Family Physicians of Canada and Canadian Society of Otolaryngology, and 'acceptability and feasibility of implementation including access to testing' is listed among the formal formulation considerations, with a defined proposal-discussion-revision-voting cycle and an 80% agreement threshold. The guideline differentiates where clinical flexibility remains (Recommendation 2's clinical remarks explicitly preserve PSQ and oximetry as adjuncts 'commonly used in clinical practice as initial screening or for triaging'), and notes that adoption will need 'education and training for providers'. However, no clinician values were sought outside the panel and its six peer reviewers, workflow adaptation and new skills required for L3/HSAT are named only in passing, and the range of actions acceptable to the wider clinical community is inferred from the vote rather than described.
items.rationaleB: Clinician values were captured principally through a 14-member multidisciplinary voting panel nominated by CSS, the Canadian Paediatric Society, the College of Family Physicians and the Canadian Society of Otolaryngology, using a documented five-option ballot with an 80% threshold and iterative re-voting; the guideline reports the resulting agreement ("All recommendations ultimately received 100% support ... with some recommendations requiring additional discussion and a second round of voting"). Acceptability and feasibility were named as formulation criteria, and Recommendation 2 is a direct accommodation of clinical practice — rather than banning the PSQ and oximetry outright, the panel preserved their established roles "as initial screening or for triaging of polysomnography, to determine post-operative surgical risks." What is missing is any elicitation beyond the panel itself: no survey or consultation of practising target users, and almost nothing on workflow disruption, new skills or the practical burden of adopting home testing beyond a single clause about "education and training for providers."

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target patients/populations
items.rationaleA: The guideline is commendably transparent that 'there were no children or parents with lived experience of OSA participating in the guideline panel', and the entire patient input consists of one 60-minute consultation with the KidsCan YPRAG (youths aged 13-19), summarised to the Chair and presented to the panel; a parent representative appears only in the acknowledgments as a reviewer. That input demonstrably shaped the text - burden factors are named ('limits costs of travel and time away from school or work'), and the panel qualifies the preference honestly: 'while patient and family preferences support testing that is close to or in the home, this preference was expressed in the context of an accurate test'. But no families of younger children or children with comorbidities were consulted, the guideline never differentiates where patient choice should carry more or less weight in the testing decision, and no patient decision aids or information tools are proposed or recommended.
items.rationaleB: The panel ran a structured consultation with the KidsCan Young Persons Research Advisory Group (a 60-minute session with youth aged 13-19, materials reviewed plus facilitated open-ended questions, summarised back to the panel as a formulation input), and its output is traceable through the recommendations: the preference for home testing is invoked in support of Recommendation 1, in the burden argument ("limits costs of travel and time away from school or work"), and in the closing call for "further investment ... in developing accurate and accessible home-based testing options." The panel also handled the preference with appropriate nuance, noting it "was expressed in the context of an accurate test. Accordingly, access to PSG must be maintained, if not enhanced." Against this, the guideline states plainly that "There were no children or parents with lived experience of OSA participating in the guideline panel"; a single youth consultation cannot represent parents of infants or children with medical complexity, no formal preference elicitation was done, and the guideline never states where patient choice should carry more or less weight nor whether decision aids would help.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of policy/decision makers
items.rationaleA: Decision-makers are an explicitly named audience ('local, provincial, and national policy makers and funders'), and the guideline states the policy changes needed: implementation 'will require the development of standards for L3/HSAT testing and reporting in children, potential updates to provincial/territorial regulatory and funding approvals and education and training for providers', alongside calls that 'access to PSG must be maintained, if not enhanced' and that 'further investment is needed in developing accurate and accessible home-based testing options'. It cites the CDA/AMC report on federal, provincial and territorial coverage of diagnostic sleep studies, noting coverage varies and pediatric-specific data are absent. Equity is treated substantively rather than as boilerplate - health equity was a formal formulation consideration, geographic disparities are cited, and the panel warns that the lack of alternatives for high-risk groups 'may perpetuate limitations in access to diagnostic testing and health disparities'. What is missing is any economic modelling or budget-impact estimate; the claim that L3/HSAT 'may reduce costs to the healthcare system' is asserted, not analysed, and no payer or policy representative sat on the panel.
items.rationaleB: Policy considerations are not an afterthought here — they generate the guideline's central recommendation. Decision makers are named as an intended audience ("local, provincial, and national policy makers and funders"), resource use and health equity are listed among the explicit formulation criteria, and the panel cites the CDA/AMC report on "federal, provincial and territorial coverage of diagnostic sleep studies" while noting it contains nothing pediatric-specific. The document names the precise policy levers required: "potential updates to provincial/territorial regulatory and funding approvals," development of L3/HSAT standards, and continued investment in PSG capacity to "reduce wait times." Equity runs through the text (geographic disparities in PSG access, the risk of perpetuating "health disparities in children at risk for OSA," and a call for future studies in racially diverse and socioeconomically disadvantaged children). The gap is that no funder or policy maker appears to have been consulted or seated on the panel, and no costing accompanies the funding recommendations.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of the guideline developers
items.rationaleA: Beyond the conflict-of-interest declarations and the editorial independence statement, the guideline does name the value set the panel applied - 'the quality of the evidence, the balance of desirable and undesirable effects, child and family preferences and values, resource use, health equity and acceptability and feasibility of implementation' - and describes the voting mechanism as its method for integrating differing views, reporting that all recommendations ultimately reached 100% support with some requiring a second round. A clear developer value is visible in the reasoning for diverging from the AASM 2017 position, justified by the panel's judgment that 'access to testing is the most pressing issue in the field of pediatric OSA'. What is absent is any account of the values individual members or the represented disciplines brought (surgical versus sleep-medicine versus primary-care perspectives), which recommendations were contested and how disagreement was resolved beyond a tally, and, most importantly, an explicit statement of how developer values tipped the benefit-harm interpretation far enough to justify a 'Strong' recommendation over acknowledged strangulation and misclassification risks.
items.rationaleB: There is a well-specified method for integrating differing perspectives — the iterative propose/discuss/revise/vote cycle with an 80% agreement threshold, revised ballot options if the threshold failed, and a confirmatory online poll — plus a list of the considerations panellists were asked to weigh ("the quality of the evidence, the balance of desirable and undesirable effects, child and family preferences and values, resource use, health equity and acceptability and feasibility of implementation"). Editorial independence and annual COI declarations under the CTS policy are documented, but the rubric treats COI disclosure as insufficient on its own. What is absent is any statement of the values the developers themselves brought: the panel plainly weighted access and equity heavily enough to issue a Strong recommendation on Low-to-Moderate evidence and to depart from the AASM 2017 position, yet that value judgement is never declared as such, nor is it explained how developer values shaped the interpretation of benefits versus harms (for example, tolerance for the false-positive rate implied by an L3/HSAT specificity of 0.57).

items.text: The purpose of the recommendation is clear and actionable
items.rationaleA: The Objectives section states a clear implementation goal - 'to help clinicians to choose appropriate testing to identify OSA in children' and 'to offer practical guidance to all clinical practitioners... in order to improve the care and clinical outcomes of these children' - and each recommendation is a directly actionable testing decision that serves it. Anticipated impacts are described across levels: for patients and families (Recommendation 1's clinical remark that L3/HSAT 'is likely to improve access to testing in areas where polysomnography is effectively absent', with reduced travel and time away from school or work), for systems (possible cost reduction, regulatory and funding change, preserving PSG capacity), and as an advocacy and research agenda directed at 'scientists and private industry'. Anticipated harms of adoption are also stated rather than glossed. It falls short of exemplary because no impact is quantified and no framework is offered for evaluating whether adoption achieves the stated goals.
items.rationaleB: The stated purpose — "to help clinicians to choose appropriate testing to identify OSA in children" and "to offer practical guidance to all clinical practitioners ... in order to improve the care and clinical outcomes of these children" — matches what the three recommendations actually do, and the guideline pursues all three implementation goals the item names: practice change (adopt L3/HSAT where PSG is absent; stop using PSQ, oximetry, BMI and airway descriptors as diagnostic tests), policy change (regulatory/funding approvals, PSG investment), and advocacy plus a detailed research agenda for industry and researchers. Anticipated impacts are described across levels: for children and families (improved access, less travel, less time away from school and work, but also the safety risk of unmonitored testing), for the system ("may reduce costs to the healthcare system," "likely to improve access to testing in areas where polysomnography is effectively absent"), and for organisations (need for L3/HSAT testing and reporting standards). These impacts remain qualitative and unquantified — no projected uptake, no estimate of how many children would be diagnosed differently.

items.text: The recommendation is feasible for local application and adoption
items.rationaleA: The guideline is clear about the change required from current practice - it explicitly diverges from the AASM 2017 position against HSAT in children, and constrains tests (PSQ, oximetry) that it acknowledges are already in routine use - and it is unusually good at flagging where local adaptation governs, conceding that 'effectively absent' will be 'impacted by provincial/territorial regulatory frameworks' and wait, travel and cost realities. Prerequisites for adoption are named (testing and reporting standards for children, regulatory and funding approvals, provider education), resource considerations are discussed qualitatively, a knowledge mobilization specialist supported the project, and a three-year living-guideline update cycle with McMaster Plus alerting is defined. However the guideline supplies no implementation tools at all: no care algorithm, no patient or family materials, no formal cost-effectiveness or economic analysis, no specified competencies or training curriculum, no data or audit criteria for monitoring uptake, and no strategies for overcoming the funding and provider acceptability barriers it itself identifies.
items.rationaleB: The guideline is clear about the magnitude of change required — Recommendation 1 "diverges from the AASM 2017 recommendation that recommends L3/HSAT should not be used in children" — and it explicitly flags where local adaptation governs, conceding that "the definition of 'effectively absent' may vary across jurisdictions and will be impacted by provincial/territorial regulatory frameworks" and by wait times, travel and cost. It names real implementation prerequisites (testing and reporting standards, regulatory and funding approvals, provider education) and one concrete safety barrier (accidental strangulation from unmonitored home equipment), and the CTS Living Guideline Model with three-yearly review and McMaster Plus alerts covers currency. But almost none of the item's tooling is delivered: no formal economic or cost-effectiveness analysis despite recommendations that require new provincial funding, no algorithm, checklist, patient material or audit tool, no specification of the personnel competencies needed to score pediatric L3/HSAT, no data requirements or monitoring plan, and no criteria for measuring implementation or quality improvement. "Effectively absent" is left operationally undefined, which is candid but leaves adopters without a usable threshold.

guidelineTitle: Clinical practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of melanoma
recommendationText: There is insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of automated instruments for the clinical diagnosis of primary melanoma. However, particularly when a benign measurement is found using the cited protocols of Nevisense™ and MelaFind™, this information may aid the clinician.
aiInput: Multispectral skin images (MelaFind), eElectrical impedance signals (Nevisense)

pico.outcomes: Diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity/specificity); potential usefulness of benign measurement to aid clinician

items.appraisal: The purpose is clear: revision of the previous melanoma guideline in response to major developments in melanoma diagnosis, staging and management. The development appendix explains why revision was necessary, particularly because of major changes in treatment and evidence since the earlier guideline.

Excellent. Twenty-three priority questions were initially identified, and the guideline provides a detailed list of clinical questions covering risk, diagnosis, biopsy, treatment, follow-up and other areas.

The population is generally clear throughout the guideline—people with or at risk of melanoma—with subpopulations defined for individual questions, including high-risk patients, different melanoma stages, children, pregnancy and uncommon melanoma types. However, there is not one exceptionally concise overarching population statement covering all inclusion/exclusion characteristics.

Strong multidisciplinary development. A Management Committee established a wider multidisciplinary working party and question-specific expert subcommittees. GP representatives were also specifically included.

Two consumer representatives were formally appointed to the working party. In addition, drafts underwent public consultation, with submissions invited from the public, consumer groups, professional societies and other stakeholders.

The intended clinical audience is evident and includes clinicians involved in melanoma diagnosis and management, including primary care and specialist disciplines. The dissemination strategy specifically targets professional groups, medical students, learned colleges, residents and registrars. However, the target-user definition could have been presented more explicitly in a single dedicated statement.

items.text: Systematic methods used to search evidence
items.appraisal: Excellent. PICO-based systematic searches were undertaken using PubMed, Embase, TRIP, Cochrane and other databases, with CINAHL and PsycINFO for psychosocial questions. Snowballing and other sources were also used.
Predefined inclusion/exclusion criteria were used. Title/abstract screening was followed by full-text screening; two reviewers assessed full texts, with a third reviewer resolving disagreements.

items.text: Strengths and limitations of evidence described
items.appraisal: Evidence was critically appraised and graded, and limitations are explicitly discussed. For example, individual sections describe limitations such as short follow-up, recruitment issues and applicability concerns.

Very strong. Recommendations were developed by subcommittees, circulated to the full working party, discussed individually and approved through a consensus/voting process. Evidence-based recommendations, consensus recommendations and practice points are distinguished.

Benefits and harms are repeatedly considered in recommendation development—for example survival, morbidity, toxicity, quality of life and complications. The guideline explicitly contrasts treatment benefits against adverse outcomes in relevant sections.

items.text: Explicit link between recommendations and evidence
items.appraisal: Excellent. Evidence summaries, levels of evidence, references, recommendations and grades are presented together. The guideline explicitly distinguishes evidence-based recommendations from consensus recommendations and practice points.

There was extensive staged public consultation. Professional societies, consumer organisations, other stakeholders and the public were invited to comment, and submitted evidence was methodologically assessed. This is strong external consultation, although it is not described quite as clearly as a separately constituted independent expert peer-review panel.

Excellent. The wiki infrastructure permits continuous evidence surveillance. Literature updates are monitored, the working party can trigger revision when new high-level evidence emerges, and external stakeholders can flag new evidence.
Recommendations generally identify the population/intervention and intended action clearly. For example, recommendations specify surveillance intervals and modalities for very-high-risk patients.

Multiple diagnostic and treatment alternatives are presented across the guideline, including surgery, systemic therapy, radiotherapy, surveillance and other approaches. Treatment algorithms/flowcharts are also used.
Excellent presentation. Evidence summaries, evidence-based recommendations, grades, consensus recommendations and practice points are visually/structurally distinguished throughout.

The guideline explicitly recognizes that implementation barriers differ by setting and that incentives and planned implementation strategies may be required. However, specific barriers and facilitators are not systematically identified for each major recommendation.

Several implementation mechanisms are proposed: CME, interactive learning, electronic decision support, decision aids and clinical/audit tools. The wiki itself improves accessibility. However, several tools are described as things that may be developed rather than fully operational implementation packages.

Resource/cost implications are considered for some clinical questions. For example, structured surveillance is discussed in terms of cost-effectiveness and estimated savings/QALY gains. However, there is not a comprehensive resource-impact assessment accompanying all major recommendations.

The developers plan web-analytics monitoring and mention development of audit/clinical tools. However, the guideline does not provide a strong, systematic set of measurable clinical audit criteria, performance indicators, thresholds or explicit monitoring outcomes for implementation.

Funding and in-kind contributions are transparently reported: Cancer Council Australia and Melanoma Institute Australia contributed resources, and Skin Cancer College Australasia provided additional funding for a project officer. However, I do not find an equally explicit statement that the funding bodies had no influence on guideline content, which AGREE II specifically looks for.

Very strong. Declarations were collected from nominated members, evaluated by the Management Committee, and members were required to update them throughout development, with reminders before formal meetings. A declarations-of-interest register is included.
