items.text: The evidence supporting the recommendation is applicable to the clinical question at hand
items.rationaleA: Each evidence-based recommendation sits directly beneath an 'Evidence summary' table giving evidence statements, NHMRC levels (I to IV) and citations, and each recommendation carries an A-D grade formally derived from volume, consistency, clinical impact, generalisability and applicability (Appendix 19.1, Tables 1-3); risk of bias was assessed in duplicate. However, the NHMRC scheme is design-based rather than a certainty-of-evidence judgement: precision (confidence intervals), publication bias, confounding and dose-response are nowhere addressed, and the evidence tables report levels but not effect estimates. The larger problem for recommendation quality is dilution - roughly twice as many 'practice points' as graded recommendations, all expert opinion 'outside the scope of the search strategy', with no evidence link at all. There are also congruence lapses: acral/subungual melanoma is directed to 'partial digital amputation' and margins 'might be modified' on a Grade D body of evidence, phrased as settled practice rather than with the caution Grade D demands.
items.rationaleB: Every evidence-based recommendation carries an NHMRC Grade (A-D) and is preceded by an evidence summary table giving NHMRC levels of evidence and citations, and the grading matrix in Table 2 explicitly scores volume/risk of bias, consistency, clinical impact, generalisability and applicability, so risk of bias, consistency and directness are systematically handled. However, precision (confidence intervals) and publication bias are nowhere assessed, there are no summary-of-findings tables giving absolute magnitudes of benefit and harm, and much of the base is adapted from the 2012 German S3 systematic reviews with only updated searches. Congruence between strength and certainty is inconsistent: the melanoma in situ margin recommendation is Grade D yet states margins 'should be 5-10 mm' and that 'positive histological margins are unacceptable', and the Grade C follow-up recommendation prescribes an exact interval schedule (annually for 10 years for stage I, etc.) despite a weak body of evidence. A very large share of the guidance (hundreds of 'practice points') is expert opinion outside the systematic review scope and is presented in the same visual format as graded recommendations.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target users it is intended for
items.rationaleA: The clinical problem is maximally relevant to the intended Australasian audience ('Australia and New Zealand have the highest incidence of melanoma in the world'), and most recommendations are concretely actionable within a defined scope of practice - specific radial margins per T category (1 cm for pT1, 2 cm for pT4), SLNB thresholds (>1 mm, or >0.75 mm with high-risk features), 6-monthly full skin examination with total body photography, and practice points that route work appropriately ('SLNB should be performed in a centre with expertise in the procedure, including nuclear medicine, surgery and pathology'). The working party included two GP representatives alongside dermatology, surgery, pathology, radiation and medical oncology. The guideline nevertheless never states its intended target users anywhere: there is no scope-and-purpose statement, so a GP must infer unaided which of the 19 chapters are primary-care actionable and which belong to tertiary melanoma centres, and the imperative wording of several Grade C/D recommendations overstates the harm-benefit certainty.
items.rationaleB: The recommendations map onto the full Australian melanoma care pathway and are largely actionable, specifying who should act and where: 'Clinicians who are performing skin examinations ... should be trained in and use dermoscopy' (Grade A), 'SLNB should be performed in a centre with expertise in the procedure, including nuclear medicine, surgery and pathology', BRAF testing 'in an accredited laboratory', and referral of >1 mm melanomas for multidisciplinary discussion. Applicability to the Australian healthcare context is a formal component of the NHMRC grading matrix, and two GP representatives sat on the working party, so primary care as well as specialist scope of practice is represented. Weaknesses: the document never states its intended target users in a scope statement (they must be inferred from the Multidisciplinary care chapter, section 18.1), and directive 'should' phrasing on Grade C/D recommendations overstates the benefit-harm trade-off for users who cannot see the underlying uncertainty.

items.text: The recommendation is applicable to the target patients/populations it is intended for
items.rationaleA: Outcomes used are patient-important - melanoma-specific and overall survival, recurrence, complication rates, lymphoedema, disfigurement, anxiety and quality of life (e.g. the CLND chapter states all patients 'are exposed to the risk of morbidity that can compromise quality of life', listing wound problems, fibrosis and lymphoedema). Tailoring by disease characteristics is a real strength: dedicated chapters for melanoma in children, melanoma in pregnancy, MelTUMPs, desmoplastic/neurotropic, mucosal and ocular melanoma, plus site-specific advice for head and neck and acral lesions. But the guideline never reports how the importance of outcomes to patients was determined - PICO outcomes were set by lead authors, not rated by patients - and quality of life is repeatedly named as a gap ('there are no good data assessing the quality of life implications of avoiding CLND') rather than built into recommendations. Demographic tailoring is absent: no mention of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Māori (despite the New Zealand scope), skin of colour, comorbidity or socioeconomic circumstance.
items.rationaleB: Patient-important outcomes are genuinely present in the reasoning, not just survival: the complete node dissection chapter weighs 3-year melanoma-specific survival against 'wound healing problems, cosmetic issues, sensory and motor neural disruption, fibrosis and tightness, limitations in range of movement and lymphoedema', and section 6.1.2 quotes the Cochrane review that 'quality of life after surgery is an important consideration and unnecessary disfigurement should be avoided'. Recommendations are well tailored by Breslow thickness, stage, tumour subtype (lentigo maligna, desmoplastic/neurotropic, acral, ocular, mucosal) and by population, with dedicated chapters on melanoma in children (Ch. 7), MelTUMPs (Ch. 8) and melanoma in pregnancy (Ch. 9). The guideline never reports how the importance of outcomes to patients was determined (no rating exercise, no patient-prioritised outcome set in the PICOs), and the acknowledged gap that 'there are no good data assessing the quality of life implications of avoiding CLND' is flagged as future research rather than reflected in the recommendation. There is also no consideration of skin type/ethnicity or of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations anywhere in the document.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target users
items.rationaleA: Clinician views were procedurally sought - every recommendation and practice point was 'tabled as an agenda point', discussed and 'approved once the eligible panelists reached consensus, which was reached by voting', and six rounds of public consultation invited submissions from professional societies. Acceptability and feasibility for users are addressed in substance in places: dermoscopy carries a Grade A recommendation that clinicians 'should be trained in and use' it, and SLNB is restricted to high-volume centres because 'complication rates are inversely related to procedure volume'. Clinical flexibility is signalled ('Excision margins might be modified to accommodate individual anatomic sites or functional considerations'; margins depending on 'prevailing surgeon/patient preferences'). What is missing is any explicit account of user values: no elicitation or survey of clinician preferences, no discussion of workflow or routine adaptation burden, no description of the range of practice acceptable to the clinical community, and no acknowledgement of the genuine professional disagreement over SLNB and CLND, which is presented as evidentially settled.
items.rationaleB: Clinician acceptability is addressed indirectly but concretely: practice points describe workflow and setting ('Most primary melanomas can be treated as an outpatient under local anaesthesia or as a day-case'), new skills are named as prerequisites (formal dermoscopy training, expert SLNB centres, expert dermatopathology review), and clinical flexibility is explicitly demarcated - partial biopsies are acceptable 'in carefully selected clinical circumstances ... and in the hands of experienced clinicians'. Six rounds of public consultation with professional societies and a face-to-face working party meeting at which 'each recommendation and practice point was tabled as an agenda point' and approved by voting are the mechanisms by which the clinical community's views entered. But no survey or formal elicitation of target users' values was undertaken, the range of actions acceptable to the clinical community is not described except by implication, and the one acknowledged practice-context tension - 'This may present logistic difficulties in regional and remote areas' - is left as an unfinished sentence with no guidance attached.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of target patients/populations
items.rationaleA: Two consumer/patient advocates sat on the working party and are named on some question subcommittees, and one chapter handles preference-sensitivity well: the follow-up recommendation states 'individual patient's needs should be considered before appropriate follow-up is offered', with Notes explaining that some patients 'may prefer more frequent follow-up for reassurance, while others may prefer less frequent follow-up because of the anxiety... or the time and expense associated with attendance'. Practice points require that patients being considered for SLNB 'be given an opportunity to fully discuss the risks and benefits' and that they be informed of specific surgical harms. Against this, patient values were never systematically sought or reviewed - the margins chapter concedes the trials 'do not assess economic outcomes and patient preferences' and falls back on a quoted Cochrane opinion - preference-sensitive recommendations are not flagged as a class, and no patient decision aid or patient-facing tool is recommended or supplied (the sole 'decision aid' reference is to computer-assisted clinician decision support in the implementation plan).
items.rationaleB: Two consumer representatives sat on the multidisciplinary working party and consumer groups were invited to each public consultation, and patient preference evidence is actually reviewed in places: section 10.6.2 summarises interview studies of patients' follow-up preferences (concerns about 'travelling times, costs, brevity of consultations, and poor continuity', pre-visit anxiety), and section 6.1.2 candidly reports that the excision-margin RCTs 'do not assess economic outcomes and patient preferences'. Several recommendations are explicitly preference-sensitive - patients 'may choose to have the procedure' for CLND, 'individual patient's needs should be considered before appropriate follow-up is offered', 'Routine follow-up by the patient's preferred doctor may be appropriate', and a practice point requiring that SLNB candidates 'be given an opportunity to fully discuss the risks and benefits'. What is missing is systematic treatment: the guideline does not consistently differentiate high- from low-preference-sensitivity recommendations, offers no patient decision aids or statement that they would be beneficial (decision aids appear only as a future dissemination idea in the implementation section), and provides no patient-facing versions of the recommendations.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of policy/decision makers
items.rationaleA: There is more system-level awareness than most guidelines carry: PBS/TGA reimbursement status is flagged repeatedly against specific drug recommendations, an entire section addresses 'The use of adjuvant systemic therapies in the Australian setting' (noting that only IFN-α is PBS-funded and that self-funding is an option), Medicare rebate status is noted for a pathology consultation, and Australian cost-effectiveness evidence is cited for high-risk surveillance clinics (0.31 QALY gain) and for SLNB, with a health economist on the working party. But policy-makers' needs were never sought, and the guideline stops at describing funding status rather than saying what should change: it identifies that effective adjuvant therapies are unsubsidised yet makes no policy recommendation. There is no system resource or workforce impact assessment for population-level recommendations such as six-monthly surveillance with total body photography, and health equity is entirely absent - no mention of equity, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander or Māori populations, socioeconomic disadvantage, or rural and remote access anywhere in 524 pages.
items.rationaleB: System-level considerations surface sporadically rather than systematically: cost-effectiveness analyses are cited for SNB (Morton et al.), for specialised high-risk skin surveillance clinics, and for follow-up imaging strategies; regulatory and funding status is flagged for systemic agents ('nivolumab is TGA approved but not PBS reimbursed'); one recommendation is justified partly on 'reduced resource utilisation' (isolated limb infusion over perfusion); and referral to specialist centres is recommended in part 'for the collection of national outcome data'. However, no chapter presents a structured resource or budget-impact assessment tied to a recommendation, and there is no analysis at all of the service implications of major practice shifts such as abandoning routine CLND. Health equity is essentially absent - there is no mention of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, socioeconomic disadvantage, or access; rural and remote access appears only as a passing acknowledgement of 'logistic difficulties'. The guideline nowhere identifies policy or funding changes needed to align the system with its recommendations.

items.text: The recommendation reflects the values and preferences of the guideline developers
items.rationaleA: The methods state that 'Declarations of interest were collected from all nominated members and evaluated (see COI register)' with management strategies where necessary, but the register is an external link and no individual disclosure appears anywhere in the document; the phrases 'conflict of interest' and 'disclosure' occur essentially nowhere in the body text. More importantly for this item, the guideline never articulates the values the panel brought or how those values shaped its interpretation of benefits and harms - for example, the decision to keep recommending SLNB (Grade B) despite its own evidence statement that SLNB with immediate CLND 'does not prolong melanoma specific survival or overall survival' rests on an unstated valuation of prognostic information over procedural morbidity. The method for integrating differing stakeholder perspectives is described only as consensus 'reached by voting', with no thresholds, no rules and no record of dissent, and the concentration of authorship in Melanoma Institute Australia - including chairs who co-authored the pivotal MSLT trials relied upon - is never acknowledged.
items.rationaleB: The appendix documents a process for reaching agreement - working party review, a face-to-face meeting where each recommendation was 'reviewed and approved by consensus, which was reached by voting', and consensus resolution of public consultation comments - and declarations of interest were collected, evaluated by the Management Committee and posted in a COI register. But the guideline nowhere articulates what values or preferences the developers themselves brought, how those values shaped the weighting of benefits against harms (for example the evident preference for oncological safety over cosmesis in the margin recommendations, or the tolerance for directive language on Grade C/D evidence), or how divergent views within a largely surgical/dermatological panel were reconciled with the consumer and GP members' perspectives. Voting outcomes, dissenting positions and the substance of any COI management strategies are not reported, so a COI register plus 'consensus by voting' is the whole of it - process disclosure standing in for a declaration of values.

items.text: The purpose of the recommendation is clear and actionable
items.rationaleA: The Foreword states an explicit tripartite purpose - 'to achieve early diagnosis whenever possible, make doctors and patients aware of the most effective treatment options, and minimise the financial burden on the health system by documenting investigations and therapies that are inappropriate' - and the recommendations track it credibly, including de-implementation guidance (routine frozen section of sentinel nodes 'is not recommended'; 'insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of automated instruments'; CLND largely abandoned after MSLT-II/DeCOG-SLT; interferon displaced by routine follow-up given 'minimal overall survival benefit and significant toxicity'). The living wiki model is itself framed as an implementation goal, so guidance does not go stale. What is not done is any description of anticipated impact: the guideline nowhere estimates how adoption would change stage at diagnosis, service volumes, organisational workload or system cost, so the stated aim of minimising financial burden is asserted rather than demonstrated.
items.rationaleB: The Foreword sets an implementation goal - 'It is hoped that wide dissemination of these guidelines and adherence to their recommendations will benefit melanoma patients in Australia by ensuring that they receive the most appropriate care' - and the living wiki format is explicitly justified as serving that goal ('a living document, rather than a static printed publication that would inevitably be out of date within a very short time'). The recommendations are consistent with that practice-change purpose, and some are clearly intended to change behaviour (Grade B: 'CLND is no longer the preferred treatment for patients with a positive SLNB'). What is not done is any description of the anticipated impact of adoption: no estimate of how many patients would be affected, what workload or service reconfiguration would follow from, say, replacing CLND with structured ultrasound surveillance every 3-4 months for two years, or what outcome improvement is expected at population level. Advocacy and policy goals are not stated at all.

items.text: The recommendation is feasible for local application and adoption
items.rationaleA: The 'Dissemination and implementation' section is more developed than most: a multi-strategy approach, distribution via colleges, conferences and CME, identification of 'local expert leaders... to act as champions', integration into undergraduate and registrar teaching, a machine-readable semantic-web format enabling integration with Australian clinical systems, listing on guideline portals, web analytics to track usage, and explicit recognition that 'a planned approach is necessary to overcome specific barriers to implementation in particular settings'. Competency and infrastructure requirements are embedded in recommendations (dermoscopy training, SLNB centre expertise across nuclear medicine/surgery/pathology, MDT discussion), and some Australian economic evidence is provided. However this is almost entirely prospective - audit tools, decision support and clinical tools 'may include' being created but none is supplied; no quality indicators, monitoring criteria or implementation data requirements are specified; the degree of change from current practice is never characterised; and no guidance is given on which recommendations require local adaptation where total body photography, confocal microscopy, nuclear medicine or specialist melanoma centres are unavailable.
items.rationaleB: The Dissemination and implementation section is unusually specific for a guideline of this type: distribution through colleges, conferences and CME, identification of 'local expert leaders ... to act as champions', integration into undergraduate and registrar teaching, linking from EviQ and healthdirect and international guideline portals, and a machine-readable semantic wiki that can be embedded in Australian clinical systems with web analytics tracking usage. Personnel competencies needed to implement specific recommendations are named at the recommendation level (dermoscopy training, expertise-based SLNB centres, accredited molecular pathology laboratories, expert melanocytic-lesion pathologists), and some cost-effectiveness evidence is cited. Against this, the concrete implementation tooling is aspirational rather than supplied - decision-support systems and 'the creation of audit and other clinical tools' are things implementation 'may include', and no audit criteria, quality indicators, monitoring data elements or measurable implementation targets are actually provided. There is also no guidance on local adaptation, no costing attached to individual recommendations, and the degree of change required from current practice is characterised for only a few topics (notably CLND) rather than across the guideline.
